The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is a waterproof running shoe designed primarily for gravel, but it’s also very capable on roads and other light trails. It will suit some runners’ needs perfectly, but the waterproof upper can run hot.

Comfortable midsole with good energy return

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

For those of us in the Northern Hemisphere, the cold, wet days of winter are approaching fast, and if you plan on running through the season, there are some benefits to buying a specialist set of running shoes for it.

The two features I look for in the best running shoes for the winter are an outsole that grips well in wet conditions and a water-repellent or waterproof upper.

Both boxes are ticked by the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX, which has a Gore-Tex membrane in the upper, is fully waterproof, and has a gravel-ready outsole that works well on a wide variety of terrain.

I’ve used the shoe for a mix of runs on roads, light trails and grassy hills and it’s impressed me as a winter-ready daily trainer. If you don’t need its waterproof upper or versatile outsole, though, you’ll get a better ride from some lighter, bouncier road options like the Asics Novablast 6.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX launched in fall 2026 and costs $160 in the U.S. and £145 in the U.K., which is $20/£20 more expensive than the standard model of the shoe without the Gore-Tex upper.

Salomon also released the Aero Glide 4 GRVL in its line-up, which is a slightly softer and more cushioned option than the Blaze, which some runners might prefer for easy long runs in particular.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is currently available in four colors, including Vanilla Ice, the model I tested for those who want to show off the dirt they run through, and an all-black design for those who don’t.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My US men’s size 10 weighs exactly 10oz, which is light for a shoe with a thick outsole, waterproof upper, and tall stack of foam in the midsole.

The stack height is 37mm at the heel and 29mm at the forefoot for an 8mm drop, which is a little lower than the stack on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL.

I found the shoe fit me well in my normal running shoe size, and the Gore-Tex upper wasn’t stiff or uncomfortable during my testing.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a mesh upper with Gore-Tex lining and padding on the tongue and around the collar.

During my testing, I was able to run in heavy rain and splash through puddles without my feet getting wet, and I also like that it’s quick and easy to clean the waterproof upper after muddy runs.

However, the drawback is that it’s not the most breathable material, and when running in warm conditions or using the shoe for walks, my feet got sweatier than normal.

Rather than traditional laces, it has Salomon’s QuickLace Neo system so you can loosen and tighten the fit quickly with the pull toggle, which you can then tuck under an elastic band so it doesn’t bounce around on the run.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a supercritical TPU foam called OptiFoam Squared in its midsole, with a mild rocker shape helping to roll you from heel to toe with each stride.

I’m a fan of this foam, which is also used on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL. It’s soft enough to be comfortable without being overly squishy, and it gives a good amount of energy return when you hit faster paces.

The rubber outsole on the shoe has 2.5mm deep, chevron-shaped lugs that are built to grip on gravel tracks but also work well on roads and other light trails.

This outsole is a star feature on the shoe because it allows you to tackle such a wide variety of terrain with confidence, even in wet conditions.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX proved to be an enjoyably versatile shoe in my testing. I used it as my main daily trainer, tackling easy, steady-paced runs mainly on the road and forest trails.

I also used it for one run on slightly more technical trails with rocky and grassy sections, and throughout all my testing, the grip was impressively reliable, even in very wet conditions. It’s not a good option for deep mud, but can handle most other trails well.

That versatility extends to the paces the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX can handle. The midsole has a responsive feel at faster paces while soft enough for long, easy runs — it felt good at all the paces I’d run at outside dedicated interval workouts.

The waterproof upper does its job on rainy days well, and also helps keep your feet warm on easy runs in cold conditions.

However, this upper did limit me because it can be a bit too hot at times. My feet got very sweaty on longer runs on dry days, and if you’re a runner who uses one shoe for everything, a fully waterproof sneaker like this probably isn't the best buy.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX does a great job in the role it’s built for. The waterproof upper is great on wet, cold days; the outsole grips well in wet and dry conditions on both the road and light trails, and the midsole is enjoyably energetic.

If that all sounds good but you want something a little softer and more cushioned, the Salomon Aero Glide 4 GRVL also comes in a Gore-Tex model, and Salomon also has non-GTX models of both shoes, and road versions with less substantial outsoles.

There are a lot of choices in the line-up, and I’d say all are good shoes thanks to the OptiFoam Squared midsole at the heart of them, so you can tailor your Blaze or Glide to suit your needs and preferences.

If you’re sticking to the roads during your winter runs, I’d also consider the Adidas Adizero Evo SL ATR, which has a water-repellent upper and small lugs on its outsole. It’s a good option if the full waterproof upper and thick outsole on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is overkill for your needs.

#3257. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3256. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3255. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

“over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

The word “by” seems important here. That quote is clearly not about the apps used to track ICE, it’s about apps that ICE uses itself.

That makes me wonder if the original article is confused, though. Is ICE really “hosting” its own internal apps on the App Store rather than deploying through some enterprise/MDM distribution method? I guess Apple is involved in that process, too? And if the incoming Congress takes the posture that ICE has been operating an illegal human trafficking ring, then assisting them is a crime.

Apple was pathetic and ridiculous for removing ICEBlock and similar apps. It was also blatantly unconstitutional for the DOJ to threaten them into doing it.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

You can read the full Reuters report here, and The Washington Post’s here.

#3254. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

#3252. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3251. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

#3249. Apple TV renews ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ for season three

Award-winning culinary show ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is getting a third season, in an announcement that came hours after its second season came to a close. Here are the details.

Just as ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ premiered with a two-episode combo, and ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ aired its second season finale, the company confirmed that the latter will return for an eight-episode third season.

‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is hosted by Topjaw’s Jesse Burgess and executive produced by Gordon Ramsay. Each season tells the story of several restaurants around the world as they compete to earn, retain, or increase their Michelin Star ratings.

The show premiered on Apple TV in 2025 to a perfect 100% Tomatometer score and has since been nominated for a BAFTA Television Award in the Factual Entertainment category, and won Best Popular Factual Programme at the 2026 Broadcast Digital Awards.

With eight episodes in each season, the show has taken viewers inside some of the world’s most acclaimed restaurants, including Brazil’s Evvai, the first in Latin America to earn three Michelin Stars, and Ynyshir, a two-star restaurant in rural Wales.

“What I love most about making ‘Knife Edge’ is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover. Behind every restaurant is a very personal journey, and for the chefs we follow, a Michelin Star can represent years of sacrifice, obsession and an enormous amount of hard work. It’s a privilege to be able to tell these stories, and I’m absolutely thrilled that we get to do it all again for a third season”

#3248. TELUS (TU) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management details a $900 million efficiency push and an AI infrastructure bet.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

TELUS Corporation (TU -3.29%) reported a strategic focus on its core telecommunications assets while launching a multiyear efficiency program designed to reduce debt and improve margins. Management stated that the company is advancing an asset monetization strategy for its non-core Health and Agriculture units and is exploring a partnership model to unlock equity from its PureFibre network. The company is also expanding into the Canadian AI infrastructure market, leveraging its existing data center footprint and secured power capacity. These initiatives aim to restore the leverage ratio to 3.0x or lower by the end of 2028 while funding organic growth in the domestic telecom market.

Operator: Good day, everyone. Welcome to the TELUS 2026 Q3 Earnings Conference Call. I would like to introduce your speaker, Ian McMillan. Please go ahead.

Ian McMillan: Thank you, Carl, and hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us. Our third quarter 2026 news release, MD&A, financial statements and detailed supplemental investor information were posted on our website earlier this morning, along with the earnings presentation referenced on this webcast. Today's agenda will include opening remarks from Victor Dodig, TELUS President and Chief Executive Officer; and Gopi Chande, our Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. After the presentation, there will be a question-and-answer period where we will be joined by David Fuller, Executive Vice President and Group President, TELUS Communications; and Navin Arora, Executive Vice President and Group President, Global Platform Businesses. This will be followed by brief closing remarks by Victor. Turning to Slide 2.

Prepared remarks, slides and answers to questions contain forward-looking statements. Actual results could vary from these statements. The assumptions on which they are based and the material risks that could cause them to differ are outlined in our public filings with securities commissions in Canada and the United States, including our third quarter 2026 and 2025 annual MD&A. Please note that all reference dollar amounts are in Canadian dollars unless otherwise stated. Additionally, financial performance is compared to prior year period unless otherwise noted. With that, let me turn the meeting over to Victor.

Victor Dodig: Thanks, Ian, and hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us for our third quarter earnings call. As I promised on our second quarter call in July, today we'll provide you with more granularity on our priorities. My remarks will focus on our transformation strategy, while Gopi will provide an overview of our third quarter results and financial details behind our plan. So let's start on Slide 5. Our transformation strategy has one clear objective, and that is to solidify TELUS' position as the leading communications and AI infrastructure player in Canada. It's an intentional and a strategic pivot to profitable growth.

To achieve this, we're executing against 3 key priorities that I outlined during our second quarter call and results in July. The first is to strengthen our financial foundation. We will continue to strengthen our balance sheet by reducing our debt and by focusing our efforts on our core telecom business and pursuing a monetization strategy for our noncore assets. Our second priority is to hone our operational discipline. This means that we're transforming our cost base, how we do business, particularly in our telecommunications business as well as streamlining and improving processes across our enterprise to deliver a more seamless experience for our TELUS customers and for our TELUS team members.

And our third priority is to deploy these resources to drive profitable and sustainable growth and returns. So I want to go through each of these priorities in greater detail, beginning on Slide 6 with our first priority, which is strengthening our financial foundation. With our second quarter results, we announced 3 key actions. We reset our dividend payout ratio to a sustainable level. We terminated the dilutive discount on the dividend investment -- reinvestment plan, and we put a moratorium on acquisitions. These decisions were difficult, but they were necessary, and they demonstrate our commitment to financial discipline.

We're committed to strengthening our balance sheet and have a clear path to achieving a net debt to adjusted EBITDA leverage ratio of 3x or lower by the end of 2028. To that end, we're intentionally pursuing an asset monetization strategy and prioritizing our TELUS Health and TELUS Agriculture & Consumer Goods businesses. We are advancing this plan with one asset in our health portfolio, which is in an advanced stage with a prospective buyer. We'll manage these engagements on our terms to ensure we maximize the value of our businesses to our shareholders. And as we sign these agreements, we'll share those developments with you.

We're also reviewing how we can unlock equity value from our PureFibre network while maintaining control, similar to the successful partnership approach we took with our wireless towers through Terrion. Now we're early in the process and conversations with potential investment partners are encouraging. So let's turn to Slide 7, our second priority, which is to hone our operational discipline. With our new leadership team in place, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of our business, and we identified a clear set of levers to simplify our operations, improve our cost structure and concentrate resources behind profitable growth.

Today, we are announcing a program that targets $900 million in annualized cash savings exiting 2028, driven by operational cost and margin improvement as well as CapEx efficiencies. Up to 80% of these run rate savings are expected to come from telecom with the balance coming from the global platform businesses. Within telecom, we've already made a number of strategic pivots in our consumer business that prioritize profitability and capital efficiency. Under Dave Fuller's leadership, we have refocused our consumer Internet business on our fiber built communities and moved both our home security business and our TV offerings to a capital-light model that will dramatically improve our return on capital for these businesses.

Our team has also streamlined our organizational structure and simplified our product portfolio by winding down unprofitable and capital-intensive initiatives. These actions will deliver approximately $250 million in structural cash savings, predominantly capital with the full run rate benefit expected beginning in 2027. These savings are also captured within the $900 million target that I just referred to. Let me now detail the initiatives that underpin these additional benefits. I'll start with our core telecom business. This program will be executed across 5 key areas.

The first is focused on streamlining our customer experience, reducing customer pain points and reasons to call us and leveraging AI to automate and ensure that TELUS is the easiest provider to do business with, all in the name of improving our Net Promoter Score and ensuring that our customers are happy customers. The second is focused around driving higher revenue per customer and enhancing our already industry-leading customer retention metrics. The third stream is to optimize our sales mix toward lower-cost channels and digital onboarding. The fourth is procurement enhancement across both operating and capital spend, while the fifth is focused on network and field force effectiveness and capital optimization.

We know how to do this, and we're going to get it done. In our Global Platform business, we're focused on 3 things: first, leveraging AI and automation to deliver better results for our customers with less effort. Second is earning more from each customer by deepening the relationship with them across higher-margin services and tightening pricing and contract terms. And the third is running leaner by simplifying how we deliver and how we trim overhead. Again, we know how to do this, and we'll get this done. These actions target a stronger margin profile across TELUS Digital, Health and Ag & Consumer Goods.

So taken together, our efforts will support achieving our target of $900 million in annualized cash savings exiting 2028. So moving to Slide 8, which is our third priority, and that's to deploy the resources that we free up to drive growth and returns in our core business. First, we're committed to reducing our leverage, and we'll use proceeds from the dividend reset and asset monetization strategy to achieve our leverage ratio target of 3x or lower by the end of 2028. In parallel, we will strategically invest in organic growth in our core telecom assets. We'll fund this growth through disciplined CapEx with a focus on preserving premium economics.

This includes growing our PureFibre footprint, the gold standard for broadband connectivity, delivering capabilities that alternative technologies, including cable and satellite, simply cannot match. We began building our fiber network more than a decade ago, and it now reaches over 3.8 million homes and businesses with strong penetration rates across our footprint. We continue to grow this footprint in high-return underserved markets in urban and suburban communities where we are quickly driving strong penetration gains and product intensity. Our PureFibre network is a highly valuable asset and a critical differentiator across our business. It strengthens our competitive position in the markets we serve and our AI infrastructure more broadly.

Our PureFibre network is also the foundation for an accelerated source of growth, and we're well positioned to meet one of the fastest areas of growing demand in the economy, and that's in AI infrastructure. So Slide 9 shows how we're pursuing the AI infrastructure opportunity, something that we mentioned we covered with you in the second quarter call. And that's to leverage our core strengths and advantages that we have invested in and developed over decades.

And those advantages are our PureFibre network, which I've mentioned a couple of times, data centers where we already own and operate them with the scale and technical expertise to operate them, telecom and AI infrastructure offered together and a brand trusted by both businesses and government. Importantly, we're committed to Canadian sovereignty and data residency. Canadian data stays in Canada, which is the foundation of our sovereign approach. Together, these support a disciplined, capital-efficient strategy built on TELUS' core strengths aimed at sustainable, profitable growth. So in that vein, we have 3 initiatives, the first 2 of which are near-term priority. And that first one is we're using our fiber to connect other data center operators to the grid.

This is where our PureFibre network gives us a real edge. Several deals are underway and the economics of these transactions and our win rates so far are strong. Second, we're building sovereign AI capabilities for Canadian businesses and governments. This is where owning our data centers sets us apart. We'll start with our data centers in Rimouski and Kamloops, both operating today, plus our strategically located central offices. This includes both GPU as a service and ready-to-use wholesale solutions. Across our sites, we've secured 38 megawatts of power, which we plan to bring online steadily through to the end of 2028. Our approach is to use the assets we have first, then add GPU capacity as customer demand materializes.

We'll do this ourselves or with an investment partner, whichever delivers the best returns to our shareholders while staying disciplined with how we deploy capital. We're focused on winning more of the opportunities already in front of us, and we'll invest carefully while staying committed to reducing debt and growing free cash flow. The demand is strong. I think we all know that. Canada needs more data center capacity than it has today. Canada, I think, represents 1% of compute globally. The EU represents 5%, and you know that the U.S. and China is where most of it is. So we need to build that.

We have a pipeline today of more than $1 billion in total contract value across our digital infrastructure business. And over the next 3 years, we project about $500 million in revenue with healthy margins, depending, of course, on market factors such as supply chain conditions. And third, we're exploring data center shells with power already secured. This would be done through partnerships, again, capital investment partnerships that protect our balance sheet and our commitment to paying down debt. So it's still early, and it's not included in the estimates that I just shared. You can expect to hear more of that on future calls.

In closing, our efficiency program will deliver significant cash savings through growth and through cost efficiencies and free up resources and focus management attention on our core business. Our telecom strategy ensures we maintain and grow our core business and our AI infrastructure initiative positions TELUS in a high-growth market with strong cash flow benefits where we have the right to win. Our monetization strategy alongside the equitization of our PureFibre network, which we will control, will strengthen our balance sheet and enhance our financial flexibility to invest organically in these high-growth, high-return areas. And the result of our efforts to date is clear.

We have a seasoned leadership team that is focused and moving swiftly to drive greater efficiency and better position TELUS to deliver sustainable, profitable growth and returns for our shareholders. We expect our actions to gain traction and translate into improved revenue, improved margins and improved cash flow. And now with that, let me turn the call over to Gopi for a detailed review of our results.

Gopi Chande: Thank you, Victor. Today, I will cover our third quarter operating and financial performance and provide further financial details for the key progress areas Victor just outlined. Let me begin on Slide 11 and our third quarter consolidated results. Consolidated service revenue of $4.5 billion was lower by 1% year-over-year. Growth in our core telecom business, including mobile network and fixed data service revenue was offset by TELUS Digital. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $1.8 billion declined by 5%, primarily due to weaker results in TELUS Digital and from $78 million of onetime items recognized in the third quarter last year as we shared on our Q2 earnings call. Normalized for those, consolidated adjusted EBITDA was lower by 2%.

Basic EPS was negative $0.42 due to the TELUS Health noncash impairment, which I'll discuss shortly. Adjusted EPS was $0.16, down from $0.24 a year ago, reflecting after-tax impacts of lower operating income. Cash flow from operations -- cash from operations of $1.5 billion was close to flat and free cash flow of $396 million was lower by 35%, reflecting lower EBITDA and higher CapEx, both as expected. Slide 12 outlines our results for our core TTech business. TTech service revenues of $3.3 billion was higher by 1% and adjusted EBITDA of $1.6 billion was down 5% as expected due to onetime items in Q3 of last year. Normalized TTech adjusted EBITDA was lower by 1%.

Our Internet net additions totaled 10,000 due to lower gross loading, reflecting a deliberate shift to prioritize sustainable margins and capital efficiency over subsidized volume, partially offset by lower churn. Turning to our global platform businesses on Slide 13. Service revenue at TELUS Digital was $637 million, and it declined 11%, while adjusted EBITDA of $62 million was lower by 9%. These results reflected the impacts from hyperscale client volume ramp-downs as we discussed last quarter. In TELUS Health, we saw an improvement in year-over-year growth in service revenue, up 2% and adjusted EBITDA declined by 5% due to lower other income.

As outlined in our disclosure today, we recorded a noncash goodwill impairment of $800 million for our TELUS Health business, reflecting updated growth expectations, broader market conditions and current valuation perspectives from ongoing strategic processes. Importantly, it does not change our commitment to TELUS Health or our focus on strengthening our operating performance, optimizing our portfolio and unlocking long-term shareholder value. We remain disciplined and deliberate in advancing these opportunities for our teams with a clear focus on maximizing value for shareholders while continuing to position TELUS Health for sustainable, profitable growth. Turning to Slide 14. Let me provide the financial details supporting our strategic priorities, specifically honing our operational discipline.

As we've shared today, we have embarked upon a multiyear efficiency program targeting annualized cash savings of approximately $900 million exiting 2028. This will be achieved through operational costs and margin improvements as well as CapEx efficiencies. We are already seeing this discipline in action through several key initiatives driving significant capital efficiencies, giving us confidence in our ability to reduce our core capital expenditure profile in 2027. In order to achieve the $900 million target, we expect to invest approximately $150 million across the various focus areas Victor outlined. Our comprehensive transformation strategy is designed to deliver a durable impact, building a more focused, efficient growth-oriented organization positioned for sustainable profitability.

Now let me review our balance sheet on Slide 15. We remain well capitalized with total available liquidity of $3 billion and a net debt to adjusted EBITDA leverage ratio as of September 30 of 3.6x. As expected, this was up modestly from 3.5x a year ago due to higher debt levels and lower EBITDA, consistent with our updated outlook provided on the Q2 call. Our operational execution, improving capital intensity over the longer term, free cash flow growth and asset monetization strategy will continue to strengthen our balance sheet. Let me review our capital allocation framework on Slide 16.

To reiterate, we are committed to paying down debt to achieve a leverage ratio target of 3x or lower by the end of 2028 and are fully committed to maintaining our investment-grade credit profile -- credit rating profile. Our enterprise-wide mandate is clear. We are only deploying capital to initiatives that generate strong, sustainable returns that exceed our cost of capital. We also remain committed to ongoing shareholder returns through a sustainable quarterly dividend of $0.1875 per share. Looking ahead, this disciplined approach ensures we remain focused on driving greater capital efficiency and maintaining disciplined investment in our core telecom and AI infrastructure businesses to deliver attractive financial returns and sustainable shareholder value.

Turning to our annual financial guidance on Slide 17. For the full year 2026, we are reaffirming our consolidated guidance as updated with our Q2 results in July. This includes service revenue of flat to negative 2%, adjusted EBITDA of negative 2% to negative 4%, capital expenditures of approximately $2.6 billion and free cash flow of approximately $1.8 billion. In closing, we have a clear line of sight to deliver on our transformation strategy. We are moving swiftly and with conviction and commit to communicating our progress with transparency. We are confident that our actions will position us for stronger performance as we head into 2027 and beyond.

Now let me pass the call back to Ian to begin questions and answers.

Ian McMillan: Thank you, Gopi. Carl, please proceed with questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question is from Maher Yaghi from Scotiabank.

Maher Yaghi: Victor, I wanted to follow up. I mean you guys have laid out a very strong plan for reducing the operational and CapEx cost of the company going forward and the results will hit in the coming years. I wanted to follow up on that beyond the cost savings, and this goes to a conversation we had when you joined early on, is to figure out the revenue opportunity for TELUS going forward? And where do you see the company growing into in the next couple of years? Where is the growth could come from mostly?

And if you can maybe just give us an idea of what you think the company can grow at -- on a more normalized basis now that the wireless business seems to be stabilizing.

Victor Dodig: I'm going to share a couple of comments. I'll also pass it on to Dave on the telecom front as well. Look, the goal here is to capitalize on what we see as a real opportunity in our domestic market in Canada and both the telecom sector and digital infrastructure, broadly speaking. To do that, we need to free up resources within our company. And it has several component parts. The first is that transformation strategy that we outlined that will free up $900 million in net cash savings through exiting 2028. We're going to work really, really hard to get that done.

So a lot of work, a lot of heavy lifting and a lot of change in the way we do business. The second piece is to monetize our noncore assets. All good businesses, and like I said, we're in advanced stages with one. We're going to activate another TELUS Health asset this month so that we can free up those resources. And the third, as I mentioned in my remarks, is to unlock some of the equity value, which is at very early stage in discussions in our PureFibre network. All of those resources will be redeployed to paying down our debt and to organic growth.

When you think about capital allocation at TELUS, you think about those 2 side by side and getting that leverage level to a better place and growing organically, especially in the -- by growing fiber, our fiber presence in Ontario and Quebec and in our Western region. That is the best defense against these technologies that are emerging. That is a real growth opportunity in addition to our data center strategy, and I'm sure you'll hear from Navin as well in a moment on that. So Dave, do you want to talk a little bit about telecom because we're off to a good start in terms of stopping certain things. The results are really strong.

But I think you're going to continue to see us methodically progress into better premium relationships across the telecom spectrum with our customers.

David Fuller: Yes. Thanks, Victor. Yes, Maher, we fundamentally believe that we can continue to grow the telecom business in the low single digits, both top and bottom line going forward. I would say that growth is driven by 3 areas. First of all, in the consumer business, continued strength in our mobility franchise, I think, is something we forecast through '27 and '28, provided that the sensible and stable market that we saw throughout Q3 persists in 2027 and beyond. Plus, we think on the consumer side, there's continued opportunity to progress our PureFibre build in communities across the country. Secondly, moving to B2B.

I would say that there's a significant opportunity, as Victor has already alluded to, around infrastructure build and fiber network builds associated with AI data centers. And more broadly, when you look at the tax changes that the government recently announced around the mega tax donation (sic) [ deduction ], a boom in potential infrastructure spending across the technology space that can benefit us from that increased spend from many of our B2B customers in the enterprise space and the public sector space. And then the third is operational efficiency. Victor outlined kind of the areas that we're focused on.

But when I think you -- when you look at AI and the automation benefits that it can bring, I believe it's a generational opportunity to significantly transform how we support and service our customers to allow them to support and service what they want to do through self-serve tools to automate significant portions of our processes today that are manual and to remove friction and improve the customer experience on a substantive basis. That all has then knock-on second order benefits across continued churn reductions against our already class-leading churn results as well as lower cost of acquisition, lower cost of renewal and lower operational support costs within our organization.

Operator: The next question is from Drew McReynolds from RBC Capital Markets.

Drew McReynolds: Just want to unpack just 2 numbers that you thrown out. First, on the $900 million cash savings. Just trying to understand all the moving parts here. So I think, Victor, if I understand your prepared remarks, of the $900 million, there's $250 million that you highlighted as CapEx efficiencies that begin run rate in 2027. If I've got that right, so does that imply the rest of it is $650 million in OpEx? And then where does the $150 million in investment come in?

Victor Dodig: Okay. All good questions. I'm going to hand that off to Gopi just to take you through that because I think it's important they understand how that all kind of fits together.

Gopi Chande: Perfect. Drew. So the way to think about that $900 million cash, first of all, just defining our nomenclature, think about it as $75 million in December 2028 times 12. And so that's how we get to the $900 million cash. Specifically to your question, really pleased that we have decisions that are made that already give us line of sight into $250 million CapEx. The split is roughly 50-50 CapEx and EBITDA. As you noted, there are investments we need to make. So $150 million, as Victor noted, as these programs typically run, those investments are needed more upfront to unlock some of the benefits.

And so we'll give the specifics around 2027 when we give our guidance in February. And the last comment I'll make is the split between where those savings will show up. So about 80% in our core telecom business, which, as you know, is more than 90% of our EBITDA and 20% in the global platform businesses. So I'm really pleased with the detailed action plans that both Dave and Navin have to execute on this. So we're confident in its delivery.

Drew McReynolds: And if I could just add one more clarification on the data center -- or sorry, AI infrastructure piece, you quantified some $500 million over the next 3 years in revenues, and I think those are from the first 2 buckets, so the existing data center plus the connectivity. Is that $500 million a cumulative revenue recognition over the 3 years? Or do you hit run rate $500 million kind of by year 3? I'm just trying to understand that.

Victor Dodig: Yes. Navin, do you want to go?

Navin Arora: Yes, sure. That is a cumulative number. And maybe I'll give a little bit more color on the strategy there. So as Dave mentioned, actually, the first thing I'm going to say is that we're not going to boil the ocean around speculative or volatile data center type decisions. So we're really going to be executing on 2 immediate high-return, low-risk priorities where we have a competitive advantage. And so Dave mentioned the first one around our fiber connectivity of other developers' data centers. Our incumbent territory of B.C. and Alberta has large campus style data centers that come in -- that are coming in, and we're going to be plugging them into our -- into our PureFibre network.

And these are high-margin, long-term transport deals. And what we really like about them is that customers fund the network build capital right upfront. So that is a big part of our growth and as part of that $500 million number. And then the second is the sovereign Canadian AI compute and we're using our existing data center facilities, Rimouski, Kamloops and the central offices that Victor mentioned. We already own them. We have the power. We have the talent. We have the expertise, and we're going to be thoughtful about how we expand that from the current 2 megawatts to the 38 megawatts of secured power that we have.

And we'll be really matching the demand build-out of the GPU capacity with signed customer contracts. And we'll be thoughtful about how we fund that within the debt commitments that Gopi and Victor talked about. The business case is really strong with high IRR, and we're excited about those expansions.

Operator: The next question is from Stephanie Price from CIBC World Markets.

Stephanie Price: I was hoping to get a little bit more color on the potential equitization of the fiber assets. #3247. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3245. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.
