#3207. Here's the Maximum Social Security Benefit for 2027 and How to Get It

The wealthiest seniors will take home more than $64,000 from Social Security next year.

Social Security's wealthiest beneficiaries will take home $5,358 per month in 2027, up from $5,181 in 2026. This is the largest the maximum benefit has ever been, and seniors lucky enough to qualify for this amount will receive more than $64,000 from the program next year.

There are only three boxes you have to tick to take home the maximum checks, but most people won't pull it off. Still, if you understand the elements that influence your benefits, you may be able to increase your Social Security checks.

The Social Security Administration bases your benefit amount on your average monthly earnings over your 35 highest-earning years. If you want to take home the $5,358 maximum check in 2027, you need to work at least this long before applying for benefits.

You can still qualify for Social Security retirement checks with as little as 10 years of work history, but you will have zero-income years factored into your benefit calculation. This will significantly reduce your monthly payment. On the other hand, there's no downside to working longer than 35 years. Doing so could increase your benefits if you're earning more now than in the past.

To claim the maximum Social Security check in 2027, you must have paid the maximum Social Security payroll tax in all 35 of your highest-earning years. That means earning the equivalent of $184,500 in 2026 dollars or $192,300 in 2027. These limits were lower in years past, but they still represented a significant challenge to workers.

This is why most people never claim the maximum Social Security benefits. Most people never earn enough throughout their careers. But that's OK. Even if you only manage to increase your income slightly, it will still lead to permanently larger checks.

You must wait until age 70 to apply for Social Security if you want to receive the maximum monthly checks in 2027. Do not wait any longer than this, though. It will not grow your benefit any further.

Signing up at 70 could be the right move for you if you have other ways to cover your living expenses in the meantime and you expect to have an average or above-average life expectancy. But those lacking personal savings or in poor health may do better by signing up earlier.

Explore a few different claiming ages before deciding which one is right for you. If you don't manage to max out your benefit, that's OK. Go with what makes sense for you, and then figure out how you plan to cover the rest of your expenses.

#3205. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

Mini PC or all-in-one? Here’s how Apple’s M6 desktops stack up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re looking for a new computer and want a Mac, your first instinct might be to pick up one of the best MacBooks. However, opting for Apple’s premium laptops or even the much more affordable MacBook Neo has its drawbacks — especially if you're paying a portability premium for a machine that will rarely leave your desk.

Sure, the new MacBook Pro OLED looks fantastic with that illuminated Apple logo on the lid, and it is the first Mac with a touchscreen. For the majority of people, though, it’s total overkill. Unless you plan on editing 8K video or running demanding local AI models on the go, you’re buying far more computer than you need.

If you just want a reliable, fast Mac to use at home, Apple’s desktops are a much better bet. The powerhouse Mac Studio will be overkill for most, too. That’s why, if you’re setting up a dedicated home office or just need a shared family machine for the living room, the new Mac mini and iMac with Apple’s M6 chips make a whole lot more sense.

While you can configure either with beefier specs, I’ll be focusing on the entry-level models for this comparison: the base Mac mini with M6 and the base iMac with M6. The latest Mac mini landed in September of 2026, followed shortly by the new iMac in November. Since both sport the latest Apple Silicon, either will easily last you for years to come.

Having reviewed both the Mac mini M6 and the iMac M6, the question is: which one actually deserves a spot on your desk and is worth your hard-earned cash? Here’s a full breakdown of their real-world performance, design, ergonomics, and value to help you decide between one of the best mini PCs and one of the best all-in-one computers you can buy right now.

2 x USB-C, 3.5mm headphone jack (front), 3 x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 2.5 gigabit Ethernet (back)

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, Gigabit Ethernet

Even though the Mac mini with M6 and iMac with M6 are new Apple desktops, they share one very important thing in common: neither sports a radical redesign. Instead, they feature almost identical designs to their predecessors.

The Mac mini was completely redesigned back in 2024 with the Mac mini M4. Like that machine, this new model is much more compact at 5 x 5 x 2 inches and retains those front ports — specifically two USB-C ports and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Besides charging, you can use those front ports to quickly connect your iPhone to transfer data, and having a headphone jack on the front means you can use wired headphones without having to plug them in at the back.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Then around back on the Mac mini M6, you get three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an HDMI port, a Gigabit Ethernet port, and a power port. Those Thunderbolt ports are great if you want to use one of Apple’s first-party monitors like the Studio Display or Studio Display XDR, but they also work with most portable monitors. Meanwhile, the Mac mini M6’s HDMI port is ideal for traditional monitors without a USB-C port.

The iMac with M6’s design is even older, though, as Apple first introduced it back in 2021 with the iMac M1. Though it has a much larger footprint than the Mac mini, the iMac M6 is still quite compact for an all-in-one at 21.5 x 18.1 x 5.8 inches.

Given the iMac M6 is an all-in-one, you don’t get nearly as many ports as you do on the Mac mini since you don’t need to hook it up to a separate monitor. While my review unit has four ports, on the base model, you just get two Thunderbolt 4 ports.

Then on the left edge of the device, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack and that’s it. You can get an Ethernet port on its power adapter, but you’ll have to pay extra for it. The iMac M6 also features a six-speaker system and a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for video calls.

Overall, you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini or the iMac when it comes to their respective designs. Both desktops look sleek, but if you want a computer with the smallest footprint and the most ports, the Mac mini is the better choice. You will have to bring your own display, webcam, and other accessories, though.

Although the latest Mac mini and iMac both sport Apple’s new M6 chips, there is a slight difference between them when it comes to the base models.

While the Mac mini has an M6 chip with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores, the M6 chip in the iMac only has 10 of each. In my testing, both machines feel quite snappy for everyday tasks like opening apps and browsing the web thanks to the improved efficiency that comes with the 2nm process Apple used with its M6 chips. It’s with more demanding tasks where you’ll notice a difference.

For instance, if you’re editing a lot of photos, rendering video, or are a power user with dozens of browser tabs open simultaneously, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini will certainly make a difference. If you just want a Mac for watching videos, writing emails, and basic daily tasks, the difference between these two M6 chips will be negligible.

One other area where you will definitely see an impact though is with gaming. While neither of these Macs can serve as a replacement for one of the best gaming PCs, they’re surprisingly capable when it comes to gaming and this is especially true with older titles. Here, the two extra GPU cores in the Mac mini help keep frame rates smoother.

For those who plan on pushing their new Apple desktop to the limit or playing games on it, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini is the better choice. However, if you just need a reliable machine for day-to-day use, the 10-core M6 in the base iMac has plenty of power to get the job done.

If you opt for a Mac mini over an iMac, you’re obviously going to need to get a monitor to go along with it — or you could use one you already have, just like with your mouse and keyboard, to bring your total overall cost down. However, if you want an excellent display with a high pixel count without having to do a ton of research first, there’s no screen quite like the one on the iMac.

The iMac features a 24-inch, 4.5K display with a resolution of 4480 x 2520. Since this panel is manufactured specifically for Apple, you won’t find another standalone monitor on the market with that exact screen size, resolution, and pixel density.

Most monitors that deliver around 218 pixels per inch like the iMac cost as much or more than a Mac mini M6 on their own. Samsung’s 27-inch ViewFinity S9 runs around $800 to $1,000, while LG’s 27-inch UltraFine 5K costs around $1,000 to $1,200. Granted, those panels are slightly larger than 24 inches, but they demand a hefty premium.

If you want something larger and more affordable, 27-inch 4K panels like the Dell UltraSharp or Asus ProArt can be had for around $400 to $500. However, because they aren’t native Apple displays, you do miss out on native features — like using the brightness keys on a Magic Keyboard to dim the screen without third-party software.

Even though 24 inches might sound modest, the high pixel density of the iMac gives you plenty of usable canvas. In my testing with the iMac M6, I was able to comfortably work with two browser windows side by side without feeling cramped.

There is one big catch with the iMac, though: ergonomics. Unlike the Studio Display or Pro Display XDR, there is no height-adjustable stand option. The built-in stand only tilts about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back.

To get your iMac to a proper ergonomic height — where your eyes naturally align just below the top third of the panel — you’ll likely need to set it on a monitor riser or desk shelf. Alternatively, you can ditch the stand altogether at checkout and order the factory VESA mount version, though you'll need to budget for one of the best monitor arms alongside your new all-in-one.

If you want a massive display, dual or even triple-monitor flexibility, or full control over your desk layout, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you want a compact, incredibly sharp screen built right into the machine, the iMac’s display is tough to beat.

As the Mac mini doesn’t give you that computer-in-a-box experience that the iMac does, there’s a whole host of optional 3rd-party accessories available for it. From stands and hubs that sit underneath to enclosures that rest on top to add extra ports and even M.2 SSD slots for expanded storage, you can really accessorize Apple’s smallest Mac to your heart’s desire.

You’ll find a few USB hubs and add-ons for the iMac, but nowhere near as many as you will for the Mac mini. One new accessory I’m looking forward to testing with the iMac M6 is BenQ’s iScreenBar, a monitor light bar designed specifically to match the color and aluminum aesthetic of Apple’s all-in-one.

Likewise, Satechi makes a slim dock that sits directly over the iMac’s base to add front-facing ports and an SSD slot — similar to its popular stand and hub for the Mac mini. It’s a clean setup, but overall, the 3rd-party accessory ecosystem for the iMac remains much smaller, and for obvious reasons: there's just less to add to an all-in-one.

When it comes to first-party upgrades from Apple, you can configure both machines with extra unified memory and internal storage. Keep in mind that because everything is soldered down, these upgrades have to be chosen at checkout when ordering through Apple’s website — you can't crack either machine open to upgrade them later.

The most unique upgrade for the iMac M6 is Apple’s nano-texture glass. Just like on high-end MacBooks, instead of standard glossy glass that catches reflections, you can pay an extra $200 at checkout to add a matte finish. The catch? Apple doesn't offer nano-texture on the base 10-core iMac. You have to step up to the higher-tier model first before tacking on that $200 display upgrade, which widens the price gap between it and the Mac mini considerably. Still, there’s no other all-in-one on the market that offers a matte display quite like it.

If you want a vast ecosystem of desk mounts, docks, and external drives to completely personalize your workstation, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you work in a sunlit room with nearby windows and glare constantly drives you crazy, stepping up to an iMac with nano-texture glass might be worth the extra investment.

Although the Mac mini M4 could be had for $599 at launch, thanks to RAMaggedon and the ongoing component crunch, Apple bumped up the starting price of the new Mac mini M6 to $899. As a result, when you factor in the cost of a display, keyboard, mouse, webcam, and speakers, the Mac mini is suddenly playing in the exact same price bracket as the iMac.

The iMac M6 saw a price increase of its own. While the iMac M4 started at $1,299, the new M6-powered version climbs to $1,499. The Mac mini used to be an unbeatable bargain compared to the rest of Apple’s lineup, but if you don’t already have a desk full of peripherals at home, you could easily spend $1,350 to $1,450 just to get a setup comparable to the iMac.

The real value proposition between the two comes down to your existing hardware. If you already have a spare monitor, keyboard, and mouse sitting on your desk, the Mac mini M6 delivers better raw performance for significantly less cash. But if you’re starting completely from scratch, the iMac’s $1,499 sticker price includes a built-in 4.5K display, crisp speakers, a 12MP Center Stage camera, and a color-matched Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse right in the box.

If this is your first dedicated desktop, the iMac is the easier, better-value buy — unless you prefer an à la carte approach where you handpick every screen, dock, and keyboard yourself. If total customization is the goal, or you already have the accessories to make it work, go with the Mac mini instead.

While you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini M6 or the iMac M6, the choice between the two ultimately comes down to how complicated you want your desk setup to be.

Let’s say you just moved and need to get to work right away in a new apartment where space is at a premium. One trip to the Apple Store later, you have a complete desktop in a box that you can set up in less than 30 minutes. If you want to heavily personalize your workspace, however — or if you prefer a much larger display or even multiple screens — then the Mac mini makes far more sense.

Regardless of which entry-level Apple desktop you choose, make sure you know what you’ll be using it for and how demanding your workflow will be before hitting checkout. When it comes to their internal components, neither the Mac mini M6 nor the iMac M6 can be upgraded after the fact. It’s essential that you configure the right chip, memory, and storage the first time around.

Although I review mini PCs for a living and have always been a big fan of the Mac mini, setting up and testing the iMac gave me a whole new appreciation for its simplicity. Sometimes, there is undeniable value in not having to overthink your monitor, cables, and peripherals.

#3203. Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The iPhone Duo likely won't make it into Santa's sleigh this year. Here's what Apple had to say about it.

Apple is unsure when it will have more of its foldable iPhone Duo in stock for customers to purchase ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

During Apple’s earnings call on Monday, Nov. 2, Apple’s chief operating officer, Sabih Khan, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo would catch up with current demand.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: Some magical touches

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today … We’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan told investors.

The stock and shipping delays were among the broader concerns on an earnings call riddled with questions about rising memory chip costs driven by the AI industry, according to reports from TechCrunch.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

Last month, the iPhone Duo (Apple’s priciest smartphone to date) sold out shortly after its official launch on Oct. 23. Apple told the Financial Times that demand for the new Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary” after the smashing sell-outs, though veteran techies like Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman posited that Apple knew it would encounter supply chain issues, yet it was still the plan all along.

Those who didn’t initially jump to preorder the new device or wait in line at an Apple store are still facing shipping times that extend into 2027. Some outlets are even reporting that carriers like Verizon have offered gift cards as apologies for the extended delays.

Apple CEO John Ternus signaled the company’s effort to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, announcing that Apple will be “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer supplying pieces for the device.

Also: iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Ternus said during his opening remarks on the earnings call.

While the iPhone Duo snafu is a rare event for Apple, which traditionally has a strong reputation for a smooth supply chain, rising demand for memory chips is raising hardware costs across the industry, and it’s something Apple can’t circumvent. On the call, Khan noted that Apple has had to increase prices on numerous products, though he said those decisions were made rather “reluctantly.”

Back in June, MacBooks and iPads saw price increases of up to 25% due to rising hardware and chip costs.

As Apple works to iron out its kinks, customers may be looking elsewhere. Reports from Korea indicate that Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales jumped 20% in the week after the iPhone Duo became available, and recent reports of cracked displays are another strike for Apple.

Also: Want an iPhone Duo before 2027? Try this

So, Santa may not be able to deliver the iPhone Duo this year, but Samsung’s foldables may make it onto Christmas lists across the globe instead.

#3202. A Wall-Mounted Smart Garden Is Peak Winter Decor (and a Great Gift)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I tested Modern Sprout's handsome Growframe for a pop of green during fall and winter.

My pursuit of good houseplant tools means I’m always looking for shops and resources. That led me to Modern Sprout, a Chicago-based online store that sells plants and plant-care accessories. When they reached out offering a chance to test some of its high-design indoor garden tech, I decided to see what, if anything, is worth considering for your houseplant needs or as a place to get gifts for the plant parents in your life. I found a few pleasant surprises.

Whether I’m tending to houseplants in winter or gardening in summer, I’m always looking for tools to improve plant care. For houseplants in particular, this means watering, trimming, fertilizing, occasionally repotting and providing as much real estate in sunny windows as possible. When that’s not enough, I harness the power of full-spectrum LED grow lights, so I can have greenery in practically every room of my apartment.

A quick look at Modern Sprout’s website shows it sells most of what you’d expect from a boutique plant nursery: live plants, potting soil, gardening accessories, grow lights, grow kits, candles, bird feeders and gift sets. While Modern Sprout carries plenty of its own products, it also curates items from other small businesses instead of relying on large mainstream gardening brands. This is a nice bonus for folks who prefer to support smart business owners. Modern Sprout also offers wholesale accounts, so you might even see it at a nursery near you.

For my tests, I stuck to the Modern Sprout brand, which is also available on Amazon. Since I review a lot of smart home gear, I wanted to try out the Smart Landscape Growframe ($229) and compare it with other plant light options I use. I also wanted to see if Modern Sprout’s tools are any good, so I rounded out my experience with three essentials behind effective houseplant care: Pruning Shears ($20), a Glass Watering Can ($48) and Dissolving Plant Food Sheets ($20).

I don’t think anything could’ve prepared me for the size of the Smart Landscape Growframe: 32.1 inches long, 11.5 inches tall and 5.3 inches deep. For some context, that’s wider than my kitchen table and large enough to require a careful survey of my home to find a suitable location. I found a nice spot above my stairs next to the front door.

Additionally, its durable powder-coated steel frame weighs an incredible 8 pounds. That’s roughly the weight of a gallon of milk, which makes wall mounting tricky. I agree with Modern Sprout’s recommendation to place the mounting screws in studs, so you’ll need a stud finder, a level, and a power drill if you want it on the wall. You can use drywall anchors, but they aren’t included.

Make sure you visually line up the Growframe’s mounting holes with your marks before driving screws into the wall. This is easier with a second person, but I managed it alone. However, I relied purely on my measurements and had to redo the screws after one was slightly off. I suggest marking one stud first, then holding the planter and using a level to see where the other should go. Similarly, keep in mind that the 9-foot power cord needs to reach an outlet.

The app isn’t complex and is really easy to use. I really like that there are preset schedules for shade, partial sun and full sun light levels — these options always start at 8 a.m., providing 8, 12 and 16 hours of lighting at different intensities, respectively. The presets aren’t customizable, so you must use one of the app’s two other scheduling options to adjust the timing and other settings. I noticed that toggling a preset works as intended, but closing and reopening the menu shows an inactive toggle — a minor visual bug that doesn’t seem to affect the feature. (It might even get patched by the time you read this review.)

You can also set a schedule using specific times of day in the Growframe device menu. While this particular scheduling menu lacks an option to tie the lighting controls to sunrise and sunset, you can find that on the Scenario tab. (Sunrise/sunset automation isn’t necessary for most tropical plants and herbs people put in the planter, but it’s nice to have a temperate lighting option that changes throughout the year.)

The Scenario tab offers a few automation options based on device status, scheduling and weather changes, plus a way to set up manual Tap-to-Run automations. Beyond that, there isn’t much else to the app, which makes sense and aligns with the company’s goal of keeping things simple. However, folks wanting smart home integrations with a platform like Home Assistant or Samsung SmartThings might be better off using a smart plug with a different grow light brand.

Speaking of grow lights, the full-spectrum unit inside the top of the Smart Landscape Growframe can reach up to 1,480 lumens, which is very bright considering most plants in the planter will be within 6 inches or less. Given the size limit on the plants you can put in the planter, I doubt you’ll have any issues with giving your plants enough light. I want to note that the adhesive holding one of the grow light strips in my sample unit came loose during shipping, but it was easy enough to reattach.

Planting in the Smart Landscape Growframe is fairly easy. It comfortably holds up to seven potted plants (2- to 3-inch pots), though I ended up putting five 4-inch potted herbs in my setup. One pot in particular is a little taller than the planter box lip, but it doesn’t bother me.

Be mindful of pot size in the planter, as rims that press up against the side can cause water to overflow onto the floor, as it did with mine. The best solution is to remove a little soil from overfilled pots and to add a small notch or hole in a side of the pot that drains into the basin.

The potted herbs I got from my local garden center needed a little trimming before I could put them in the Smart Landscape Growframe, so it was a good opportunity to try out the Pruning Shears. I’m a huge fan of the all-metal design, which is easily one of the most comfortable pairs of gardening shears I’ve used. The nifty locking latch at the end of the handle isn’t metal — it doesn’t need to be — but it’s easy to use and doesn’t require any fiddling.

I also love the needle-nose blades, which are easy to maneuver into tight spaces when trimming dead growth off plants — they are great for trimming all of my herbs. Although I’ll admit that the densely packed chives tested my patience, that’s hardly the shears’ fault.

Of the items I tested, the glass watering can was my least favorite. For instance, the borosilicate glass may be more durable than other types of glass, but it’s still glass and still fragile. I’m not sure if I trust my clumsy self with it when I water my plants. Similarly, the 1-quart size is great for folks caring for a handful of plants, but it can’t keep up with the gallon-size watering can that I sometimes empty completely just to water my dwarf lemon tree in a large container.

Another issue I had with the glass watering can was the upper rim. While I like that the flared rim makes it easy to fill from my bathroom sink, it can get in the way when watering the Growframe. This is especially tedious when you need to tilt the watering can nearly vertical to get the last drops out. Fortunately, you can see when the water is almost gone, but that’s the only real advantage it has over my normal watering can.

I often put off fertilizing houseplants because it feels like a hassle. My main reason is that most of the carnivorous plants I grow don’t like fertilizer, so I skip it on other houseplants. (I get around this with plant food spikes, but I’m hardly consistent at that either.) A secondary reason is that keeping the fertilizer out where I’ll use it isn’t the best use of space in my apartment. While Modern Sprout’s Dissolving Plant Food Sheets don’t really solve the former problem, they’re very convenient for the latter.

Just like when I tested dishwasher detergent sheets, I really like how easy it is to toss Modern Sprout’s fertilizer into the watering can. A full sheet treats a gallon and has perforations so you can tear it into segments to fit your watering can. Since the glass watering can holds one quart, I needed only one-quarter of a sheet. The sheets dissolved a little slowly, and I had to stir them for a minute or two before no fragments were left.

I’m a fan of the seaweed sheets, which are a great option for plant food that isn’t entirely a collection of processed chemicals. Despite the seaweed ingredient, the sheets don’t explicitly state they’re certified organic, so keep that in mind if you use them for herbs or microgreens.

All of the Modern Sprout products I tested have a premium design and build quality that makes them easy to recommend for people who value form as much as function. I consider the Pruning Shears the best value in the bunch. They feel incredibly sturdy and capable for $20 and are a huge step up from my $10 Vivosun Gardening Scissors in every way. I haven’t tested Modern Sprout Bypass Hand Pruners, but I suspect they’ll easily rival the Fiskars Shears I use for thicker growth.

While $229 is a lot to ask for the Smart Landscape Growframe, keep in mind that premium heavy-duty steel planters without smart lighting already cost more than those made from other materials. Likewise, more affordable — and more powerful — grow lights are on the market, but Modern Sprout’s intuitive app includes every scheduling and customization feature I consider essential. Even people who don’t use other smart home gear should find it easy to navigate.

I think the Dissolving Plant Food Sheets are a fairly nice option for seaweed-based fertilizers, but the 20-pack will treat only 20 gallons of water at the normal dilution. This makes the sheets generally more expensive per feeding than liquid kelp fertilizers from brands like TPS Nutrients and Grow Queen. That said, Modern Sprout is more convenient to measure, and it won’t cause a liquid or powdery mess if you knock the package over. It’s a great gift, but not necessarily for an enthusiast with a large collection of houseplants.

I wouldn’t buy the Glass Watering Can, but I don’t think it’s a bad product. It’s undeniably attractive, but $48 is more than most. I’ll stick with my cheaper, larger plastic watering can. Overall, Modern Sprout suits folks with higher budgets or as an attractive gift option for your favorite plant nerd.

'The Mean Season" is a sun-drenched, stormy mystery set against 1980s Miami

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While I'd usually queue up the holiday movies as the season approaches, for some reason, I'm not quite ready this year. I miss long summer days, even if they do come with insects and heat. Like me, if you are longing for beachy days, you may want to skip the queue of winter-heavy movies and opt for a summer-based thriller instead.

I happened upon "The Mean Season" on Tubi while looking for a thriller, and it completely swept me away. Starring Kurt Russell, Mariel Hemingway, and Richard Jordan, the film is set in a stormy, beautiful Miami during its "mean season" of storms and hurricanes.

It let me put off the cold weather a little longer while keeping me captivated by an intricate serial-killer plot — the ultimate escape from the dark fall and winter days to come. And best of all, it's completely free to stream "The Mean Season" since it's on Tubi.

"The Mean Season" kicks off with a murder. Alongside shots of a newspaper's printing press, a woman is seen walking out to the beach. At first, she seems to smile, only for someone to come up behind her, pointing a gun. The camera cuts away to a looming storm as a gunshot rings out.

The next scene introduces us to the weary Malcolm Anderson (Kurt Russell), who is ready to leave behind his journalism career in Miami for a slower life with his girlfriend, Christine Connelly (Mariel Hemingway), in Colorado. But before he leaves, his editor, Bill Nolan (Richard Masur), approaches him with one final assignment: a body that's been found.

The victim turns out to be a teenage girl. Malcolm is on the scene, talking to witnesses and gathering information, then returns to the office to write up the article. After it gets printed, he gets a phone call. While initially thinking it was a prank or a strange reader, the caller (Richard Jordan) admits to being the one who killed the girl. He even shares details only the killer would know.

Thus begins a truly bizarre relationship between reporter and murderer. The killer wants Malcolm to keep writing about him. Despite Malcolm's longing to escape the entire hustle for news, he can't help but stay and see it all play out. As the news reports on the crimes, the killer becomes restless, believing that too much focus is on Malcolm and not on the killer himself. It won't be long before both Malcolm and his girlfriend are at risk.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

While "The Mean Season" has its flaws, Russell and Jordan's excellent acting and the vivid Miami setting make it an electric thriller. These types of late '80s thrillers always leave me wanting more; it's something about the gritty setting and the less-than-combed look of the entire movie that makes it feel more real than anything of our modern era.

Plus, I've always loved Kurt Russell in films. He manages to portray a charming, decent man with notable personality flaws—including the ambition shown here that leads him into a relationship with a killer, putting both his and his girlfriend's lives at risk.

Richard Jordan as the killer is downright frighteningly good. He plays a diabolical man incredibly well, reminding me of how much we lost when this actor passed away far too soon. He's one of the biggest reasons to spend time watching this flick.

I also can't resist the Miami beach setting, especially with the stormy weather looming as equally close and threatening as the killer himself.

Also, keep an eye out for a fresh-faced Andy Garcia as Detective Ray Martinez. He does an excellent job matching the intensity of the moment throughout the movie.

The AI Discover tab will be centered around themes. You’ll be able to pick from a range of themes depending on what you feel like watching, or how long you want to watch. You’ll also see selections that match what you’ve been watching lately and what’s popular.

You can refresh the list of suggestions or dive deeper with more complex search prompts. If you’d like to start over, you can pick the “Something different” option. To support AI Discover, Netflix is also adding a new button next to Play and My List that’ll let you tune your recommendations. You can press this button to keep a recommendation or to request that you don’t be recommended a title again.

Most streaming apps already rely quite heavily on machine learning and AI algorithms to offer user recommendations, even if they’re not marketed as AI features. Though most rely on traditional AI algorithms, like Prime Video’s “Recommended for you” tab, they personalize title recommendations based on your viewing history, likes and dislikes, and rental behavior.

Other platforms offer generative AI and features more similar to Netflix’s AI Discover. For example, YouTube features Gemini-powered searches that let you ask complex questions or use open-ended prompts to get results you want.

While I am itching to test this feature to see just how accurate it can be, Netflix hasn’t made it widely available yet. The company will gradually grant users access over the coming weeks, so stay tuned.

#3198. You Should Update to iOS 27.2 Now to Patch Hundreds of Bugs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The update fixes some bugs that could expose your sensitive iPhone data or worse.

Apple released iOS 27.2 on Monday, Oct. 26, just a few days after the launch of the iPhone Duo. While iOS 27.2 brings Siri AI to more languages and updates a few other features, it also patches 141 bugs and security issues, including some that could allow a third party to access data or run commands on your iPhone or leave your device inoperable.

You can download iOS 27.2 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

According to Apple’s release notes, iOS 27.2 patches dozens of issues across your iPhone. Some of these issues can cause some serious problems for you and your device.

Nine of these bugs address issues that could lead to kernel corruption on your device. The kernel is the core of your device’s operating system, and kernel corruption can cause your device to freeze or crash. The blue screen of death, for example, could be caused by kernel corruption.

Apple also wrote that seven of these bugs could lead to arbitrary code execution. That means the bug could allow a third party to steal your data or use your device for other nefarious purposes.

The update addresses a lot of other bugs, including one that you might run into if you plug a malicious USB into your device. Apple didn’t write that any of these bugs were being actively exploited, but you should still update to iOS 27.2 now to give yourself the most protection.

For as many bugs as 27.2 fixes, it’s actually a slight decrease from earlier updates. Last month’s iOS 27 update patched even more bugs at 157. The number of bug fixes in both iOS updates are unusual based on data over the past few years. In iOS 26, the most bug fixes included in an update was 88 with iOS 26.6. The update with the next highest number of patches was iOS 18.4 with 75.

Apple didn’t say why there’s been an uptick in the number of bug fixes in iOS updates. Artificial intelligence has been used recently to find and address huge numbers of software bugs; however, that doesn’t appear to be the cause behind the surge in iOS 27.2 or iOS 27. Apple usually notes when a bug is found with the help of AI, yet OpenAI is mentioned four times in iOS 27.2’s release notes, and Claude’s Anthropic is only mentioned thrice.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to my request to comment.

For more iOS news, here’s what you should know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1. You can also check out our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

According to 9to5Mac, you can ask Siri AI to create a playlist in Music and save it to your library, request messages to be scheduled for a later send, organize and label photos, and create a detailed calendar invite — all with your voice.

The same reporting also states that Siri AI features will appear in Maps, Weather, Shortcuts, and Notes, signaling that an AI-supercharged Siri will live in every crevice of your Apple devices.

Also: iOS 27 will organize your open Safari tabs now

I’m not one to complete tasks like the ones mentioned above on my iPhone — I’m far more likely to do them on my MacBook Air, since I associate the laptop with productivity. Every blue moon I’ll rearrange my entire Apple Music catalog, every month I fill out my calendar, and sometimes I’ll go through Photos and try to organize it. I can see myself automating certain steps in these tasks, and I’m excited to try it.

A WebKit blog post details that adaptive dark mode is coming to Safari, how it will work, and what users can expect. According to the post, 40% of web page loads are from dark mode users, but only 10% of web pages natively support it.

I’m particularly excited about this feature, as I set my Apple devices to automatically enable dark mode at 7 p.m. to encourage a more relaxing evening scrolling vibe, especially while reading. I read a lot on my MacBook, and in a dark room, a bright page can feel too bright, but dimming my laptop’s display doesn’t quite do the trick.

Also: Your AirPods got better in iOS 27 – three new ways I’m using them

The WebKit blog post states that adaptive dark mode uses “a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue” and distinguishes between when a page’s color is purely decorative and when it carries substantial meaning, to ensure the user experience remains consistent between light and dark modes.

Vertical browser tabs aren’t a new concept, but they’ll soon be new to Safari. I see the value in vertical tabs: a list view is easier to scan, web page titles aren’t smushed when several tabs are open, and they’re particularly useful when you’re working on a widescreen monitor.

Many people who spend hours using their Mac or MacBook may find this upcoming feature useful. I do believe that Safari is the superior browser for personal use, given its integration with your Apple devices, especially with features like Handoff.

Also: 7 AI-free iOS 27 features that make old iPhones exciting again

However, I do have one major gripe with vertical tabs: they’re usually locked to the left panel, and I prefer the right. If Safari allows this customization, I’ll seriously consider switching from horizontal tabs.

#3193. The Step-by-Step Guide to Shutting Off Apple Intelligence Features in iOS 27

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With the master Apple Intelligence toggle gone, opting out in iOS 27 means turning off Siri AI, Writing Tools, Image Playground and other features separately.

Screen Time, the iPhone feature most people know for limiting app use, has become the most direct way to block Apple Intelligence in iOS 27. That’s because Apple removed the single switch that used to turn every AI feature off at once. The Settings section once called Apple Intelligence & Siri is now just Siri, centered on the new Siri AI, and the remaining AI tools are scattered across several menus. Screen Time’s restrictions can shut down Writing Tools and image creation together, and a few other features need their own toggles. Here’s the full map.

Individual features can still be disabled, but they’re scattered across several menus in Settings and Screen Time rather than consolidated in one place. Here’s the current map of what can be turned off and where to find each control.

If your device is not running the newest software, turning off Apple Intelligence all at once only takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

You can still disable some of Apple’s AI features if your iPhone is running iOS 27. It just won’t be as easy as tapping the main toggle.

To disable Siri AI, go to Settings > Siri and toggle off the control. Beware, though, that this will disable your voice assistant entirely, as well as disable conversations in the new dedicated Siri app and block you from using Apple’s Visual Intelligence. Additionally, your HomePod speakers will not be able to recognize your voice or help with personal content if they’re on the same iCloud account as your iPhone.

Keep reading for how to disable some of the individual Apple AI features.

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Read more: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? Here’s what’s actually going on.

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas should be for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the new iPhone 18 lineup, the iPhone Duo, iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. This is what it looks like running iOS 26, but the settings flow is the same.

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, the storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an “Apple Intelligence & Siri” option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features.

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. This is what the settings look like with iOS 26. It may look different if you are using iOS 27. The settings flow is the same.

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 27 yet, make a good backup first.

If you aren’t on iOS 27, you can turn off Apple Intelligence with one tap. (You can see what software your iPhone is running by going to Settings > General > About and seeing what iOS version you’re running.)

If you’re on iOS 26 or earlier, here’s how to disable Apple Intelligence. Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch if you are running iOS 26 or an earlier software version.

Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.

#3192. Orion Energy (OESX) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

LED lighting growth offset EV charging weakness this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Orion Energy Systems, Inc. (OESX -7.67%) reported a 9% revenue increase for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and reiterated its recently upgraded full-year revenue guidance. Management attributed the growth primarily to the LED Lighting segment, which offset declines in EV charging and maintenance revenue. The company reported its eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA, supported by increased project activity with major retail and data center customers. Financial performance in the quarter was influenced by a mix shift that temporarily lowered gross margins, though management expects these rates to return to levels above 30% in the second half of the year.

Operator: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Orion Energy Systems' Fiscal 2027 Second Quarter Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] In this call, Sally Washlow, Orion's CEO; and Per Brodin, its CFO, will review the company's second quarter results as well as its fiscal 2027 outlook. Then we will open the call to investors' questions. [Operator Instructions] Today's call is being recorded. A replay will be posted in the Investors section of the company's website, orionlighting.com. I will now turn the call over to Per Brodin, Orion's CFO.

John Brodin: Thank you, Corey. First, as a reminder, prepared remarks and answers to questions on this call include statements that are forward-looking under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements generally include words such as anticipate, believe, expect, project or similar words. Also, any statements describing future objectives or goals, company plans and outlook are also forward-looking. These forward-looking statements are subject to various risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from current expectations. Risks include, among other matters, those that Orion has described in its press release issued this morning and in its SEC filings. Except as described therein, Orion disclaims any obligation to update or revise forward-looking statements made as of today.

In addition, reconciliations of certain non-GAAP financial metrics to their nearest GAAP measures are also provided in today's press release. And now I will turn the call over to Orion's CEO, Sally Washlow.

Sally Washlow: Thank you, Per. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being with us today. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, we delivered growth of 9% year-over-year. All of Orion's business segments, LED Lighting, EV charging and Maintenance recorded expected levels of financial performance in the second quarter and continue on a trajectory to meet our full fiscal year guidance. As a reminder, those expectations, which we recently increased are to achieve positive adjusted EBITDA on revenue of between $100 million and $102 million, an increase from prior guidance of $95 million to $97 million in FY '27.

As we head into the second half of the fiscal year, FY '27 shapes up as a continuation of the successful turnaround we began in FY 2026, which came in at $86 million in revenue and $2 million in positive adjusted EBITDA. FY '26 represented a return to growth for this company in both revenue and profitability. Orion's unrivaled supply chain and project management capabilities are attributes that I cannot emphasize enough. Our resilient supply chain provides a competitive advantage that is consistently cited by Orion's customers.

Many of our customers come back to Orion asking to expand the work we are doing with them, whether it is expanding the scope of work at a single facility or adding increased opportunities at additional locations. These projects run the gamut ranging from lighting only to EV infrastructure projects to electrical contracting. Our existing expectations for this fiscal year reflect our confidence in the continuing growth trajectory for the company, along with recent industry research that informs us that we are about to begin a new industrial LED lighting replacement cycle.

The October cover story of a respected industry publication, Lighting Management & Maintenance, reports that 10% to 20% of America's LED installed base may already be due for replacement. For commercial, industrial and outdoor applications, the segment that Orion serves, that replacement cycle may be 20% to 30%. Orion's recent announcements serve as early indicators of this replacement cycle. As for FY '27 specifically, the quarter included a number of milestones. Q2 marked an additional multimillion deployment of our data center lighting solution for one of the world's largest hyperscalers. This followed June's announcement of our first multimillion-dollar deployment for this globally renowned hyperscaler.

We believe we are still in the early innings of deploying our cost-saving and energy-efficient solution with this hyperscaler, and there is still growth in this segment, evidenced by our discussions of finalizing additional scope to our already announced wins. Our customizable lighting solution manufactured right here in Wisconsin is capable of delivering higher energy efficiency, resiliency and decarbonization in LED lighting. Another announcement, our latest $10 million to $15 million engagement with a major nationwide retailer. Our long-time customer made a follow-on commitment to us in the second quarter for a new LED lighting project estimated to represent $10 million to $15 million.

We believe we will achieve the higher range of this commitment, and we will keep you apprised as we execute this project in Q3 and Q4. This latest scope of work involves retrofitting interior LED lighting and IoT system installations at locations we had not previously retrofitted. This is the most recent in a multiyear sequence of engagements for us with this well-known brand. Furthermore, we believe this will expand to additional stores, which could equal or be more than our previously announced project. We've seen adoption of the full spectrum of Orion's products and services, typified by our recent announcement of a global automotive leader that is deploying both our LED lighting solutions and our EV charging infrastructure.

We will continue to focus on scaling EV charging across a broader customer base and geographic footprint. More than ever, industrial America requires full-footprint LED lighting, EV charging and electrical infrastructure. It needs it at scale and at the maximum of efficiency and cost effectiveness. We believe strongly that we will continue to be a provider of choice for AI and IoT-driven electrification to Fortune 100 corporations and other global leaders. With that, let me turn it over to Orion's CFO, Per Brodin, to review our financial performance and outlook.

John Brodin: Thank you, Sally. Today, we reported fiscal Q2 '27 revenue of $21.7 million compared to $19.9 million in Q2 '26. LED Lighting segment revenue in Q2 '27 was $14.9 million compared to $10.7 million in Q2 '26. Q2 '27 Lighting segment revenue performance reflected increased project activity and distribution channel sales, partially offset by a decrease in ESCO channel sales. Orion's expanded LED lighting project pipeline and efforts to drive growth in the distribution channel are continuing to contribute to improving performance in fiscal '27. Lighting achieved a Q2 '27 gross margin of 29.1% versus 27.5% in Q2 '26. Maintenance segment revenue was $4 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.5 million in Q2 '26.

We achieved a Maintenance segment gross margin of 25.3% in Q2 '27 versus 23.7% in Q2 '26. EV charging solutions revenue was $2.8 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.8 million in Q2 '26, reflecting a year-over-year reduction in project volume. EV achieved a gross margin of 31.4% in Q2 '27 versus 45.8% in Q2 '26. Our overall gross profit margin was 28.7% in Q2 '27 versus 31% in Q2 '26. The Q2 '27 margin decrease was largely driven by a mix shift within the Lighting segment. We expect our margin rate to normalize back to the 30-plus percent neighborhood in Q3 and Q4. Total operating expenses were $7 million in Q2 '27 compared to $6.4 million in Q2 '26.

Increases in stock-based compensation and general and administrative expenses, along with increased commission expense included in sales and marketing costs were the main drivers of the increase. Reflecting lower gross margin and higher operating expenses, Orion's Q2 '27 net loss was $0.8 million or $0.20 per share compared to a net loss of $0.6 million or $0.17 per share in Q2 '26. Adjusted EBITDA was positive in Q2 '27 and was $0.5 million in Q2 '26. As Sally pointed out, this was Orion's eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA. Regarding our outlook, as Sally highlighted, we expect a continued increase in profitable growth in fiscal '27, with positive adjusted EBITDA and revenue between $100 million and $102 million.

Given the remaining revenue needed to achieve this guidance, we expect both Q3 and Q4 revenue to be relatively even. Any upside mentioned by Sally would occur in Q4. And this concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, would you please commence the question-and-answer session?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Sameer Joshi of H.C. Wainwright.

Sameer Joshi: Congrats on the upgraded guidance. That was good to see. So on the hyperscaler wins that you are experiencing, how should we look at these? Are these for unique sites? Or are these for a set of sites? And what is the strategy going forward or rather the sales cycle going forward where do you expect the same hyperscalers to contract you for additional sites?

Sally Washlow: Yes. Thanks for the question. We expect with this hyperscaler, and as we've said earlier, how we've won is we first get approved on their campuses to install or to sell our lighting fixtures. We're not doing the installation. And then we win building by building. And each building is 7 figures of lighting fixtures alone. So we've won 2, and we're in discussions of another building as well that we expect to come shortly. So there's a lot of noise in data centers.

But with the hyperscaler that we're working with and the locations that we're in, we think that they're going to continue to grow, and we're in the early innings with this hyperscaler on the amount of buildings that we'll be able to win with them and then share the solution with others as well.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And as far as the products that they want, is there any -- are you learning of new specifications that may need upgrade to your products, new products being offered to these hyperscalers in particular?

Sally Washlow: If you're looking at it from a lens of retrofitting data centers, not anything in our line of sight. This is with new buildings that have already been announced and in flight, in construction of these data centers.

Sameer Joshi: Okay. On the EV sort of Voltrek and deployment at automakers, how is that sales process? Is it that the EV team gets the lead and they also get a lighting contract? Or is it the other way around where you are doing a lighting job and then EV gets invited?

Sally Washlow: So the good news is it's starting to work both ways. With the global automotive maker, it was a lighting project that we are doing, and then they brought the EV team in to help with that solution, in particular, and then we won EV charging at that one site. And quite frankly, we're looking at a couple of other sites with them as well. There are some other opportunities where the EV team has been in and looked at their lighting solutions and then are bringing our lighting team in to recommend solutions. So we are seeing more collaboration and a bit more opportunities in cross-selling between the 2 segments.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then just a couple of sort of financial questions. Given that at least the 2Q -- fiscal 2Q service revenue was lower, should we expect the annual mix of product versus service to skew even more towards product revenues? And a corollary of that is if that happens, should we expect gross margins -- blended gross margins to be higher, relatively higher?

John Brodin: I think as we expect the rest of the fiscal year to play out, it likely will skew a little bit more toward product based on the projects that are underway. But I wouldn't call that a markedly significant change. And as I mentioned in my comments, we do expect our margin rate to, call it, normalize back to 30-plus where it's been most recently, because we did have a mix shift change that simply impacted Q2 of this year.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then last one on accounts payable. I think, quarter-over-quarter, almost -- a little over $5 million in drop. Was there anything specific that happened there? Or is it just timing?

John Brodin: It's primarily timing. It really goes to the working capital investment we've talked about for some of these more significant projects.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gowshi Sriharan.

Sally Washlow: So we are working with the sensor or the IoT provider. It's not a system that we build or it's not our software. So we don't have a component of that. And quite frankly, in this system, I don't believe there is any component of it.

Gowshihan Sriharan: And on the pricing side of the maintenance review, compared with the previous contracts?

#3191. Want an AI job? Deployment engineers are earning executive-level pay – up to $1.45M a year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AI has ushered in new jobs, and some of them are paying handsomely, according to a new study.

AI engineers are making well over six figures in salary — and plenty more in bonuses and equity, according to data from a new report by executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Enterprises now pay “elite” AI deployment engineers between $586,000 and $1.45 million annually in total compensation, with senior leaders in the field earning up to $2.25 million, according to the report. This figure approaches the median compensation of executive officers of public companies, the authors note.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

Christian & Timbers is an AI executive search and leadership advisory firm, recruiting CEOs, board members, technology executives, and AI engineers for enterprises. The new report draws on more than 550 interviews with engineers, deployment leaders, and executives conducted from January through June 2026, along with closed and current open offers. The compensation bands are Christian & Timbers’ estimates and represent ranges rather than statistical averages.

“Enterprise CEOs are under pressure to deliver returns for their AI investments. The most important decision is how to build the team that delivers on that goal,” said Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of Christian & Timbers, in a press release.

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

The report noted that the staggering salary range includes base salary, bonus, and annualized equity. Christian & Timbers said it defines an “elite” forward deployment engineer (FDE) as “a senior AI-native deployment builder, typically with 7 to 15 years of experience, including at least two years building and deploying agentic automated workflows that deliver measurable ROI with a documented enterprise impact of $10M or more,” who has also led a team of other forward deployment engineers.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

The large salary ranges reflect increasing enterprise investments in AI talent and employee development. Microsoft, AWS, and OpenAI have announced more than $7.5 billion in corporate and partner investment in AI deployment over the past six months, Christian & Timbers noted in the release.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

There’s an increasing need to fill roles such as Senior Principal AI Engineer, AI Solutions Engineer, and Head of Deployment — but there is a limited pool of qualified candidates. The firm estimates that only 2,000 of the most senior deployment leaders exist in the US market, according to a previous Christian & Timbers study, which does not meet demand — so companies are competing for the same small group of professionals, hence the increasing salaries.

While the report underscores lucrative yields for certain engineering roles, the firm said that public job titles make comparisons more challenging.

“Christian & Timbers’ elite category spans several titles, while advertised FDE roles cover a broader range of experience and responsibilities. Experienced deployment engineers may be recruited directly or promoted into the work under titles such as staff software engineer or principal AI engineer,” the study said.

Plus, equity and bonus make up 52% to 66% of senior engineer pay, and most job postings don’t include that value in the salary, the report noted.

#3190. Will Democrats Rein in Big Tech? It Starts With Privacy and Data Centers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech critics say that real change will depend on newly elected officials keeping their campaign promises.

In this week’s midterm elections, Democrats won back control of both chambers of Congress, with stunning victories in battleground states that have voters and tech critics asking: Was this the AI election?

Artificial intelligence was central to the national conversation during the midterms, alongside concerns about affordability and the Iran war. From data centers needed to power AI to how it’s used in surveillance tech like Flock cameras, many Democratic (and a few Republican) candidates campaigned against AI.

Despite tech leaders like Elon Musk pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, tech critics say voters’ choices show a strong distrust in Big Tech and give the newly elected leaders the necessary momentum for change. But how, exactly, they deliver on those goals remains to be seen — and will have real consequences for tech consumers and companies.

“It is time for lawmakers to get real about reining in unchecked tech power and to hold these companies accountable to the people,” Butler says.

More than any other tech issue, data centers took center stage in the midterm elections. It isn’t surprising; these facilities are popping up everywhere and require vast amounts of water and electricity at the expense of nearby communities’ health and environments.

Voters showed their frustration at the ballot box. Across the country, voters rejected more than 40 ballot measures that would’ve supported data centers. It was a rare national consensus on an issue that is usually debated in city councils and statehouses. As such, “action is more likely to come on the local and state levels, at least in the short term,” says Paris Marx, tech critic and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast.

Governments may continue to adopt moratoriums on new data center construction, like New York’s first-in-the-nation pause implemented earlier this year, as they try to figure out how to mitigate the harms. State and local legislators need to continue setting environmental rules, managing electricity demand and finding real community benefits, Marx says. (OpenAI, for its part, is tackling the issue by renaming data centers as “compute campuses.”)

In many ways, “data centers are a symptom of the larger problem,” says Samir Jain, vice president of policy at the Center for Democracy and Technology. Tech companies are so focused on “winning” the global AI race that they forget (or didn’t prioritize) the impact on everyday people, he says.

But neighbors living next to data centers cannot forget. In that sense, the overwhelming public backlash to data centers and the midterm election results are “a real repudiation of that kind of approach to technology,” Jain says.

But we’ve seen very clearly over the past decade that when left unchecked, tech companies can collect and use our data in concerning ways. Despite stalled progress on a national bill in the past, there may be a new push for it, thanks to recent tech headlines. Flock cameras and other automatic license plate readers have sparked immense public concern as many cases show law enforcement officers misusing the tech to stalk and harass people.

It isn’t just major tech platforms; it’s also data brokers that sell data to companies you don’t interact with. That industry is worth more than $277 billion, and it’s the engine behind much of how Big Tech operates.

“If you are mad at this whole surveillance pricing situation where we’re going to charge you more if we feel like you can afford it, that is because of data brokers,” says McKinney. “If you are mad that the federal government can just buy information from data brokers that [it] would otherwise have to get a warrant to get, that’s a data broker problem.”

“We can’t lead the world in AI and support transformative AI innovation with a patchwork of conflicting state laws that make life harder for startups and small businesses,” Fabrizio says.

While the Democrats will have a firm majority in both chambers of Congress, many of the most contentious tech issues have bipartisan support, tech critics told me. And we’ve already seen how that can result in actionable legislation, such as the Take It Down Act, which passed nearly unanimously in 2025.

This fleeting moment of bipartisan agreement on reining in Big Tech could help lawmakers achieve the elusive task of actually fulfilling their campaign promises. But part of the challenge will be getting lawmakers to focus on real-world harm and basic protections, not whatever dystopian tech prediction is trending that day.

“It’s very likely we’ll see companies continue to push lawmakers to focus AI regulation on so-called ‘existential risks,’ meaning their claims that more advanced AI might kill humanity or end the world,” Marx says, “rather than addressing the impacts of data centers and the present-day harms.”

Those existential risks only serve to make tech companies more powerful. “These elected representatives don’t just have the power to rein in these powerful corporations; they have the obligation to do so to promote the interests of the constituents they serve,” Butler says.

We saw this election cycle how much money Big Tech is willing to spend to try to get its preferred candidates and policies. Elon Musk alone reportedly spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates such as Ken Paxton in Texas, who lost by 12 percentage points to Democrat James Talarico. Despite that, most of the tech experts I spoke to said the results showed a real desire from voters to rein in tech companies and the harms they wrought.

But that will depend on how willing the new Congress is to buck Big Tech. “If we have a new electorate that is newly emboldened to stand up to bullies,” McKinney says, “let’s start there.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
