#3189. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

#3186. Is Chrome’s settings menu getting a search bar? What we know

Chrome might receive a much-needed addition.

I’m a longtime Chrome user, but I’ve never been a fan of the browser’s user settings menu, which has grown into a dense collection of nesting submenus that can be difficult to navigate. That may be changing soon.

Also: How Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

X (formerly Twitter) user, Leopeva64, posted a short video and several still images showcasing a potential new feature in Chrome Canary, which Google uses to test new Chrome web tools and features. The posts show the search bar pinned to the top of the settings menu for instant access. By entering the name of the submenu or feature you want to access, the new search bar could save a lot of time normally spent clicking around, trying to remember exactly where it’s located.

In Chrome Canary, Google is testing removing the scroll arrows that let you automatically scroll to reveal hidden items when you hover over them in the 3-dot menu. #3185. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3184. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

And the feedback has been really, really fantastic. And the other part is we're getting great ideas from our customers.

So we really believe interacting with the customers, they've got things that take them a little bit longer or processes that they would love to see automated. And so we see a ton of opportunity on a go-forward basis to be able to add to the Ignite AI platform. And at the same time, we're going to continue to look forward to opportunities where we can create new modules, add-on modules like Recruiting Optimizer, like our absence management module that we're launching in January to be able to monetize those AI capabilities. And when you look at the breadth of our portfolio in AI, we feel like we've got a leading solution in the market.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Siti Panigrahi of Mizuho.

Sitikantha Panigrahi: Great. Just a follow-up. You said the leading solution in AI. So the question like this higher adoption, is that driving paid module attachment or pricing today? Or is that nearly -- the near-term value primarily retention and differentiation? And particularly, in the same context, are you seeing any win in terms of competitive wins in the new logo deals because your AI capability is better than competitor, anything like that?

Steven Beauchamp: Yes. Yes. So I would tell you that on an increasing basis, your AI strategy and then more specifically, the AI products that are available to customers are coming up with prospect conversations, and they're absolutely part of that evaluation process. And they not only want to know what you have today, but they also want to know what is coming because I think as the market gets educated, they realize one of the ways to take advantage of AI is to make sure that the people they're partnering with have AI tools that will really drive efficiency. And so I would say absolutely that is -- really, we've had a great start from a revenue perspective.

I think Toby talked about the momentum in the sales force from a prepared remarks perspective. And I would tell you that our AI strategy is definitely a factor there. And I think the other point I would just make is we have actual AI products that we have both launched already and announced that are coming, that are directly monetizable and then add to the ARPU equation. So it's really a combination of those 2 that gives us, kind of, the confidence in making that statement that we're seeing the benefits of having a leading platform in AI.

Sitikantha Panigrahi: Okay. And then one quick follow-up. Workforce levels, I think you said last quarter, 50, 60 bps higher than your flat assumptions. So what are those running today? And what's your assumption in the guidance?

Ryan Glenn: Yes. I think the Q1 levels were very consistent with what we saw last year. So up -- probably rounding up to a point in that 50 to 60 range, rounding up to about 1. We continue to assume flat year-over-year within the guidance, so no change to how we approached that historically.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jared Levine of TD Cowen.

Jared Levine: To start, I was hoping to talk about the managed service offerings. Can you discuss the target market for this offering, including what mix of your existing customer base would fit into that, kind of, ideal client profile for it?

Toby Williams: Jared, Toby. Yes, sure. I mean I think so far, we've seen a level of attach that we're really happy with. And I would tell you that, that is all the way through our target market from those that have under 50 employees to the heart of our market around 150 on average and then even into our enterprise clients. And I think when you look at where most of the demand has traditionally sat, it's really been in the core of our market. And I think that's what we've prepared for.

But I think as we've really launched these solutions and come through Q1, we've seen attachment penetration, I think, fairly well balanced in that -- in the core of our market, right around that 150 in the middle, but we've also seen it be relevant to those that are slightly smaller and slightly larger than that.

Jared Levine: Got it. And then, Ryan, the ex-float adjusted EBITDA beat was the smallest in the history that you've guided to float revenue here to be able to back into that. Any impact in terms of timing of investments or incremental investments made here in terms of, I guess, why that smaller than typical ex-float adjusted EBITDA beat in the quarter here?

Ryan Glenn: No. I mean I think we beat the guidance. And I think as we called out on the August earnings call, we plan to invest in R&D this fiscal year, and you saw that in Q1. R&D is up 15% versus Q1 last year. We're seeing the benefits of that investment. And I think results are consistent with expectations to a touch better. And as I mentioned on an earlier question, I think raising the year by more than that beat just points to increased margin as well and passing on the full interest income beat as well.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Daniel Jester of BMO Capital Markets.

Daniel Jester: So in the past, if I recall correctly, a lot of times when you've come out with new product, it's been easiest to attach that when you've had new customers added to the platform. And so as you think about all of the new products that you've been working on, all of the new AI tools, do you feel like you need to invest more in a back to the base motion so that your current customers will have the opportunity to use all of these tools?

Steven Beauchamp: Yes. I think you're right. You go back in our history, we've generally tried to launch products and focus on that new customer attach out of the gate. We would gain feedback from customers over time. We would stand up back to the base teams, make sure they're up and trained and ready and then we would have them go back to the client base. So that is something that we have done before. That is very much a typical motion. As you look at products like Elevate Solutions and Retirement, there's probably a little bit more pull-through demand that's already available in the client base.

And so we would stand up those back to the base teams earlier as part of that launch. I think that's probably why we called out some pretty quick momentum on both of those 2 new product launches. But it's pretty much the same formula. It's really just running that playbook a little bit earlier with the 2 new product launches. And then from an AI perspective, it's easier -- certainly easier adoption for some of the features for clients. But we really are running the same playbook for the products that are monetizable and that customers have to make a purchase decision for.

Daniel Jester: Okay. Great. And then at HR Tech a few weeks ago, it did feel like there's a diversity in the industry about how companies are evaluating, sort of, headless as the philosophy and how they're engaging with other AI tools? And so maybe just for Paylocity, like how do you think about headless? How do you think about customers using Claude and things like that to access your systems?

Steven Beauchamp: Sure. So I think if you, kind of, take a step back and our philosophy has always been very much, kind of, an open platform where if you go back in our history, we'll integrate with a bunch of different providers for things that we don't do. And if a customer is needing us to integrate with a competitor because they feel like they want to use that solution for, I don't know, recruiting or performance, we've always been very open to that. We want to be able to deliver the best possible customer experience. We've obviously expanded dramatically our marketplace over the last 5 to 7 years.

And I think that's the conversation around MCP and headless interaction is really the next iteration of that. And so if a customer wants to be able to interact in something like Claude or OpenAI or any of the frontier models, we do not have a problem with that concept at all. We want to deliver them the ideal experience, and we will meet them where they are. And so you'll see us continue with that philosophy in terms of our product road map on an ongoing basis.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Patrick Walravens of Citizens.

Kincaid LaCorte: This is Kincaid on for Pat. I was just curious, when you guys talk to customers about different pricing models, seats, consumption, outcome, what are you hearing from them? And how are they thinking about it in terms of your new products?

Toby Williams: I guess I would say there's a lot of consistency in our pricing conversations over the course of -- certainly over the course of the quarter. I think there's been a lot more talk in the market about the variability in pricing models that you're seeing with some of the different AI providers. I think in our industry at this point in time, we haven't seen any significant shifts in terms of the baseline pricing, whether that's on a PEPM basis or per seat basis for some of our other solutions. So not to say that, that doesn't evolve over the course of time. We certainly have had some of those conversations with clients.

But I think you're seeing in our industry at this point in time, grounding in the traditional pricing model. And I think for us, as we look forward, we just want to make sure that as we're rolling out new solutions, we have the flexibility to adjust from pricing standpoint if the market evolves. And I think we've done a pretty good job of making sure that's the case.

Kincaid LaCorte: And then I just wanted to touch on the 15% increase in R&D spend. Could you give a little bit of color on, kind of, where that spend flows through your teams? And then if you can, I'd love to understand how you budget out from a token perspective. Is it like on a per engineer basis? Is this something on a per team basis, a segment? I'd love some color on where that R&D money is going.

Toby Williams: Well, I think if you step back and look at all of the new products and solutions that we've launched over the course of the last 6 months or so, it's been a period of significant launch for us. A lot of those solutions we've talked about, whether it's recruiting or our Recruiting Optimizer, Retirement or the Elevate solutions and then everything we've done from the Ignite AI standpoint and as we look forward a bit, leave management. So it's been a pretty intense period of product development and launch. And so I think what you're seeing is the flow-through of the investments that we've made that we called out that we would make in the course of last year.

And all of that was positioned last year as investing for future growth. And I think what you're seeing in the quarter and with all those launches is just the pull-through of the success in the attach and penetration of those new solutions, which I think we're really excited about.

Steven Beauchamp: Yes. And then I think to the other part of your question, we're definitely seeing efficiency using code generation tools within R&D. I think the momentum that we have in terms of the number of product releases, the amount of features we're starting to -- customers are really starting to benefit from the efficiencies that we're seeing there. Obviously, this is all still early days, but we think there's a ton of opportunity for us to use tools like that to drive more innovation back to our customers. And it's pretty well adopted across our client base. We have a budget for these things. It gets managed like we do every other thing that gets looked at very frequently.

And we're pretty comfortable with the spend level and the ROI that we're getting on that investment.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Raimo Lenschow of Barclays.

Sheldon McMeans: This is Sheldon McMeans on for Raimo. I wanted to take a step back and ask about your thoughts on the durability of your AI differentiation in the market. And so it, kind of, seems like there's 2 opportunities, of course. You can agentify current solutions. You can -- maybe you talked about some solutions that wouldn't have been possible there without AI. But -- and then there's also the engineering returns and making it easier to expand into new product areas. So just, like, do you see, like, some of the things becoming table stakes and maybe the bigger opportunity is around, like, entering into new areas, getting that product velocity going?

Steven Beauchamp: Sure. I'm pretty comfortable with that part of the equation because that's really how we've operated forever. At the end of the day, we launched and we had payroll in a couple of modules when we IPO-ed in '14. We added a bunch of modules based on product feedback and market demand. We then were really the first to drive, kind of, an employee experience with community and surveys and rewards and recognition. And so the idea of, kind of, moving into this next innovation cycle for our industry and leveraging AI to be able to maybe expand beyond the traditional HCM footprint is something that we were already on that path for the last couple of years.

This is just going to unlock more opportunity. And so we're never going to sit and tell you we're completely satisfied with what we have today. We're going to drive new innovation to the market. We're going to work with customers to be able to solve more of their problems, and we think that, that's going to give us a bigger wallet share over time. And so I'm more excited today now that we've been making these investments and seeing customer interactions about the opportunities in front of us than AI than I was even a year or 2 ago.

Sheldon McMeans: That's great to hear. And on Elevate, I wanted to ask if there's any metrics around attendance and engagement there compared to last year. And I think the attendance typically leans a little bit more on the existing customer side, but would be particularly interested in any color around new prospects.

Toby Williams: Yes. I think it was really -- looking back, I mean, just fresh coming out of it, I mean, it was a really successful event again this year. And I think we had a -- what I would characterize as traditional mix of mostly, as you said, current clients with a fair number of prospects in attendance as well to give them a good sense of what it is like to be a part of the Paylocity family. And the attendance, yes, on a year-over-year basis was up slightly. So really happy with having just over 3,000 people in attendance at Elevate.

Again, thank you to all of our clients who came and spent time with us, and I think it was a really successful event again this year.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Matt VanVliet of Cantor Fitzgerald.

Mason Marion: This is Mason Marion on for Matt. I wanted to check in on Paylocity for Finance. So at the time of the Airbase deal, we discussed your longer-term ambitions of penetrating 10% to 20% of your installed base. Now that we're 2 years down the line, how are you tracking against those longer-term aspirations?

Toby Williams: Yes. I think we're tracking exactly to the plan. As we look back on the -- a little less than 2 years, I think, and certainly less than that since we launched the fully integrated solution, really happy with how the team has progressed both in terms of integrating the business, integrating the product set and really happy with how the go-to-market team has been able to sell those products, both in terms of new deals, attaching to new deals and then also back into the customer base. So in aggregate, I think we're really happy and tracking exactly to that plan.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jacob Smith of Guggenheim Securities.

Jacob Cody Smith: On Elevate, was there pent-up demand when you launched the offering? Is there a backlog that's giving you confidence to invest in the service organization so early? Or was that part of the plan? And can you just talk about what you're seeing so far in pipeline and ability to close those opportunities?

Toby Williams: Yes. I think we've seen a really strong pipeline, and we've also seen, I think, a strong ability to close those deals in the pipeline. And I think if we go back to some of the context we've given around the start of those solutions as an idea, I mean, we would frequently see clients coming to us and asking for the type of help that we are providing in the Elevate Solutions. And so I think we believe that -- and certainly had a large number of client conversations and market testing work leading up to that. But I think we believe that there was demand both in the market for new deals that we would bring in.

And I think we also believe there is demand that was in the client base. And I think that's exactly what we've seen as we've actually gotten the solutions launched and out there. It's still early days. I mean we're still in really, I think, the first full quarter of having them live. And I think that's a lot of what has given us the confidence to invest in those teams to support that business. I think we're ultimately really happy with how -- what we've seen so far from the demand standpoint coming through Q1.

Jacob Cody Smith: And just a follow-up there, too. Is the expectation still that the margin profile will be similar to the broader software business?

Toby Williams: It is. I mean, I think you heard Ryan a few minutes ago just talk about the investments that we've made across the board, both in product and tech and in service to get those solutions launched. And you see some timing difference in expense here and there. But I think on an overall basis, as you look out across the end of this fiscal year and into next year, we absolutely believe that the margin profile will be the same.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Tomer Zilberman of Bank of America.

Tomer Zilberman: I think in the Q&A, you spoke a lot about the HCM market. You also addressed finance. But I just wanted to touch a minute on the IT side of the equation, what you're seeing there. Your competitor last night called out strength there. I just wanted to see if you're also seeing good progress there as well.

Steven Beauchamp: Yes. I think we're really happy with both, kind of, finance and IT. I think on a relative basis, it's a much smaller part of our business. We're newer in that category. But we've seen really good momentum. I think the concept of being able to tie back to the employee record and know when the events are happening in real time, then being able to tie IT, particularly as you think of onboarding and offboarding and all the things that need to happen from an employee perspective, is really attractive to our customers. And so early innings for that product overall, but we are excited with the momentum that we are seeing.

And really, all the new products that Toby just, kind of, went through and mentioned, combined with the investments in finance and IT and additional HCM modules really contributed to a strong start.

Tomer Zilberman: Got it. Maybe as a follow-up in an unrelated piece, going back to the float business, your guide is $15 million above the previous guide. I think last quarter, you set out an expectation of 2 rate cuts. We've seen so far 1 rate hike with the potential for a second. Just curious what you're embedding. Is it just the one hike so far?

Ryan Glenn: Yes. So we've factored in the September 25 basis point rate increase. We have no further changes to rates over the balance of the fiscal year. So I think to the extent we see an increase, we will update you at that time with what the impact is to yields, and we provide the average daily balance every quarter. So we'll be able to provide that math if that were to happen.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Kevin McVeigh of UBS.

Kevin McVeigh: I think you mentioned seeing some green shoots in new product, kind of, the demand environment. Maybe help us understand what's been the source of that and the sustainability is your -- that's, again, the new products that are driving that, where it's a little bit better demand? Just help us dimensionalize that a little bit.

Toby Williams: Yes. I mean I think I would maybe bifurcate the new logos and then back into the client base. I think from a new logo standpoint, our view is that the demand environment remains really stable. And I think the go-to-market teams have done a really good job coming into this year from an execution standpoint and bringing new logos into the business. Fairly well-balanced quarter in terms of the growth between ARPU increase and new unit increase.

And then I think from a launching of new product standpoint, I think we're really happy with the balance that we've seen between attaching new products to new logos and then also being able to sell those products back into the client base and add value to our existing clients. So overall, I mean, I think -- we're -- we think the demand environment is very stable and pleased with the execution of the teams. And I think it's been overall from a growth standpoint, well balanced across new business, sales back into the client base, the contributions that the new products have made and then ultimately, the great job that our service team has done driving retention.

So I think overall, solid quarter and pretty well balanced from a performance standpoint.

Kevin McVeigh: That's helpful. And then I guess you've talked a little bit about AI starting to surface from a product perspective. Are you charging for that separately similar to a module? Or is it wrapping into just other packages? Or is it just -- I guess, how do you monetize it, I guess, [ is what I am asking ].

Steven Beauchamp: Yes. So if you think about our AI Ignite platform, there's multiple capabilities in a whole series of agents that are included in that platform. Some of those things are embedded in the flow of everyday work. So as you're completing your payroll process, our agent capability are going to reduce the number of errors. They're going to increase the efficiency, and they're going to produce more accurate results for you overall. And that's just embedded, and that's just part of our payroll platform. We're not charging separately for you. But I can tell you that when we demo it and we talk about it with prospects, it's a differentiation. There's a whole series of agents. That's just one example.

And then there's a second category of agents where we are really saving the customer a ton of time. It's something that they maybe don't purchase from us today. And then we are monetizing those separately. That's where Recruiting Optimizer and the leave management category come in. And so we're selling those back to existing customers. We're bundling those in for new. So it's really, kind of, a combination of both. And as we think about it over time, we'll continue to add modules that we can monetize. We'll continue to add AI capabilities across the platform that we will include just as part of differentiation.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back to Toby Williams for closing remarks.

Toby Williams: Thanks so much. Yes, I just wanted to say thanks to all of you for your interest in Paylocity and a special shout out and thank you to all of our employees for the great job they're doing serving our clients. Thank you very much, and have a great night.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

If you've never seen a Western before, these familiar faces could be enough to get you hooked

Verdict: "The Magnificent Seven" is a remake of the 1960's Western of the same name. That movie was itself a remake, adapting Akira Kurosawa's 1954 classic "Seven Samurai." This updated version is not better than either of those movies; they're two of the greatest films of all time. But with its modern stars and a few excellent shootouts, it is a great choice for those looking for an entry point into the Western genre. Just make sure to watch the other two movies once you're done.

Where to watch: Stream "The Magnificent" for free on Tubi or YouTube

Going into this, I thought that "The Magnificent Seven" (2016) would be a tough movie to recommend. It's not that I expected it to be the worst film in my 52-movie-long Denzel Watchathon. I thought it would be perfectly fine, and ultimately, it did live up to those moderate expectations. The problem is, this movie is a remake of the 1960 Western classic of the same name, and that's one of the greatest Westerns ever made.

Further complicating things is that the 1960 version of "The Magnificent Seven" isn't even the best version of that story. That honor belongs to Akira Kurosawa's "Seven Samurai," a movie you likely heard of and almost certainly saw an homage to at some point. It's been remade or copied directly over a dozen times and then indirectly probably scores more. One of my favorite clones of "Seven Samurai" is the episode "Bounty Hunters" from "Star Wars: The Clone Wars."

In short, it's tough to recommend watching a movie that's an inferior copy of a copy, even if the movie itself is perfectly fine. But as I watched this latest homage to Kurosawa, I realised that there is an audience for this movie. Especially while you can still stream it for free.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Tubi, one of the best free streaming services we've tested. You can also stream it for free on YouTube (with ads).

Malcolm has been with the Streaming team at Tom's Guide since 2023, reviewing dozens of movies each year so you don't have to watch the bad ones.

If you're a fan of Westerns, you can probably turn back now. Not only have you probably seen the original 1960 version of "The Magnificent Seven," but you've probably seen "Seven Samurai." If that's the case, the only reason for watching this movie is if you're a Denzel Washington completist like me. Again, this isn't because the movie is bad; it's just that it doesn't bring anything to the table aside from updating the call sheet.

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

But for those of you who are new to the Western genre, this movie is a great starting point. It stars Denzel Washington as Sam Chisholm, a bounty hunter from Kansas. He is in search of a fugitive, which causes him to cross paths with Emma (Haley Bennett). Her town of Rose Creek is in danger of being taken by a mining tycoon, Bartholomew Bogue (Peter Sarsgaard), and she's trying to find men who will help the townspeople keep their land.

Sam agrees to help her, so he recruits a group of six others (Chris Pratt, Ethan Hawke, Vincent D'Onofrio, Lee Byung-hun, Manuel Garcia-Rulfo and Martin Sensmeier) to help Emma and her fellow citizens make a stand against Bogue. Upon arrival in Rose Creek, they quickly dispatch Bogue's agents left behind to keep the townspeople in check, then get to work training the newly conscripted soldiers and setting up traps for when Bogue eventually returns to claim the town.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The 1960 original and Kurosawa's 1954 classic both make serious attempts to emotionally connect you to the seven soldiers and the townspeople they're defending. There are romantic entanglements, class struggles, betrayals and more. This 2016 version only ever hints at delving deeper into its characters.

That's essentially the long and short of this movie's plot, aside from the climactic battle, and that is one of the problems with this remake.

The 1960 original and Kurosawa's 1954 classic both make serious attempts to emotionally connect you to the seven soldiers and the townspeople they're defending. There are romantic entanglements, class struggles, betrayals and more.

This 2016 version only ever hints at delving deeper into its characters. We learn that Ethan Hawke's Goodnight Robicheaux is suffering from PTSD following his time as a Confederate sharpshooter in the U.S. Civil War, which Chris Pratt's Joshua Faraday refers to as "The War of Northern Aggression." Given that both these men are currently serving under Sam, a Black man — Sam and Robicheaux even clearly have a strong friendship — you'd think that there'd be some deeper exploration of the racial tensions between these characters. But clearly Robicheaux and Faraday were just fighting for states' rights.

The closest we really get to any sort of emotional connection is in the film's climactic battle, when Faraday and Vasquez (Manuel Garcia-Rulfo), who openly harbor some dislike for each other over racial animosity, find themselves bonded by blood in the movie's deadlier moments. We also learn, just at the end, why Sam really agreed to help these townspeople. This is a construct crafted completely by the 2016 movie, so I won't spoil the big reveal for you here. But I'll just say I wish the movie had chosen to let us sit with the information going into the final gunfight rather than turn it into a twist.

Still, if you're brand new to Westerns, the final showdown of this movie is undeniably epic. It's around 30 minutes of non-stop shooting and action. So, if you're just looking to dip your toe into the genre, it's okay if you pick something like this that doesn't quite get into the nuances and emotional depth that it should. Start with this, see if you can handle the violence, and then branch out into more well-crafted movies in the genre.

It's worth noting that my recommendation of this as a starter Western is only applicable as long as this movie is streaming for free. I cannot and do not advocate that you pay any of your hard-earned dollars to see this film. Not when there are other great Westerns available to stream for free, including "Seven Samurai," which, despite its setting of feudal Japan, is undeniably a Western.

But that movie is also in Japanese, so it's less accessible for those not yet fully comfortable with subtitles. It's also in black-and-white, which isn't everyone's preferred format. For me, someone who owns the Criterion Collection 4K disc of Kurosawa's masterpiece, those aspects of the film are both positives, but I can see how they'd be barriers to entry.

So if you're truly just looking for a starter-kit Western, you could do a lot worse than Denzel's version of "The Magnificent Seven," and not least of all because it has Denzel in it. Just make sure, once you're done, to branch out further into the genre. Once you're hooked, there's an entire lifetime's worth of Western movies to explore.

Stream "The Magnificent" for free right now on Tubi or for free on YouTube

#3181. Live Now! Watch as This iPhone Duo Crosses 300K Folds in Our Custom Machine

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

#3178. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

#3176. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3174. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.
