#3172. CNET People’s Picks: Readers Say This Brand Wins as the Top Laptop Choice

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

If you prefer a PC, there are still some non-Apple brands worth considering.

Shopping for a new laptop for the holidays, but not sure which brand to choose from? Our readers do.

We recently surveyed CNET readers as part of our People’s Picks awards to find out what they think about their laptop brand to help you make a more sound choice for your next laptop. We listed several well-known names, including Dell and Lenovo. We asked about everything that matters most on a daily basis, like battery life, durability and even its performance for handling tasks like gaming and graphics. Out of 10 categories, one brand wins most of them: Apple.

Apple swept up eight of the awards for its signature MacBooks and claimed the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks award. Here’s why.

Apple wins the overall award in CNET’s People’s Picks, and also takes home the overall satisfaction rating, with 74.2% of Apple users saying they’re extremely satisfied with their laptop. In comparison, 22.5% say they’re satisfied — bringing Apple to a near-perfect overall satisfaction score of 96.7%.

Apple’s overall impression also speaks to other awards it wins from CNET readers, including high ratings for its impressive battery life, display quality and high-quality build. All of those categories and more sum up Apple’s brand loyalty nod, with 68% of MacBook owners saying they would buy the same laptop and model from Apple again.

How much are people paying for MacBooks? CNET found that 43.5% of Apple users paid at least $1,500. Until earlier in 2026, the MacBook Air was Apple’s entry-level laptop, priced at least $1,299. The introduction of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo brought that down to a more reasonable $699. However, despite Apple’s laptops being more expensive than those from other brands, they still ranked high for their value proposition. Part of the reason for that is that MacBooks received high marks for hardware reliability. “Apple’s MacBooks might cost more than the average laptop, but their premium build quality means they’re built for the long haul,” said Matt Elliott, CNET’s laptop editor.

If you plan to have your laptop for a while, you may be impressed by other features that make work easier and faster, like its M-series central processing unit for task management and AI capabilities, great battery life and a one-of-a-kind operating system — currently MacOS 27. All of the features and specifications bundled together make Apple’s perception as a high-end laptop worth the investment for long-term satisfaction.

Apple clinches a near-perfect score for its value perception. According to our survey results, 44% of Apple users said their MacBook has exceptional value. Others say their MacBook is worth what they paid for it (50.9%) — for a total positive score of 94.6%.

Digging deeper into Apple’s cost-to-value rating, 81.8% of Apple owners paid at least $1,000 for their laptops, which may seem costly, but Apple users seem OK with the price. That could be because, even though Apple has only three laptop models in a handful of sizes in its lineup, each one delivers solid performance and storage.

Take Apple’s proprietary processing chips, for example — each upgrade since the M1 release has improved the laptop’s speed, battery life and performance. Now the M6 can handle the MacBook’s AI capabilities, storage and high-resolution graphics. And for all of that power, most MacBooks are relatively thin and lightweight, making them easier for mobility — just a few of the reasons Apple users may be OK with paying more for what they’re getting.

Battery life is a big deal for many laptop buyers, and that’s another area where Apple delivers. Over a quarter of those surveyed (25.7%) said their MacBook’s battery life exceeds 10 hours — which is more than enough for a full day of work in most cases. And 18.7% say their MacBook’s battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours — totaling 44.4% of MacBook users saying their battery lasts 8 hours or more.

Comparatively, non-Apple laptop brands fall short in this category. Only 16.4% of Lenovo users say their laptop’s battery lasts at least 8 hours, and even fewer for Dell (12.7%) and HP (11.8%). If you’re leaning toward a MacBook for its battery life, CNET’s lab test shows that the MacBook Neo lasts 13 hours and 26 minutes for online streaming, whereas the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch M5 (2026 model) lasts 17 hours and 2 minutes.

Apple sweeps the brightness, color accuracy and clarity category with 99.2% of its users either satisfied or extremely satisfied with their laptop’s screen performance. No Apple users reported dissatisfaction.

“Apple has long been a favorite for creative professionals and content creators for good reason: Its MacBook displays are some of the best you’ll find on any laptop,” said Josh Goldman, CNET’s managing editor for computers. “While Apple may use marketing names like Retina and Liquid Retina to describe display features, they do translate into sharp and clear text and images, with excellent brightness, contrast, color gamut coverage and color accuracy.”

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR even goes beyond what MacBook users have come to expect. It’s Apple’s first OLED touchscreen laptop and features next-level brightness, color and contrast.

Apple receives high ratings: 80% of MacBook owners say it has premium build quality, 18.2% say it’s solid, and those results don’t surprise us.

And MacBooks seem durable and reliable, with 87% of Apple users reporting no hardware failures on their MacBooks, while 8% say minor software fixes resolved their issues. Only 3% needed minor hardware repairs, and 2.2% needed major repairs — which could be fixes such as a battery or screen replacement.

Our editors say the M5 MacBook Air is thin and lightweight, but still has a well-built aluminum design. And the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is sturdy, too. What sets Apple’s laptop hardware apart could be its aluminum chassis — the casing that holds all of the components together.

“Apple makes three lines of MacBooks — the Neo, Air and Pro — and focuses on making those the best they can possibly be. They are all built to deliver a premium experience using high-quality materials, and that even includes the entry-level MacBook Neo,” said Goldman.

Lastly, Apple uses durable materials, such as the 100% recycled aluminum alloy it says encloses the 14-inch MacBook Pro. And the tech giant has several testing facilities to test MacBook durability.

When it comes to getting your daily tasks done, most CNET readers with MacBooks (70.9%) say Apple’s laptops handle workloads flawlessly. It’s worth noting that 45% use their MacBook for work tasks, but no Apple users reported poor performance.

Here’s why that might be: Apple’s laptops are packed with top-notch performance specs and features, like their powerful processors, unified memory and fast storage. Better processor performance means enhanced graphics, on-device AI capabilities and faster task speeds, all of which add up to being able to finish work, play games or stream videos without issues or lags caused by your laptop’s hardware.

On the software side, MacOS 27 Golden Gate gives you built-in AI features, like Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. And you can organize your Safari tabs by topic and use the Notify Me tool to be notified of website changes, like price drops or breaking news. Plus, you can create shortcuts to automate tasks. Coupling all of these features and specifications explains why Apple users rate MacBooks so highly for getting the job done.

Apple leads the way on brand retention with 68% of Apple users planning to buy the same MacBook model again, while 29.1% would buy another model from Apple’s lineup. Only 3% would switch to another brand that’s not Apple.

Usually, when you buy one Apple product, you’re likely to stick to the brand’s ecosystem, especially since Apple has its own operating systems to access its unique features and work seamlessly with other Apple products with Apple’s Continuity feature. For example, you can start an email on your iPhone, but finish typing it on your MacBook. Or you can call or send a text from your laptop without reaching for your iPhone. Other features work across Apple devices, including iCloud, Universal Clipboard and AirDrop.

Asus wins as a midtier laptop choice with 67% of Asus owners paying between $500 and $1,499. There’s a sweet spot in this range with 38% spending between $500 and $999, and 28% paying between $1,000 and $1,499.

If you’re planning to spend that amount on a new laptop, you may also be pleased to know that Asus earns a higher satisfaction rating compared with other non-Apple laptop brands — 48% of Asus users say they’re extremely satisfied.

Asus laptops have a few features and specifications that may speak to that rating, regardless of budget. For example, the Zenbook A14 has a thin, lightweight design that’s rigid, with long battery life and an OLED display with strong contrast and color performance. This Copilot Plus PC sells for $1,600 (but retailers like Best Buy regularly have it on sale for less). Comparatively, these premium features from other brands could cost more or sacrifice important must-have features for the price.

Asus has other laptops worth exploring depending on your needs, like the budget-friendly Asus ZenBook S 14 or the premium Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 that could be good for gamers and creators.

Over one-third of Acer laptop owners (38%) paid less than $500 for their laptop — which is greater than other laptop brands in this price range. Yet, 44% of Acer users say their laptop has exceptional value, while 50% say the value is fair — bringing a total positive cost-to-value score of over 94%. Acer also has an overall satisfaction score of 92.6% — the highest of non-Apple laptop brands.

If you’re impressed by Acer’s value and satisfaction scores, there are a few budget-friendly Acer options to consider. The Acer Aspire 16 AI wins CNET’s Editors’ Choice award. It has a big 16-inch screen but is still lightweight (3.5 pounds). And it has good battery life (over 21 hours on CNET’s battery drain test). There are a few other pluses, like the 1440p web camera that may be good for video conferencing and a sizable touchpad. All of those features and more add up to $700, which could make it a good computer for work or casual browsing. If you’re looking to spend slightly less, its predecessor, the Aspire 14 AI, is originally $639, but you may be able to score deals on both models during holiday sales.

Even though Apple is highly recommended by CNET readers, there are plenty of other laptop models and brands worth considering depending on your needs. Here are a few non-Apple laptop brands that are runner-ups to CNET’s People’s Picks winners that you shouldn’t count out of your laptop search.

Lenovo is best known for packing a powerful laptop into a compact design with tablet functionality, like its Yoga line, and its durable ThinkPad business models. But CNET readers with Lenovo laptops say the brand’s battery life stands out most compared with other non-MacBook laptops.

Survey findings show that 16% of Lenovo owners say their laptops can run for 8 hours or more. And 10.5% say their laptop battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours, while 6% say their Lenovo laptops can withstand at least 10 hours before needing a charge. That’s more than what readers say about other non-Apple brands. The Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition lasts 25 hours and 45 minutes — making it one of the best laptop batteries CNET experts have tested.

Goldman said Lenovo has such a large and varied PC selection using the latest chips from Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and Nvidia that there is something for everyone and every budget. Even those who spend less on a Lenovo laptop can expect solid performance, including battery life.

If your laptop’s hardware fails or it breaks, you may be in the market for a new laptop sooner than expected. Think about cooling fan problems, overheating or your laptop not powering on at all. Over half (68%) of Lenovo laptop owners said they haven’t had any hardware issues with their laptops — the most compared to other non-MacBooks.

Beyond hardware durability, Lenovo also scores highly for its build and construction — overall making it a sturdy laptop choice. In our survey, 38% of Lenovo laptop owners say their laptop has a premium feel, while 51% say it’s solid — totaling a positive score of 89%.

If you’re looking for recommendations, the Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 has an all-metal design. And the Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 is a business laptop with Lenovo’s well-known X1 Carbon exterior and new Space Frame design, which Elliott says makes it easier to repair or replace parts if needed.

Many Lenovo laptop users are loyal to the brand, which speaks to the overall positive satisfaction rating of 83%. If Lenovo owners were in the market for a new laptop, nearly three in four (73.2%) say they would buy another Lenovo laptop. Breaking down the percentage, 33.6% say they would buy the same model again. Meanwhile, 39.6% would buy a different model but stick to Lenovo.

Here’s why that might be. Lenovo offers a plethora of options to choose from based on your needs — while still evolving its laptops. For instance, the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 has an open M.2 slot for a second storage drive and an OLED screen for crisp, colorful images — making it perfect for gaming. Its Yoga two-in-ones let you seamlessly switch between a tablet and traditional laptop, while Lenovo’s ThinkPad and ThinkBook business laptops offer everything from ultralight 2-pound bodies to expanding rollable screens. And its new designs don’t sacrifice the must-have needs like long battery life, durability and chip efficiency that lend to strong performance.

Asus wins over nearly half of its laptop owners, with 47.5% giving it an exceptional value rating  — exceeding expectations for its price. Take our Editors’ Choice pick, the Asus Zenbook A14. It’s super thin and lightweight, but it’s still sturdy thanks to its Ceralumnium body. Plus, it has supreme 24-hour battery life, 1TB of storage and an OLED display — all for $1,200. While that’s more expensive than some laptops, it’s what’s included in that price that makes it worthwhile compared with other non-Apple laptop brands.

Asus is the top non-Apple laptop option to consider for tasks, with 47.7% of CNET readers giving it high ratings. That’s followed by 40.4% of Asus laptop owners who say it has very good task performance. When it comes to tasks, 37% primarily use their Asus laptops for work, while 5% use theirs for gaming.

Asus is well known for having lightweight laptops with all-day-and-night battery life and stunning display quality. Asus laptops like the Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 have a good port selection, which could be good for gaming, work or simply connecting different devices without the need for additional adapters. And the Asus Zenbook S 14 has a strong neural processing unit that contributes to its high-speed AI performance.

Asus scores highest for its screen brightness and clarity, with over half (51%) extremely satisfied with its screen quality and brightness, while 38.6% say they’re satisfied, giving Asus an overall satisfaction rate of 90%. One common thread we noticed in Asus laptops is their OLED screens, which deliver high-resolution video and graphics. Asus laptops also combine stunning display quality with excellent performance and at surprisingly low prices for all of their features.

For example, the Asus Zenbook 14 isn’t the highest-quality OLED we’ve seen, but it still produces clear text and graphics on a 14-inch screen, along with exceptional black levels, Elliott said. That’s still better than LCDs that many other non-MacBooks have, and could be the reason Asus owners rate it so highly in this category.

Dell wins our readers over as a top choice for high-end laptops. One-third (33.3%) of Dell owners spent over $1,500, and of that percentage, 15.2% spent over $2,000.

Dell’s premium laptops largely cater to business and gaming with their standout features and performance. The Alienware 16X Aurora is Dell’s midrange gaming laptop with user-replaceable RAM, a bright display and strong performance for $2,280. But if you want more gaming features, Dell has the Alienware 16 Area-51, which has even better gaming performance, upgradable RAM and three SSD slots for $2,530. And if you’re looking for a non-Mac alternative that comes close to MacBook quality and performance, the higher-end Dell XPS 14 is the one to choose. It has the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, Intel Arc B390 graphics and 1TB of storage for $1,950.

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,003 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from Sept. 1 to Oct. 10, 2026.

#3171. Healthcare REIT (AHR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Occupancy gains and margin expansion lifted full-year guidance this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

American Healthcare REIT, Inc. (AHR +3.34%) reported a transition into what management termed Phase 2 of its public lifespan, emphasizing platform enhancements and data-driven operational support for its regional partners. The company completed 2.1 billion in investments year to date, specifically targeting newer vintage senior housing assets in infill markets with high barriers to entry. Management increased its full-year 2026 earnings guidance based on sequential occupancy gains and expanded operating margins within its primary senior housing segments. The company also improved its leverage profile, reporting a net debt to annualized adjusted EBITDA ratio of 1.9x as it settled 1.88 billion in forward equity agreements during the quarter.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the American Healthcare REIT Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Alan Peterson, Vice President of Investor Relations and Finance. Alan, please go ahead.

Alan Peterson: Good morning. Thank you for joining us for American Healthcare REIT's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. With me today are Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Jeff Hanson; President and Chief Operating Officer, Gabe Willhite; Chief Investment Officer, Stefan Oh; and Chief Financial Officer, Aric Chang. On today's call, Jeff, Gabe, Stefan and Aric will provide high-level commentary discussing our operational results, financial position, our increased 2026 guidance and other recent news relating to American Healthcare REIT. Following these remarks, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. Please be advised that this call will include forward-looking statements.

All statements made during this call other than statements of historical fact are forward-looking statements that are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those projected in these statements. Therefore, you should exercise caution in interpreting and relying on them. I refer you to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of the risks that could impact our future operating results, financial condition and prospects. All forward-looking statements speak only as of today, November 6, 2026, or such other date as may otherwise be specified.

We assume no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise, except as required by law. During the call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, which we believe can be useful in evaluating the company's operating performance. These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP. Reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures discussed on this call to the most directly comparable measures calculated in accordance with GAAP are included in our earnings release, supplemental information package and our filings with the SEC.

You can find these documents as well as an audio webcast replay of this conference call on the Investor Relations section of our website at www.americanhealthcarereit.com. With that, I'll turn the call over to AHR's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Jeff Hanson.

Jeffrey Hanson: Thanks, Alan, and good morning, everyone. Last quarter, I discussed the durability of AHR's competitive advantages and our progress in scaling this company with both ambition and discipline to drive compounding earnings growth for shareholders. This quarter, I'd like to advance that story one step further. First, the headline results for the quarter. Total same-store NOI growth of 13.8%, our 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth with both our SHOP and ISHC or Trilogy segments benefiting from increasing operating spreads and significant margin expansion as well. Another increase in full year guidance, which now implies at the midpoint, full year NFFO per diluted share growth of over 30% versus last year.

Strong external growth with $2.1 billion in completed investments year-to-date and an awarded pipeline of more than $1 billion, a significant portion of which was secured on relationship, not price. None of that pipeline is reflected in our revised guidance, and all of it is expected to be match funded with proceeds from our unsettled forward sale agreements. And lastly, efficient balance sheet management as we continue to materially deleverage while generating significant growth, which is highlighted by net debt to EBITDA of just 1.9x at quarter end. These figures matter individually, but what matters more is what they say collectively. Our strategy is working, and it's fueling our ability to build on our track record for continued growth.

AHR has multiple engines of value creation working simultaneously. organic operating growth, accretive external investment, internally generated development and an increasingly sophisticated operating platform. And we've accelerated growth and upgraded portfolio quality while simultaneously strengthening the balance sheet, which is positioning us with real capacity to keep playing offense going forward. Put simply, this is not just a larger AHR, it's a more capable AHR, one in which our platform's core competencies are increasingly working together as an integrated system to produce consistently strong results that are beginning to compound. The sector tailwind is not the AHR advantage as we often say internally. Our platform and our execution is.

The team will run through the operating details in a moment, but the progression you'll hear is important. These results are proof points that our operating model is creating tangible value. We believe high-quality real estate is imperative, but not sufficient to produce the best results. Superior results are achieved by partnering with the strongest operators and enhancing their ability to execute. As an operating REIT, we increasingly think about AHR as a dynamic operating platform. The model combines institutional scale, resources and capital with proven regional operating expertise and then surrounds those operators with resources that can make already strong businesses even better. That's where durable value is created. And it all starts in our communities.

The quality of care and outcomes our operating partners deliver every day is the foundation of everything that we do. Strong clinical outcomes earn trust and trust is ultimately what drives occupancy, rate and payer mix. In our business has done well, quality of care and financial performance move together. Turning to external growth. The headline is more opportunity, same standard. Our external growth activity remains significant, but the emphasis must remain where it belongs. Long-term per share value creation is the objective, and that's the driving force behind everything that we've done this year. Importantly, external growth is not simply adding NOI. It's reshaping the quality and risk profile of the enterprise.

We're allocating capital towards newer vintage senior housing in affluent, supply-constrained infill markets where operating growth and pricing power is embedded in real estate that's very difficult to replicate, which is a powerful combination. Our $3 billion plus of closed and pipeline investments represent assets that are all accretive to first year NFFO, accretive to NAV per share, enhance overall portfolio quality and are expected to be meaningful contributors to both NFFO per share growth and same-store NOI growth for years to come. Importantly, these $3 billion in investments reflect an average vintage of 2019, representing some of the highest quality senior housing product in some of the best markets in the country.

On our August call, I described our approach to today's sector opportunity as measured aggression. We'll continue to move decisively when quality, basis, operator, market and expected returns meet our standard. That combination, speed and execution when opportunity meets preparedness and patience when it does not is what we mean by the measured aggression reference. And given our reputation, our relationships and our track record, much of what we pursue never reaches the broader market. We're taking the same approach to scaling the platform. We've been deliberately investing in conjunction with and ahead of robust growth. Over the last several months, we've strengthened critical leadership capabilities across our finance, investments, strategic asset management and enterprise technology divisions.

These hires introduce added depth to an already strong team, and they're the architecture for the company we're scaling AHR into. Gabe will cover these details in a moment. I also want to recognize Brian Peay, who retired on September 30 after a decade of service. He helped guide AHR through a period of remarkable growth and our listing on the New York Stock Exchange, and he leaves us with a strong financial foundation. We're grateful for his leadership and for his support of a smooth transition, and we certainly wish him well in retirement. We're also pleased to welcome Aric Chang, who joined us on October 1.

Aric comes to AHR from Public Storage, an S&P 500 operating intensive REIT, where revenue management, data and capital deployment drive results. The same discipline is at the center of AHR's operating business. His experience brings together a rare combination of what the next phase of AHR requires. We welcome Aric, and you'll hear from him later in the call. I'd like to close with a central point. The demographic opportunity in the sector is certainly extraordinary, but it will not determine the winners. Expertise and execution will. We believe AHR is increasingly positioned at the intersection of historically strong sector fundamentals and an integrated operating and capital allocation platform built to convert those fundamentals into superior long-term shareholder value.

We remain early in this opportunity, and we're intensely focused on ensuring that the best version of AHR is still ahead of us. With that, I'll turn the call over to Gabe, who will walk you through the operating results and other important details from the quarter.

Gabriel Willhite: Thanks, Jeff. 2026 marks a new phase for AHR. Trilogy's focus on care also shows up in its overall CMS star ratings across the portfolio, which are now sitting at 4.2 stars and its quality measure ratings, which are now sitting at 4.8 stars on average, both industry-leading among the largest skilled nursing operators in the country. Turning to SHOP. This quarter by every measure was a standout. Same-store NOI grew 28.2% year-over-year, accelerating from 20.5% in the second quarter and growing 9.1% sequentially. Same-store occupancy averaged 90%. Same-store revenue grew 9%, driven by accelerating RevPOR growth of 5.4% year-over-year. And notably, ExPOR grew just 0.8%. So the RevPOR to ExPOR spread expanded to roughly 460 basis points.

That widening spread unlocks tremendous value and propelled same-store NOI margin expansion of 350 basis points year-over-year to 23.5% and ultimately, strong NOI growth. When we say that execution matters, this is what we're talking about. Demographics alone do not do that work for us. All of the work that we continue to do to ensure our operators have the full strength and backing of our platform is having an effect as we evaluate the results we've achieved. And we will continue to evaluate opportunities to further enhance our operating capabilities across our portfolio through data and analytics, the Trilogy platform, our innovation forums and our strategic asset management.

It's important to note the scale of our SHOP segment has grown materially. SHOP now spans 109 properties and over 10,000 units, up from 71 properties and over 5,700 units a year ago. We're excited to have these assets on our platform and I have no doubt that our strategy of pairing the highest quality assets with the highest quality operators will allow us to continue to build upon the results we've already achieved. And in furtherance of that mission, I'm excited to expand on some of our talent acquisition.

Ann Lacey joined us in September as Executive Vice President, Portfolio and Asset Management for Senior Housing, and her mandate is to drive our multimodal operator support system across our growing portfolio. Ann is a highly capable expert who will draw from a rare and sought-after background. Jon Crosier, our new Chief Technology Officer, is leading the data and technology strategy that, among other things, puts the revenue management, analytics and reporting tools we built alongside Trilogy in the hands of more of our regional operating partners every quarter. Jon will draw on experience in both the public and the private sector, having worked at the Irvine Company, one of the most sophisticated private real estate companies in the U.S. And also just this week, we added the Jon's team from the health care REIT industry, further enhancing our capabilities. Stefan K. Oh: Thanks, Gabe. The third quarter was transformative for our SHOP portfolio. We meaningfully enhanced the quality of the portfolio through our recent acquisitions. Beyond those 2 deals, we have closed $800 million of investments this year that have been a continuation of our strategy to expand with many of our existing regional operating partners in the markets where they already excel. Looking ahead, our awarded pipeline stands at over $1 billion, which includes newly awarded deals as well as those previously disclosed.

Aric Chang: Thanks, Stefan, and thank you, Jeff, for the kind words. Before I get into the numbers, a brief word. For months before I joined, I watched this team execute on the plan AHR committed to. Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. Farrell, Jeff Hanson. Good question. Thank you for that. Gabriel Willhite: And Farrell, it's Gabe. I'd just add an important nuance to that. We don't view operators as commodities that can be traded. Jeffrey Hanson: And Stefan alluded to it briefly in his prepared remarks, our relative size advantage, and I think this is important. So they can come in as kind of a high-end consulting agency and take maybe underperforming assets or even the highest performing assets and make them better with our asset management team. All those things come together, and that's what creates the value, and that's what leads to outperform.

Operator: Your next question is from Michael Carroll with RBC Capital Markets.

Michael Carroll: I wanted to dig into Trilogy's results a little bit more. I know that, Gabe, you mentioned that they have some expense saving initiatives in place and the controllable expenses actually declined year-over-year. Can you give us a little bit of details on why the controllable expenses declined? What did they do? And is this just kind of a onetime decline? Or is this going to be ongoing over the next several quarters? Yes. So...

Gabriel Willhite: Trilogy does a lot of things well. All credit to them. If the Trilogy team is listening to this call, thank you, guys. We appreciate you, and we -- and I know you know that already, but I want the world to know it as well. So it's not -- for them, it's everything. They look at everything all the time. They're constantly looking at how they can run their business more efficiently. This quarter, it just happened to be looking at employee benefits and getting some cost savings around employee benefits without eroding the quality of those benefits is what they were able to capture.

So it is more of a onetime thing, Mike, but also at the same time, it's not -- it's repeatable because it's Trilogy being Trilogy, just finding ways to optimize the business, expand the margin and grow NOI and the best alignment in the industry.

Michael Carroll: Okay. Great. And then just looking at like the broader portfolio, I know we spent a lot of time talking about SHOP and the Trilogy portfolio. What about the other assets? I mean, is there an opportunity to maybe sell some noncore assets? Is that something that the company is looking at a little bit more in focus as you're being -- growing much more significantly in other parts of the portfolio?

Jeffrey Hanson: Sure. Yes, Jeff here. Thanks, Mike. Yes, we always do, as you know. First of all, our RIDEA vertical, both SHOP and Trilogy is the go-forward engine for AHR. So our capital, our platform expansion efforts and our external growth is exclusively focused there. I think what you're asking is as it relates to the OM portfolio, and I'll say what I think I said in the Q&A last quarter, we understand the value that's embedded in that portfolio. We've already sold 1/3 of the assets. We've taken NOI contribution from 35% down to roughly 10%, and that continues to drop rapidly. That's by design. And we've been net sellers will continue to be.

We're always looking for ways to drive long-term shareholder value and seeking optionality in doing so.

Operator: Your next question is from Wes Golladay with Baird.

Wesley Golladay: Maybe just sticking with the topic of dispositions. There is a strong transaction market for senior housing. Do you have any interest over the next year or so selling into that, maybe some of your older assets that no longer fit the go-forward criteria?

Gabriel Willhite: Yes. Thanks, Wes. We're constantly looking at the portfolio and evaluating disposition candidates. Sometimes it's because they're older and noncore. Sometimes it's because we feel like we've gotten all the value out of it that we can, and we've taken it to the highest level, and that might be a market-driven decision. At the end of the day, it might be you're looking at your micro markets and where new supply is coming. So tracking that is pretty critical to seeing where you might have vulnerability. So we are doing that. We -- and it's something we'll continue to do. Nothing to announce just yet on what types of dispositions you might expect for 2027.

But I'd expect early in 2027, we may have more to report there.

Wesley Golladay: Okay. And then with the election results earlier in the week, did anything stand out to you, either positive or negative at the local level?

Gabriel Willhite: At the national level, I think it's most relevant to Trilogy's business. And having a split Congress and White House means that the base case for us is that there's not going to be a lot of change in the skilled nursing industry, both from a regulation perspective and a reimbursement perspective. So I think it's business as usual there and predictability in an environment where Trilogy has been able to drive outperformance seems to be a favorable outcome. At the local level, nothing to really highlight just yet. We'll see how things play out.

Of course, we are always tracking what states we're in and what's happening in those states to make sure that we're regarding our risks from regulation as well. And I think at this point, nothing meaningful that's going to change our strategy.

Operator: Your next question is from Austin Wurschmidt with KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Austin Wurschmidt: Just going back to Trilogy for a minute, recognizing NOI growth hasn't slowed. You have seen revenue growth slow a little bit for maybe some of the reasons you highlighted on the call of occupancy being a little bit higher, even though that does continue to ratchet up. But can the Med Advantage opportunity and just Q mix shifts that you've talked about as well as the opportunity set on the private pay senior housing side of the business, can those increases continue to drive or drive re-acceleration in the top line over time?

Gabriel Willhite: Yes. And I think a part of that, Austin, is Trilogy's unique business, having this integrated campus model. So for those unfamiliar, Trilogy has got post-acute care and private pay senior housing under one roof. And those 2 businesses have almost opposite inflection points on seasonality, where the senior housing part of the business from an occupancy perspective is strongest at the end of the summer and in the early fall. At the same time, the skilled nursing occupancy tends to be the weakest, and they are at vastly different revenue numbers, right?

So the post-acute care business might be 2x or 3x what the Trilogy private pay business is on the senior housing side, but with a margin that is correspondingly half or 1/3 of what the senior housing margin would be. So the NOI works out to, on a per bed basis back of the napkin kind of roughly similar.

So you're seeing good NOI growth and maintained NOI numbers, but you might see a more nuanced thing on the revenue side of Trilogy, where there's a mix shift happening where there's more people in senior housing beds at a lower revenue rate than there are on the skilled nursing side, and it looks like a decel in revenue when actually it's just Trilogy's business as usual. To the overarching question of how can Trilogy grow and how long can this last?

That is the question that we've been asked every quarter for the last 11 quarters and every quarter for the last 11 quarters, Trilogy has surprised us on how well they can continue to grow and the different levers that they find to grow. Part of that is the alignment, like Jeff said, not only do we have a great RIDEA contract, but we had -- we were the first people in the space to create an operator incentive equity plan where Trilogy's long-term incentive plan is actually paid in AHR stock. So they're riding the wave of the value creation at Trilogy and fully aligned to do that. I wouldn't bet against them.

Austin Wurschmidt: Yes. And we're going to keep asking you don't worry within the non-same-store pool portion of Trilogy, I mean, it's still half of Trilogy's overall portfolio. I think you're approaching about 1 year since you guys acquired the Kingston portfolio. You're adding IL Villas. How does the growth compare within that pool of assets relative to the same-store pool? And anything specific we should be thinking about as we head into next year?

Gabriel Willhite: Yes. So maybe the most undervalued part of our entire platform is Trilogy's development capabilities, right, and how that flows through in the Trilogy non-same-store. So we have Trilogy doing 3 to 5 new campuses a year of development. They're de-risked. Trilogy has built over 80 properties themselves, developed themselves, and they value engineered the prototype. So we get asked a lot of questions how can you actually still do development in Trilogy? How does it make sense when nobody else really is. That's part of the reason. It's the value engineering of the building, not only from a cost perspective from -- but also from an operations perspective.

It's taking -- stripping out the developer returns that are part of the development. And now Trilogy is actually doing their own general contractor work on some of the projects as well, which further takes the cost down. So as those enter the total portfolio pool when they come online, they do provide a growth opportunity that I think is going to be sustainable and repeatable over the long term. And like I said, 3 to 5 campuses a year is what Trilogy kind of -- you can expect from Trilogy.

But on top of that, we have over 30 campuses with excess land or a direct path to excess land where we can do campus expansions at Trilogy, which are typically private pay senior housing, either IL or memory care or assisted living expansions. Those have great returns, maybe smaller dollars attached to the overall project. On the Kingston portfolio, specifically, that's a deal that we closed at the end of 2025, where Trilogy is a great operator, is able to take over assets and start to implement their own operational plans in those assets. We're seeing really good progress within those buildings.

And I think they will fuel the -- they'll be -- they'll enter the same-store pool, I believe, next year, and they'll fuel some powerful same-store NOI growth next year as well.

Operator: Your next question is from Michael Lewis with Truist Securities.

Michael Lewis: I was hoping I'd be the one that asked the election question, so I could say the term bluenami, which I think is fun to say. Instead, I'm going to ask about acquisitions. You talked about going into new regions of the country, maybe higher quality and price per pound was up. So are going-in yield and expected stabilized yield changing because of the mix or maybe just because things got more expensive for levered buyers or for any reason? And a second part of that, how do you feel about the acquisitions you made prior to 3Q versus the product you're buying now? Would you still buy it today?

Stefan K. Oh: Thanks for the question, Michael. So I guess just to answer your second question first. I mean, obviously, we're very proud of the acquisitions that we did prior to 3Q. I mean maybe the Kensington portfolio and the LCB portfolio, maybe there's a different geographic layout and maybe a quality difference in terms of the build-out and such. But at the end of the day, all of the acquisitions we're doing are really based around what is the performance level, what is the -- what can the operator do in these properties? Are these long-term assets where they are going to be competitive for many years to come.

I think there's definitely with some of the assets that we've recently acquired a built-in fortress there where these markets are not going to be seeing a lot of supply increase -- it's just very difficult to build in these areas. There's a lot a long process that goes -- that has to happen for someone to do that. But at the end of the day, it's all a matter of what is the long-term performance that we can generate out of our entire portfolio. And I think we've built a very good mix of assets that are going to continue to do that.

To your first question about price per unit, I think, again, it just plays into where are we buying, what is the quality of the real estate, what is the age. But -- and again, what is the ability to actually build in those locations. We're just not going to see a whole lot. And these are very high-performing assets that are generating very good RevPOR based on the fact the quality is very high. The rates are very good. And they're serving a market that is for a more affluent customer. So that's just a factor of the type of assets, has nothing to do necessarily with the yields or the pricing.

All of that has remained consistent throughout our entire portfolio and all the acquisitions we've been doing recently. So that's not a function of us paying more or accepting less of a yield from these assets. And at the end of the day, too, even though maybe there's some of these assets that are being priced at a higher per unit, they're still all below replacement costs. So we know that they're good investments for us, and they're going to be protected investments as well.

Jeffrey Hanson: And Mike, Jeff here. Thanks, Stefan. I'd add the entire $3-plus billion for context here, that's closed year-to-date plus pipeline, the yields are consistent with everything that we've been communicating all year long, mid-5s to mid-6s initial stabilized real yields -- initial yields was stabilized above 7%. And with 2019 vintage, it's some of the highest quality, best located senior housing product in the country. And Stefan referred to high barrier to entry and also as a distinction, fortress markets.

What we mean by fortress markets is much of what we bought, not all, but much of what we bought this year is in fortress markets where it's 5 to 8 to 9 years concept to delivery because there is no developable land. You have to assemble parcels to go through the entitlement process and then develop or redevelop. And in terms of higher price per unit, the economics support it. Kensington is a perfect example. All those assets are in these fortress markets.

They're super high acuity, almost 100% -- well, 100% of 7 of those 8 assets, all 7 that they built, purpose-built for their plan is all AL and memory care with RevPOR between 16,000 to 26,000 units. So the economics are fully supported. And you've got not only additional occupancy lift in everything we're buying this year, but also enhanced pricing power with material barrier to entry -- barrier to entry, rather.

Gabriel Willhite: And one more thing we haven't touched on that I want to bring up because I think people are just getting this wrong by quoting price per unit too much. We're seeing the boomer generation wanting more space and focus on bigger units. So the price per unit that you might be thinking of historically in senior housing for a studio room is -- that is not what we're buying. We're buying the bigger units, which is where the demand is showing up the most. Many times, there's 2 bedroom units that people are wanting to move into.

So maybe we need to shift as an industry to start talking more about the price per square foot and how much amenity space there is and what those amenities look like because all of that goes into that per pound equation that we're talking about. So I think if you're out there buying studio AL right now, you may -- I like where we're positioned on a relative basis where we have more bedrooms, bigger units. Oftentimes, we have 2 bedrooms and they're highly amenitized buildings. I think that's where the demand is going to be the highest. We could be wrong. We could be making the wrong bet, of course, but I like where we're at.

Jeffrey Hanson: And everything we bought this year is still below replacement cost. So that's a good cross-check.

Michael Lewis: Great. Maybe I cheated, I asked a multipart question there. But my second question, given the cost of equity and the cost of debt, -- is it safe to assume you're going to fund all your capital needs with equity for the foreseeable future? And to the extent you could talk about it, how much forward equity capacity do you like to have in reserve at any given time?

Aric Chang: Mike, it's Aric. Great question. So I'll clarify one thing, like based on the visibility we have on the pipeline and then some, we don't have any plan to go out to the market. We are fully funded for that pipeline. To ask your question, whenever we do go to the market, we intend to have match-funded opportunities. So we are raising capital with identified accretive investments. Now in the terms of -- you asked about sort of capacity and what we like to have. Again, it would be based on the opportunities at hand.

Operator: Your next question is from Dave Rogers with Raymond James.

David Rodgers: Just one question for me to follow up on maintenance CapEx of Trilogy. It looks like it's growing much faster than the size of the portfolio. Just not sure if that was related to some acquisitions and deferred CapEx that you saw specifically there. And then maybe just a broader question around how much deferred CapEx are you seeing as you're looking at assets and as that acquisition pipeline for SHOP or within the Trilogy business continues to grow.

Aric Chang: Well, one thing is on the maintenance CapEx that we've disclosed, it's only on the total portfolio basis. So that is sort of a reflection of -- as we increased the portfolio in the campuses.

Gabriel Willhite: Yes. And not only that, that's spot on. Not only that, but the Kingston portfolio that we bought, we built in some maintenance CapEx into that, that we knew about when we came into the deal. So you're seeing that show up in the numbers as well.

Operator: Your next question is from Seth Bergey with Citi.

Seth Bergey: I just wanted to follow up with some of the kind of hiring that you've done and specifically on the technology side. Can you go into a little bit more detail on kind of what technology capabilities or initiatives that you'd kind of like to add to the platform that maybe you don't currently have?

Gabriel Willhite: Yes. It's a combination of enhancing what we already have and adding to it. So it's not just adding new things, it's making things better. We want market data and intel that our investments team can use to be a competitive advantage when we're evaluating sites. Some of that means tapping into the data that we already have to use it more efficiently. Some of that is looking at the alternative data sources where we feel like it's giving us an edge. We're looking at things that may be other -- may be different than what the world broadly is looking at.

On the asset management side, it's about further building out the connection points with our operators, so we have more insight faster into what's going on within the buildings beyond just the financial data that we're getting and really digging into the operational data so that we can give more insights and help them be better at executing their business plans. And it's layering on AI to those -- to all that data so that we can better use the data that we have. Jon Crosier, our new CTO, has been at the company for a little over 2 months now, and everybody is excited about the progress that we made in that short amount of time.

I think getting better on this front is really exciting right now. The senior housing business is one that rewards innovation, and it shows up in the NOI. So we're going to lean in and be innovators in the space, use the information that we have and use our new tech team to help drive total portfolio performance.

Seth Bergey: Great. And then maybe just a second, I want to follow up on some of the comments you made earlier around kind of SHOP and Trilogy being the go-forward engines as a company and being not sellers of OM. -- would you kind of look to do that just kind of as you have been in terms of kind of one-off transactions as they arise? Or would you look to do that as a portfolio -- larger portfolio sale? And can you just talk about kind of the demand out there for outpatient medical and kind of the depth of the buyer pool that's out there for those types of assets?

Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. Thanks, Seth. This is Jeff. Look, we're opportunistic. As I've said before, I'll say it again, nothing's bolted down. It's a stable asset class. There's always -- the 35 years I've been in this business, there's always been strong demand from a variety of capital sources.

Operator: Your next question is from Nick Yulico from Scotiabank.

Nicholas Yulico: I just want to go back to the RevPOR growth in the third quarter in SHOP, 5.4%, that number that strengthened this year. I just want to make sure that there's not like a comp issue affecting that number this quarter, making it artificially high.

Gabriel Willhite: No, great question. That's not what's driving it. It's actual execution within each building operator by operator, building by building. And it's a focus on street rate, right? It's not one-off in-place increases that happened midyear. It's execution on especially the rent concession front. So as you get more occupied, it's not only do you have more pricing power on rate, but you should stop using rent concessions as much as well. So we actually took our rent concession number down 34% year-over-year because of a hyper focus on that. And that's kind of circling back to the question before on data and analytics and what are you providing to your operators and how do you leverage that?

It's many different operational data points that you're drawing from to say, hey, I think we've got an opportunity here. Let's go out and attack it. And the great thing about having great operators is when you bring those types of ideas to them, they actually can go out and execute.

Nicholas Yulico: Okay. Great. And then second question, Aric, for the balance sheet. I think you have the swaps maturing in January. I think the term loan as well. Just latest thoughts on refinancing.

Aric Chang: Yes. Great question. Obviously, with the maturity in January, we're working on that. Right now, we want to maintain flexibility and optionality there. So we'll get into exactly on '27 capital markets execution. One thing I will note is if you look at our Q, we did put in place a swap in October, and that's to hedge some of our floating rate exposure going into '27. It's basically effective in January '27 concurrently when the existing swaps mature and the term loan matures. So you know that we're being mindful of floating rate exposure and working on things.

Jeffrey Hanson: Yes. We're working on refi opportunities and alternatives now, and we'll advise accordingly.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Jeff Hanson, Chairman and CEO, for closing remarks.

Jeffrey Hanson: Well, thank you, ladies and gentlemen, for your continued support and confidence, and we hope everybody has a great weekend.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you so much for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3170. The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

The outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds.

The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term.

There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.

Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy.

"It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."

Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats.

For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031.

"The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.

It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.

If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities.

"It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.

Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close.

"Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said.

Other voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply.

Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said.

Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election.

"That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said.

Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted.

The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said.

"There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."

Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.

For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.

"At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.

Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."

Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds.

"The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

#3169. 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

#3168. Do You Speak Geek? 5 Tech Terms That Endure, and 5 That Got Defragged

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Level up your vocab with these tech phrases that'll give you major rizz.

Real talk: I’m not that up to speed on today’s tech vocabulary. That realization clocked me over the head this week when the Scotland-based Collins dictionary came out with its list of new and notable words for 2026. The words include p(doom), which refers to the probability of AI-caused doom; mogging, meaning to outshine or upstage someone; friendslop, a type of low-budget video game played among friends; and ghost jobs, jobs advertised with no real position or intent to hire someone.

Vibe-coding, which was Collins’ Word of the Year for 2025, refers to a conversational way to teach an AI model without typing in all that pesky code. Enshittification, which the American Dialect Society chose as its 2023 Word of the Year, means the gradual, profit-driven decline in the quality of, well, I guess, everything.

Maybe you know and use these terms regularly; maybe you don’t. But, in an effort to stop myself from becoming that Steve Buscemi faking-it-in-high-school meme, I wanted to lay out some tech terms that have a permanent home in the popular lexicon and the words, phrases and abbreviations that haven’t quite stood the test of time. (Note to self: Stop saying “emoticon.”)

Selfie: You know what a selfie is; my mother, on the other hand, may not. The word for taking a photo of yourself with any camera-enabled device was first coined in 2002 on an Australian internet chat forum, of all places, but didn’t become mainstream until 2013.

Content creator: “Influencer” also works here, to refer to a person who shares information on a tech platform and builds an audience of online followers. A related word, “parasocial,” refers to the one-sided relationship listeners or viewers may have with the creator or influencer, who, in contrast, doesn’t know they exist.

Podcast: The Oxford Dictionary named podcast the Word of the Year back in 2005. Since then, the term, which is a mashup of iPod and broadcast and refers to a digital program made available on-demand for streaming or download, has remained relevant. The iPod, however? Not so much. It was discontinued in 2022.

WFH (work from home): The trend of working from your own home via computer saw a substantial uptick during and after the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. According to a 2022 survey by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 23% of Americans work remotely.

Unfriend: The New Oxford American Dictionary‘s 2009 Word of the Year became popularized thanks to Facebook, but the term that means ending a friendship has actually been around for quite some time. NPR called it “the Sleeping Beauty of words,” as the term dates back to the 17th century, when it basically meant the same thing.

Metaverse: Remember when Mark Zuckerberg poured like $80 billion into a virtual reality project that was being touted as the internet platform of the future? The metaverse and its flagship app, Horizon Worlds, were announced in 2021. Five years later, it all fell apart. Now, Zuck is investing a ton in AI, which he’s touting as the internet technology of the future. Second verse, same as the first?

NFT: Just a couple of years ago, you couldn’t go online without reading about NFTs. Nonfungible tokens are digital identifiers to certify ownership of, well, a digital thing of value. Heck, remember when President Donald Trump released an NFT? After the boom in popularity, and the subsequent crash in value of most of them, the term NFT has all but left the public consciousness.

World Wide Web: It’s the internet, folks. Or, the information superhighway if you’re nasty.

Defrag: Back in my day, when we needed better performance from our Windows-based computers, we’d defragment the hard drive. There were plenty of tools you could use to do so. Apparently, this is no longer a thing people do, which is fun, since I still like to use the term in everyday situations. While we’re at it, I’ll be right back. I need to go defrag the car.

Emoticon: Technically, emoticons are made from standard keyboard characters read sideways, such as 🙂 to generate a smiley face. Emoji are graphical images that you can select in various communication programs. (Sometimes, if you try to type an old-school emoticon, the program you’re working in will just grab it and turn it into an emoji.) These days, we just say emoji, even if the word sounds more like a dessert.

Tesla will begin winding down production of the wedge-shaped pickup at its Texas Gigafactory “around the middle of next year,” Musk said, to boost manufacturing capacity for its Cybercab robotaxi.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

The Cybertruck will not be missed by many. Sales have been so low that Tesla doesn’t even separate them out in its financials — lumping it into an “Other models” column — with experts estimating numbers significantly lower than Tesla’s built-out manufacturing capacity and far below Musk’s sales goals. Meanwhile, Tesla and Musk have increasingly shifted their focus to AI, robotics and autonomy as the brand’s future.

Tesla unveiled the edgy, all-electric pickup truck at an event in 2019, and the cracks were already beginning to show in many of Musk’s most outlandish claims surrounding the truck. (In the case of the “bulletproof” glass, the cracks literally showed.)

After multiple delays, deliveries finally began in 2023. Musk had spent the intervening four years baffling people by making (and subsequently retracting) many truly bizarre statements about the EV’s capabilities, but the first nail in the Cybertruck’s coffin was the starting price, which had ballooned to $60,990, up from the initial $40,000 target touted at debut.

Customers were presented with a niche EV that was more expensive than expected, unsafe, unreliable, unpopular and unattractive. It’s no surprise that sales have suffered, with some experts predicting that since its arrival on US roads, Tesla has sold only about 10% of Musk’s Cybertruck goals. That’s despite Tesla building out an estimated 125,000-unit annual manufacturing capacity at the Texas Gigafactory where the truck is built, leaving the automaker with a huge stock of unsold, unwanted inventory sitting on its lots. One of Musk’s other companies, SpaceX, bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks last year.

The Cybertruck’s 2027 wind-down will make way for increased capacity for the fully autonomous Cybercab, which debuted in 2024 and is slated to ramp up production in Texas next year. Pitched as a robotaxi that you could own for “under $30,000,” Tesla began offering rides in its steering-wheel-free Cybercab in limited parts of Austin in early September — a stunt that immediately prompted a federal investigation into whether the self-driving vehicle meets federal safety standards.

The Cybertruck joins the Model S and X on Tesla’s 2026 chopping block. The electric sedan and SUV were discontinued in January to make room for production of the Optimus humanoid robot at Tesla’s factory in Fremont, California. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. There are a handful of things Apple’s iPhone Duo and Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 have in common. They both feature a passport-size design, two rear cameras and roughly the same battery capacity. They’re also two of my favorite phones I’ve reviewed this year.

The compact, book-style configuration feels like the future of foldables, and Apple and Samsung have each nailed their offerings. Both phones are incredibly versatile, giving you the option to quickly swipe through apps on the palm-sized cover display or open up to a more sprawling 7.6-inch inner screen that’s great for watching videos and multitasking. That innovation comes at a cost, though, with the Duo starting at $1,999 for 256GB and the Z Fold 8 starting at $1,900 for the same storage level.

There are some drawbacks to having a more compact design, namely when it comes to the rear cameras. There’s no telephoto camera on either phone, which can make the high price tags a little harder to swallow. Plus, the wide and ultra-wide cameras aren’t quite as capable as what you’ll get on premium non-folding phones such as the iPhone 18 Pro and Galaxy S26 Ultra, which have more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors.

Still, the iPhone Duo’s and Z Fold 8’s cameras are nothing to scoff at. The Duo has a 48-megapixel wide and 48-megapixel ultrawide camera, as well as a 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen and a FaceTime camera on the inner display (Apple hasn’t shared the resolution). Meanwhile, the Z Fold 8 has a 50-megapixel wide and 50-megapixel ultrawide camera, plus 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the cover and inner displays. That means you should still get photos that impress, whether you’re in the brightly lit outdoors or in a dark, moody setting.

To compare the cameras, I took the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 to Filoli, a historic house and garden in the San Francisco Bay Area. These are some of my favorite shots, highlighting the strengths and unique characteristics of each phone’s cameras.

Both phones do a great job depicting the vibrancy of the lush background, but the iPhone Duo has the edge here. It better preserves the detail in the stone bench and flooring, and the greenery takes on a deeper, more satisfying hue.

These photos turned out very similarly, and both are equally dazzling. But the Z Fold 8 image is slightly sharper, as seen in the lines on the tree bark and the brighter, more pigmented greenery and flora. So I’m giving this one to the Z Fold 8.

These portrait images highlight some of the key differences in color and tone between the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8. I prefer the richer blacks and more vibrant colors captured by the iPhone Duo. It also does a better job of keeping the raven in focus, allowing the bird to stand out more distinctly against the background and creating a more striking overall image. By comparison, the Z Fold 8 produces a softer, gentler look, with a more subdued overall tone.

I like the brightness of the iPhone Duo image, and while the Z Fold 8 shot has slightly deeper shadows, the hydrangeas are also more vibrant. The blues and greens pop more on the Z Fold 8, as does the sky, which is a little washed out on the Duo. So this one goes to the Z Fold 8.

I keep flipping on this one, but ultimately, the richer colors and texture on the Duo image have won me over. The iPhone’s camera tends to cast a warmer glow, as you can see in the stone benches, while the Z Fold 8 takes on a more neutral tone. In the end, the differences are subtle and a matter of personal preference.

And finally, here’s me unwinding with a book. By default, the iPhone Duo applies a pleasing background blur, which I appreciate for the added dramatic effect. (This effect can be disabled when taking a photo, but I rarely choose to do so.) The Z Fold 8, by comparison, keeps the distant lawns and forested hills in sharper focus, preserving those details remarkably well. Ultimately, I prefer the Duo’s approach, which keeps the book in sharper focus and makes it stand out from the background. That said, I do appreciate the Z Fold 8’s ability to capture finer details throughout the scene, particularly the crisp individual blades of grass.

Because I’m a fan of both the iPhone Duo and the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it’s difficult to wholeheartedly recommend one camera over the other. Each has its strengths, and there are moments where one preserves detail and color better than the other.

In general, photos from the iPhone Duo tend to have warmer tones and richer, deeper colors, which can also lead to more pronounced shadows. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 often produces brighter images, though this can sometimes come at the expense of finer details. But these results can vary depending on factors such as lighting and angles.

Ultimately, both foldable phones deliver impressive results, and the choice comes down to which image characteristics you value most. Thankfully, you really can’t go wrong with either.
