#3161. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

Management reported that core growth in the commercial aftermarket offset the headwind from the intentional elimination of low-margin pass-through material revenue. Operational focus centered on scaling the LEAP engine program and expanding component repair capabilities through internal development and strategic acquisitions.

Then inside that, Seth, I would say I'm particularly confident about the positioning of StandardAero and what we can do as a partner to CFM and what we can do for our customers, and that's proving itself every day as we win additional contracts.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Ronald Epstein with Bank of America.

Andrew Steinhardt: This is Andrew Steinhardt on for Ron. Congrats, Russ, on your retirement and Paul on the transition. I wanted to ask if you guys could quantify the impact of the pass-through eliminations on commercial revenue in Q3. What would underlying growth be excluding the pass-through eliminations? And for the full year, if you could ballpark commercial end market growth accounting for those eliminations, that would be helpful, too.

Daniel Satterfield: That's right. Yes. Commercial was, what, 1.3% growth. Excluding that, it's high single digits, you'll see that on the page. And then the -- for the full year commercial growth, we're calling high teens, ex material takeout.

Andrew Steinhardt: Could you quantify what's the takeout?

Daniel Satterfield: It's right. We think -- we called the material takeout for the full year, we were saying $350 million to $400 million. It's now going to be closer to $300 million. As you recall, in Q1, it was a minimal impact. Then Q2, it was significant and Q3 and Q4 are going to be right in line with expectations. We kind of lost the quarter, and we're saying the full material takeout impact instead of $350 million to $400 million would be closer to $300 million for the full year.

Andrew Steinhardt: Got you. Okay. And just on CRS margins, can you talk about how the work migration efforts have progressed since last quarter?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. There's a great opportunity there that between -- that we launched between our -- some of our back shops and the Cincinnati site, where capability and on that repair was already in place. That continues to occur. There are even more opportunities out in the future that we're going to take advantage of across our -- we have 50 sites in total at StandardAero. Most of the MRO sites have what are called back shops that do component repair for the engines in the shop, right, for a quick turnaround. When these back shops have additional capability and capacity, that's an opportunity for the overloaded CRS sites to offload, and we're taking full advantage of that.

Paul McElhinney: Andrew, this is Paul. Just a couple of comments. Firstly, CRS is a very strategic part of the business. I've spent a lot of my career running repair businesses in the aftermarket. Quite apart from the fact that they're financially very attractive for the company, their impact on customers is very important and very impactful to their turnaround times, lowering the cost of maintenance. It's a key part of our offering to our customers. In the first 3 weeks here, I've spent time with our repair teams in both Dallas and Cincinnati, which are 2 of our larger repair locations. Demand is not an issue here. Commercial demand, very robust, I would say.

The entire focus of the team is on internal execution, increasing and improving throughput. You can expect me to be spending quite a bit of time with that team, and I look forward to sharing some of the results of the work we're doing here, improving that as we go forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Kristine Liwag with Morgan Stanley.

Kristine Liwag: Congrats, Russ. We'll miss you on the earnings call, and welcome, Paul. I guess, Paul, given your involvement in shaping the LEAP's aftermarket strategy in your prior role, how do you assess StandardAero's competitive position today? You must have seen good things for you to join the company. And are there any areas you want to invest in more or expand capabilities to be able to capture more market share or a greater share of the aftermarket economics as the platform matures?

Paul McElhinney: Thanks for the question, Kristine. The investments we did, the company has positioned itself extraordinarily well for LEAP. You're right, LEAP is near and dear to my heart as an engine product. It's exciting for me to now sit on this side of the table and be able to talk to customers about how we support them and their needs. We are quoting shop visit slots all the way out to the mid-2030s at this stage, really robust demand. I like where StandardAero is competitively. We will continue to invest -- you can expect us to continue to invest in repair development.

You can continue to expect us to work on attractive commercial offerings for our customers that allow them to lower their maintenance costs over time. But I feel really good about LEAP, and I feel good about what that will be candidly for StandardAero for 3 decades or more to come.

Kristine Liwag: Great. Super helpful. And if I could add a second question. On the 4Q CRS margins, the implied for the quarter will be 27.5%, so a sequential increase versus this quarter. So how do you -- how much visibility do you have into that recovery? And is that sequential margin expansion dependent on the return of the military programs you guys have previously discussed?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. Thanks, Kristine. The decline in margins that we called out had to do with some -- 2 things, really the residual effects from the labor ramp. Don't forget, the commercial business of CRS is booming. A lot of strong volumes there. Their volumes are being somewhat depressed because of the military issues that we mentioned before due to the outlay change as a result of the Middle Eastern conflict. What that has an impact on the margin rates is that military business is a pretty good business. Losing that has a negative mix impact. Then we have some residual effects from the labor ramp on the commercial business, which is quite strong.

That we're working through that we have a better line of sight to recovery than on the military side, which is dependent on the macro.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gavin Parsons with UBS.

Gavin Parsons: Russ and Paul, congrats to you guys both. Paul, I guess sort of echoing Seth's question a little bit on CRS, which you brought up as a priority. I've talked about. I mean it's a smaller growing business, but one that -- smaller business, but one that I would think would have more idiosyncratic growth opportunities. So I've been a little surprised that one has grown slower than ES for a couple of years now. So just any insights you can shed on that and how you might quantify the growth opportunity there over the medium term would be helpful.

Paul McElhinney: Thanks for the question, Gavin. CRS is very strategic for me, a very important part of our customer tool set and the offerings that we can give them. I would say, right now, I see a lot of demand. I see good backlog, and frankly, I'll spend my time on working with the teams and accelerating some of the efficiency, productivity, throughput, turnaround time activity that's already going on in the company. We have a lot of capacity across the network. Dan talked about the fact that we've been involved in this work transfer from Cincinnati to some of the other back shops. That's complicated work, frankly.

It's not something that happens overnight, but it is something that I intend to continue to focus on. I think you should expect to see CRS continue to be a big piece of the business in terms of strategic importance, both to us and to our customers. I intend to spend a fair amount of time with the team helping them get to where we need to be with the offerings.

Gavin Parsons: And then on the military side, I think you guys do have a lot of exposure to deployed assets, something like C-130, V-22. I mean any way to help us frame your exposure to those versus, say, the training platforms where the drag is today, rough order of magnitude?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. So we're really -- those are our fixed wing transport aircraft that we support, and they're in good shape. When we talk about the military issues, it is primarily related in large part to these training programs that are -- the demand is not going away, it will definitely come back. These are programs that the U.S. Air Force needs more pilots on. As far as the C-130 or the AE2100 and the Osprey or the 1107 programs, those are looking good. That's why we're having still a strong military guide, low double digits for the full year.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Andre Madrid with U.S. Bancorp.

Edward Morgan: This is Ned Morgan on for Andre. Russ, congrats on a great tenure as CEO. And Paul, we look forward to working with you. As we start thinking about '27, I understand you're not going to provide any guidance today, but are you willing to rank the growth outlook across commercial, business aviation and military?

Daniel Satterfield: The 2027 guide, we're going to give you better information on that in February.

Russell Ford: It should be roughly about the same. I mean it's just the general growth of those end markets, right?

Edward Morgan: Okay. And then another GE lowered its CFM56 retirement outlook. Just curious on the puts and takes of that for you guys and what it means for you on the CFM56 platform?

Paul McElhinney: Yes. CFM56, a very strong platform for us. It's still actually quite early in the life cycle of that motor. 2/3 of those engines have not even seen their second shop visit yet. I think that you're going to see continued strength certainly in StandardAero on CFM56, a lot of customer demand for us, constrained capacity. But yes, as I look at that program, I see continued growth. The retirement rate, which GE called to 1.5% to 2% of the fleet, frankly, not having an impact on the demand that we're seeing for slots from our customers.

Russell Ford: And Ned, keep in mind, the OEMs, when they refer to their shop visits, it's shop visits of 500 labor hours or more. It doesn't include module swaps, exchanges, those type of things that we do quite a bit of.

Paul McElhinney: Thanks very much. Thank you all for joining us and for your continued interest in our company, and we look forward to sharing more details with you on our next call.

#3158. The built-in iPhone app for creativity you may be ignoring (but shouldn't)

Apple's free digital whiteboard lets you organize messy ideas, sketch plans and work with others without another subscription.

Your iPhone is great for capturing screenshots you'll likely never revisit. So organizing all that mess into something coherent might be just what you need. Apple's Freeform app has been available on iPhones since 2022, giving you room to spread out ideas instead of adding them to another list.

It's a digital whiteboard with an infinite canvas, so you can organize photos, sketches, links, and PDFs in any way you want. From there, you can connect them and change your mind without having to rewrite everything. The Freeform app is good for visual plans that are easier to show than explain, and others can participate too.

Now, Freeform isn't some miracle app that can organize your life, but it could be just the thing that makes your next messy project less of a headache. Best of all, the app is free.

When you open a new Freeform board, you're presented with a blank canvas that expands as you add to it. You can use your finger to scribble on the board, add a photo or sticky note, and drag items around until they begin to make sense. It also lets you draw arrows between related items, zoom out to see the bigger picture or zoom in to work on smaller details. An Apple Pencil isn't required, either, although iPhone Duo owners running iOS 27.2 or later can use the Apple Pencil (USB-C) to sketch directly in Freeform.

It also allows for videos, PDFs, website links, and text boxes. Photos app and Safari can also send images and links directly to a board from the Share menu, without copying and pasting.

You could storyboard a video by laying out reference images and notes for each shot, then shuffle the scenes around as your ideas evolve. Or sketch out a DIY project on the canvas, where drawings and measurements are right where you need them. But things like your grocery list, for instance, probably don't need an infinite whiteboard.

Since its introduction with iOS 16.2, Freeform has gained Dark Mode and folders in iOS 27. On compatible iPhones, Image Playground can also create illustrations for boards, but Freeform itself doesn't require Apple Intelligence.

You can also invite others to a Freeform board and see their changes in real time. That means a group can plan a vacation or collaborate on a project without having to search through message threads. Boards are synced via iCloud to iPhone, iPad, and Mac, and if you have a crowded board, you'll be glad to have the larger screen on an iPad or Mac.

There is one tiny hiccup, though. Everyone on the board needs a compatible Apple device, an Apple Account with two-factor authentication, and Freeform turned on in iCloud. There's no Android app or browser-based editor, so a cross-platform whiteboard like Miro would be more appropriate for mixed-device groups. Alternatively, if someone just needs to view the final product, the board can be exported as a PDF.

There are downsides to the expanding canvas, as well. Bigger boards can be hard to maneuver, particularly on the smaller screen of an iPhone, but maybe this is a problem for the iPhone Duo to solve.

Board creation and sharing are still free. You don't need Apple's optional Creator Studio subscription, which costs $12.99 per month in the U.S., to do basic brainstorming, but it does provide access to premium assets, plus advanced AI image-generation tools on compatible iPhones. If you previously deleted Freeform thinking it was some Samsung-like bloatware, you can reinstall it from the App Store.

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3156. Nvidia Stock Has More Than 60% Upside According to Analysts' Average Price Target. Should You Buy While the AI Trade Wobbles?

Nvidia stock looks cheaper, and its growth prospects are well intact.

Investors are skeptical of many AI stocks right now, questioning the long-term return on investment for tech companies spending so much on data center infrastructure. And as a leading semiconductor company for AI infrastructure, Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%) has felt the pain from the sell-off, with its share price falling 13% over the past month.

That's put Nvidia's share price at around $202, far below analysts' average price target for Nvidia stock of $327. If it reaches that target, investors stand to gain around 62%. So, is now the right time to buy Nvidia stock, despite the concerns about AI spending?

I think so, especially given that recent tech earnings reports indicate tech companies are likely to continue investing in infrastructure over the next few years.

Let's start with SK Hynix's (SKHY +2.78%) recently reported third-quarter results. The company is the leading high-bandwidth (HBM) memory company with 50% market share and the second-largest DRAM and NAND flash memory company with 24% and 19% market share, respectively.

The company has benefited immensely from a ramp-up in AI spending, sending its sales 328% higher in the quarter and its operating profit up 632%. Even more impressive is that the company's management said in a press release that 50% of its available memory supply for 2027-2028 is already sold out -- and that it expects its supply to remain constrained through 2030.

What does this have to do with Nvidia? Well, SK Hynix is the leading supplier of HBM memory for many of Nvidia's data center components. If SK Hynix is experiencing exponential demand for its memory processors, part of that is due to Nvidia placing substantial orders. And if Nvidia is placing large orders for memory, it's because AI spending continues to rise.

This leads me to Alphabet's and Microsoft's recent cloud sales. These two companies hold a combined 35% of the cloud market, and they're both experiencing impressive sales gains from their AI spending. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the third quarter to $30.7 billion and Microsoft's Azure sales rose 48% to $33.2 billion.

Alphabet says it will spend up to $205 billion this year in capital expenditures (capex), mostly for AI. Microsoft says it will spend $170 billion in fiscal 2027. That's an acceleration of spending for both companies and it's a result of Microsoft and Alphabet realizing that their cloud investments are paying off.

And they're not the only ones. Bank of America said recently that AI data center spending is estimated to more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028. While investors are rightly concerned that some AI spending is too high and won't be worth the investment, Alphabet and Microsoft are already benefiting from their spending and are doubling down.

Again, that's great news for Nvidia because these two companies are critical customers for Nvidia, and it's a good indicator that AI infrastructure investments aren't slowing down yet.

Nvidia's shares have a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 26 right now, which makes them slightly cheaper than the tech sector P/E average of 28.5. Investors don't have to back the truck up and go all-in on Nvidia stock right now. But the recent pullback does present a buying opportunity for some investors to start a small position or add to an existing one.

The chipmaker will report its fiscal 2027's third quarter results on Nov. 17 and Wall Street's consensus estimates are for earnings per share of $2.47 and nearly $109 billion in sales. Considering Nvidia has beaten analysts' earnings estimates in seven of the past eight quarters, shareholders could be pleasantly surprised again soon.

More importantly, with Nvidia's customers already experiencing significant growth and continuing to invest in AI, Nvidia's long-term growth prospects remain intact.

You’ll also get an in-stay credit when you book a vacation home through The Edit for four nights or more.

Starting in 2027, Chase’s The Edit collection of upscale hotel and resort stays will broaden to include more than 10,000 vacation homes. If you carry the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, that means you’ll soon have more ways to use The Edit credits on those cards.

This addition will significantly expand The Edit’s footprint — currently at more than 1,500 hotels and resorts — although its usefulness will depend on your travel style. The new properties are curated in partnership with Plum Guide, a vacation-rental booking platform.

Plus, when you book a stay of four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use at your vacation home.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming changes to The Edit.

Eligible Chase cardholders can currently book vacation homes through the issuer’s travel portal. However, those bookings are not eligible to receive The Edit benefits. That changes Jan. 1, 2027, with select listings.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

#3154. IAMGOLD: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Essakane's cash flow is funding buybacks while the company holds more cash than debt, a position that leaves room to pursue 2027 catalysts.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, IAMGOLD (IAG +7.20%) announced it is repurchasing half of the gross margin royalty on its Côté Gold mine for $525 million. This transaction lowers operational cash costs at the company's flagship asset starting in 2027 while keeping a greater share of future cash flows. Three takeaways from management's presentation stand out for long-term investors.

IAMGOLD is using balance-sheet liquidity to repurchase half of the 7.5% gross-margin royalty on the Côté mine for $525 million. This transaction reduces Côté's cash costs, including royalties (fees paid to third-party rights holders based on mine revenue), by roughly $150 per ounce starting in 2027.

Operational performance at Côté reached a turning point during the quarter following the transition from contractor crushing to owner-operated crushing. Processing rates averaged 37,100 tons per day in September, surpassing the plant's nameplate capacity (its designed full-scale operating throughput target) of 36,000 tons per day.

Cash flow generated by the Essakane mine in Burkina Faso continues to fund IAMGOLD's share repurchases and debt reduction. The company has repurchased over 32 million shares for nearly $600 million since December 2025 while maintaining a net cash position (holding more cash than total debt).

Operations across key sites are executing steadily while cash flows reinforce financial strength. Operational efficiency, reserve expansion, and debt control underpin future asset value, while management monitors inflation in input costs.

Upcoming technical reports across the asset portfolio provide strategic catalysts through 2027.

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3152. SoundHound AI: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its shift from one-time license fees to recurring hosted subscriptions makes future revenue easier to forecast, a change worth weighing before the margin story.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, SoundHound AI (SOUN -3.52%) announced that it expects to reach sustainable profitability within the second half of 2027. It's swapping lumpy upfront software license fees for steady hosted subscriptions. Management is also cutting operational expenses across the business. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Upfront licensing deals historically created unpredictable swings in quarterly revenue. Management is now using its enterprise platform, OASYS -- which runs software agents across voice and text -- to convert those single-point customer commitments into steady annualized recurring revenue by positioning OASYS as a hosted service.

Integrating recent acquisitions allows the company to eliminate duplicate corporate functions, optimize cloud spending, and drop unprofitable customer contracts. Consequently, management expects to achieve positive adjusted EBITDA -- earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, which is a key measure of core operating profitability -- even at the low end of its revenue guidance.

Relying on external providers for complex software tasks drives up computing expenses for enterprise customers. SoundHound is migrating customer traffic to its proprietary models, cutting operating costs while improving processing speed and accuracy.

Quarterly revenue grew 48% year over year to a record $62.4 million, and enterprise demand for voice technology is accelerating. Management is institutionalizing financial discipline across the business.

SoundHound relies on structural advantages including over 800 patents and proprietary models that insulate it from third-party vendor fees. Management is watching pricing discipline and hosted customer transitions to drive long-term value.

#3151. 3 Dividend Stocks I'd Buy With $5,000 Before the End of November

Splitting $5,000 equally across these stocks would pay a blended dividend yield of about 3.5%.

Dividend stocks can turn savings into a growing stream of income. If I had $5,000 to invest in dividend stocks before the end of November, I'd split it equally among PepsiCo (PEP -0.96%), Hershey (HSY +0.37%), and Home Depot (HD -1.85%).

All three have long records of paying dividends, and research shows that companies that pay dividends have historically outperformed those that don't. According to Hartford Funds and Ned Davis Research, S&P 500 stocks that grew or initiated dividends returned about 10% per year from 1973 through 2025, versus about 4% for stocks that paid no dividends.

At Nov. 3 prices, investing $1,667 into each stock would earn about $176 a year in dividends, a blended yield of about 3.5% -- more than three times the S&P 500 average. Here's why now is a good time to buy these stocks.

PepsiCo sells some of the world's best-known snacks and drinks, from Doritos to Gatorade. A $1,667 investment would buy about 12 shares at current prices, yielding about $71 per year based on Pepsi's current annualized dividend of $5.92 per share.

The business is gaining momentum, especially overseas. Organic revenue, which excludes the impact of foreign currency fluctuations, grew 3% year over year in the third quarter -- the highest rate of growth since the fourth quarter of 2023. The international business performed well, with organic revenue up 8%.

PepsiCo is also cutting costs to fund more growth. CEO Ramon Laguarta said additional structural cost reductions "will be implemented in the coming months to help fund investments that aim to accelerate organic revenue growth."

The stock yields about 4.3%, and the dividend accounted for about 75% of trailing free cash flow (cash from operations minus business investments). This year marked PepsiCo's 54th consecutive annual dividend increase, making it a Dividend King (a category of companies that have increased their dividends for at least 50 years without interruption).

With international growth looking strong and management focused on reducing costs, Pepsi's high yield looks very attractive.

Hershey owns iconic treats like Reese's and Kit Kat, plus fast-growing salty snacks like Dot's pretzels. A $1,667 stake buys almost 10 shares, which would pay about $58 a year based on the annualized dividend of $5.808 per share.

Hershey's profits are rebounding as price increases and productivity savings kick in. Its adjusted gross margin jumped nearly 11 percentage points last quarter to about 43%. Management sees more progress ahead. CFO Dave Hulays said, "We do expect meaningful margin improvement in 2027."

Sales should grow, too. CEO Kirk Tanner reaffirmed that 2027 sales growth should land within the company's long-term range of 2% to 4%. He added that the 2027 innovation pipeline is 50% larger than this year's, citing new product ideas that could drive healthy sales.

It's a good bet that people won't lose their taste for chocolate, and Tanner described its convenience-store sales channel as a "robust category" that remains "resilient" despite consumer headwinds. The stock yields about 3.5%, and the dividend totaled about 55% of trailing free cash flow.

Hershey just declared its 387th consecutive regular dividend, payable on Dec. 15 to shareholders of record on Nov. 16. Its iconic brands and pricing power should continue to reward patient investors.

Home Depot is the world's largest home improvement retailer, with more than 2,300 stores. A $1,667 stake buys about five shares, which would pay about $47 a year based on the annualized dividend of $9.32 per share.

Even with a sluggish housing market, Home Depot is holding up well. In the fiscal second quarter of 2026, comparable-store sales, which measure performance at stores open at least a year, increased 1.7% year over year, with sales through digital platforms up 11%.

Home Depot also shows steady profitability even during a weak housing market. CFO Richard McPhail pointed to the company's "consistent ability to deliver results and maintain stable gross margin," even through "unprecedented volatility in our cost environment."

The stock yields about 2.8%, and the dividend totaled about 61% of free cash flow. Home Depot has paid 158 consecutive quarterly dividends. With its scale and growing reach with professional contractors, Home Depot is positioned to deliver long-term shareholder returns.

Together, these three stocks would turn $5,000 into about $176 a year in dividend income. Each company has the brands, scale, and cost discipline to keep raising its payout over time, which makes this a portfolio I'd be comfortable holding for the long term.

#3150. What Does a ‘Blue Wave’ Mean for Mortgage Rates?

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.

#3149. Choosing a Tech ETF: Low Fees vs. Targeted Exposure

FTEC's lower 0.08% expense ratio and broader 294-holding portfolio delivered stronger 12-month performance, while IYW offers a more concentrated bet on semiconductors, software, and hardware.

The choice between Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC +1.38%) and iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW +1.31%) often comes down to cost and diversification within the domestic technology sector.

Both funds offer broad exposure to U.S.-listed technology companies, serving as core building blocks for growth-oriented portfolios. While they target the same market segment, their underlying indexes lead to different holding counts and cost structures that may influence long-term efficiency for buy-and-hold investors.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The Fidelity fund is more affordable, with an expense ratio of 0.08% versus 0.37% for the iShares fund. Additionally, the Fidelity fund offers a higher payout, providing a 0.30 percentage point advantage in distribution yield.

Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF allocates 99% of its portfolio to technology and holds 294 securities. Its largest positions include Apple Inc (AAPL -0.52%) at 17.73%, Nvidia Corp (NVDA +2.77%) at 16.95%, and Microsoft Corp (MSFT -0.99%) at 12.22%. It was launched in 2013. Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF has paid $1.11 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$271.6 share price, works out to a 0.4% yield.

iShares U.S. Technology ETF holds a leaner group of 148 positions, with heavy tilts toward semiconductors (38%), software (30%), and hardware (22%). Top holdings include Apple at 17.41%, Nvidia at 16.68%, and Microsoft at 13.56%. It was launched in 2000. iShares U.S. Technology ETF has paid $0.25 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$236.5 share price, works out to a 0.1% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

When comparing the Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC) and the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. FTEC is focused on mid-cap and small-cap tech stocks. It holds about 300 stocks across the software and hardware subsectors. IYW, meanwhile, holds about 150 stocks, giving it a narrower portfolio.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Here, the funds are very similar. Over the last five years, FTEC has generated a total return of 103%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.2%. IYW, on the other hand, has delivered a total return of 102%, with a 15.1% CAGR. Neither fund delivers significant income. However, IYW has a modestly higher dividend yield of 0.4%, while FTEC's is only 0.1%.

One final factor to weigh is cost. Here, FTEC has an edge. Its annual expense ratio is 0.08%, while IYW's is 0.37%. For context, if a person buys $10,000 worth of each fund, they should expect to pay only $8 in annual fees for their FTEC shares but $37 in annual fees for their IYW shares.In summary, FTEC and IYW are both tech ETFs, but due differing strategies and fees, they will appeal to different types of investors. Overall FTEC may appeal to the larger group of investors, given its lower fees. IYW, however, may still appeal to investors seeking a tighter basket of tech stocks.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3147. Eli Lilly Just Raised Its 2026 Revenue Forecast by $5.5 Billion. Is the Stock Still a Buy?

The stock is expensive, but the potential market for GLP-1 drugs is likely much larger than forecast.

After a 57% run-up over the past 52 weeks, Eli Lilly (LLY -0.79%) shares are expensive. The stock is now trading at 47 times trailing earnings. That's more than double the price-to-earnings ratio of the pharmaceutical industry. There are some sound reasons for that, which, put together, make the stock a buy, in my opinion.

First, sales are growing rapidly. Revenue was $24.4 billion in the third quarter, 39% higher than the same period a year ago. Profits are soaring, too. Earnings per share increased 16% in the quarter, to $7.22. Even better, management raised its guidance for full-year revenue from $85 billion to $87 billion to $91 billion to $92 billion.

It's no wonder, as Lilly's GLP-1 drug tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, dethroned Merck's cancer drug Keytruda last year to become the world's best-selling drug.

In the third quarter, Zepbound sales climbed 49% to about $5.4 billion, while Mounjaro sales jumped 65% to more than $10.7 billion. Foundayo, an oral weight-loss drug, contributed sales of $184 million in the quarter.

I believe those numbers are just the beginning. Morgan Stanley forecasts that the market for obesity drugs will reach $190 billion by 2035, more than double its 2025 level. Right now, that growth is being driven by new oral treatments, expected to be adopted by consumers at a faster pace than injection-based delivery systems, and by expanded coverage from Medicare, the largest payer for healthcare services in the U.S.

Even those predictions may fall well short of the actual market for GLP-1 drugs. That's because medical researchers continue to find new uses for the drugs beyond obesity and weight loss. GLP-1s are beginning to look like miracle drugs that will cause a tectonic shift in the healthcare industry.

First, there are international markets, largely untapped so far (outside of Europe). Morgan Stanley estimates there are more than 1 billion people with obesity living outside the U.S. To date, adoption in foreign markets has been constrained by several factors, including affordability, needle aversion, and safety concerns -- all of which can be overcome. The investment bank's research mentions Brazil and China, in particular.

There are also new use cases for GLP-1 drugs. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) says that the medicines also improve outcomes in people with cardiovascular, kidney, liver, arthritis, and sleep apnea disorders. Those improvements are mediated in part through anti-inflammatory and metabolic pathways.

I predict that there will be more uses in the future for GLP-1 drugs, some of them astounding. For instance, the drugs have shown promise in treating and preventing substance use disorders. One study conducted by Washington University found the drugs are tied to a reduced risk of such disorders across all major addictive substances, and to a reduction of severe harm, like overdose or death, in people who already have those disorders.

According to Stanford researchers, GLP-1 drugs control appetite -- and potentially addictions -- by influencing the release of dopamine in the part of the brain linked to motivation, pleasure, and reward. That sounds extremely promising to me.

There are potentially other, even more miraculous, uses for GLP-1 drugs. A recent study conducted on mice and funded by the NIH has shown that the GLP-1 drug semaglutide, which is made by Novo Nordisk, extended lifespan in older, healthy mice by tempering the detrimental effects of aging.

Of course, researchers have long known that calorie restriction -- one of the primary benefits of the drugs -- can have anti-aging effects. But the new study, conducted at the University of California, found that the drugs' effects on mice could be more than just a consequence of lower-calorie diets.

In fact, the new study in mice offers evidence that these drugs may slow physiological aging itself. While the study on mice and aging was conducted with semaglutide and will need more research before it can be used in humans in this way, I think we can assume the anti-aging effects could be replicated with Lilly's tirzepatide.

So, the uses, benefits, and market for GLP-1 drugs have massive potential, possibly much greater than current forecasts predict. Lilly is currently the leader of that market. That makes it a buy in my book, despite the price tag.

Matthew Benjamin has positions in Novo Nordisk. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Eli Lilly, Merck, and Novo Nordisk. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3146. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3145. Where Will Rigetti Computing Stock Be in 3 Years?

Will Rigetti Computing hit its quantum milestones by 2029? Here is how to judge the stock's risk before it does.

As of Nov. 6, Rigetti Computing (RGTI +19.29%) stock is down 48.1% in 2026. That's not a typo, and it's not the first quantum stock I've watched do this.

The shares fell 18.7% over the past month, mostly because the whole group got dragged down when quantum computing rival IonQ (IONQ +23.42%) announced a $2.0 billion equity offering in mid-October. Investors sold the whole pile, including Rigetti. The stock traded at more than 300 times trailing sales at the time, and there's not much room for error on those lofty heights.

The sell-off hit the whole group, even companies with little direct exposure to the offering.

Rigetti's most significant recent development is a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100.0 million over three years, aimed at superconducting quantum research under the CHIPS Act. The deal is not definitive yet.

The government would receive an equity stake, which means new shares. Existing shareholders would face share dilution if and when the deal closes.

Rigetti's headline numbers are fine. Q2 revenue hit $5.1 million, up from $1.8 million, mostly from on-premises Novera sales. The company's flagship 108-qubit chip runs at about 99.1% median two-qubit fidelity, which sounds great until you remember the three-year goal is 99.9% -- nearly a whole order of magnitude tighter.

Management says the holdup is coherence time, meaning how long a qubit can keep its quantum state before information is lost. That figure is 25 to 30 microseconds in Rigetti's systems. Management hopes to double or triple it over several years, but lab results don't always carry over to production chips.

"Coherence time is the limiting factor for 2-qubit gate fidelity at this time, and that's why we are so focused on improving coherence time," CEO Subodh Kulkarni said on the Q2 earnings call.

Rigetti has committed to a three-year roadmap, and that window is the most useful yardstick for investors. If it reaches the stated fidelity and scale targets around 2029, the stock's current valuation could look more reasonable in hindsight. But if it misses one or more of the official goals, a stock priced this high has a long way to fall.

Investors who want exposure to quantum computing should size their Rigetti position for the non-zero risk of a poor outcome. Share count rose 3.1% year over year to 333.7 million, and the Commerce deal would add more. I would only buy Rigetti as part of a broader multi-ticker quantum computing sleeve, not as a stand-alone bet. And I'd say the same thing about IonQ, D-Wave Quantum (QBTS +18.01%), or Quantinuum (QNT +25.99%), too.

#3144. MercadoLibre's Profits Fall Again. What It Means for Investors

The Latin American e-commerce operator fell again on earnings. Is a recovery near?

MercadoLibre (MELI -1.32%) delivered another round of strong top-line growth, but falling profits again sank the stock.

Shares fell 12% on Thursday as investors have grown impatient with the company's investment cycle, as it spends on lower free shipping thresholds, expanded logistics, and growing its credit business. However, that again led to narrower margins.

Revenue in the quarter jumped 45% to $10.75 billion, edging out estimates of $10.71 billion. Both core businesses delivered strong growth, with gross merchandise volume up 38% to $23 billion, and total payment volume jumped 53% to $109 billion.

Operating income in the quarter fell from $636 million to $601 million, and the company reported a net income margin of just 4.2%. On a per-share basis, earnings rose from $8.32 to $8.83 as the company benefited from lower tax expense. Still, that was below analyst estimates at $9.27.

MercadoLibre doesn't give guidance, so estimates are a bit of a guessing game, which works against the stock at times like these when it's investing in the business.

The top-line metrics are clearly moving in the right direction, and management said it gained share in its three largest markets, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina, which should quell concerns about competition from Amazon and Sea Limited's Shopee.

Importantly, the company continued to see engagement strengthening, and it sees a significant opportunity to grow purchase frequency, noting that its buyers make an average of 12 purchases a year, compared to more than 50 for e-commerce shoppers in developed countries. Faster shipping, lowering the free shipping threshold, and expanding its selection are part of its strategy to build a sticky habit and strengthen its competitive advantage, much like Amazon has done in the U.S.

The company is also seeing more customers adopt multiple products, which drive both revenue and margin improvement over the long run. As the business has scaled up, its cost per shipment in Brazil has fallen, down 5% in constant currency over the last year and 14% since the first quarter of 2025, a sign that it's effectively scaling its logistics operations.

Its credit card portfolio has been another source of headwinds on the bottom line, as the company needs to book a provision for expected losses when it issues new cards, even before it's earned any profits. The credit portfolio grew 62% to $18 billion in the quarter, and default and interest metrics remained stable.

Management noted tailwinds picking up with e-commerce penetration in Latin America increasing at its fastest pace since the pandemic, further justifying its investments in grabbing market share.

Finally, the company argued that the structural long-term profit drivers like lower cost per shipment, operating leverage in product development, and profitable growth in its credit business will deliver overall profit growth over time.

With Thursday's decline, MercadoLibre is now trading down 42% from its peak in 2025, and the stock is at its lowest point in more than two years. That certainly makes it look oversold.

The concerns about lower profit margins are reasonable, but any business putting up 45% revenue growth, especially in scalable industries like e-commerce and fintech, should eventually see profit growth. Investors would like some more details about when margin expansion will return, and that uncertainty is reflected in the weak stock performance.

However, MercadoLibre looks about as cheap as it's been right now, and the stock has significant long-term growth potential across several industries. Taking advantage of the sell-off looks like a smart move, even if a recovery could take at least a few quarters.

Jeremy Bowman has positions in Amazon and MercadoLibre. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon, MercadoLibre, and Sea Limited. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.
