#3143. IRS Announces 2027 Income Tax Brackets, Updated Standard Deduction

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3141. Warren Buffett Warned Investors About This Number 27 Years Ago. It's Never Been Higher. Should AI Investors Worry?

In 1999, Buffett said corporate profits couldn't stay much above 6% of the economy for long. They're now more than double that, and the AI spending boom is a big reason why.

In 1999, near the peak of the dot-com boom, Warren Buffett explained in a Fortune magazine article, drawn from speeches he gave that year, why stock investors were expecting too much. One of his reasons: "In my opinion, you have to be wildly optimistic to believe that corporate profits as a percent of GDP can, for any sustained period, hold much above 6%."At the time, after-tax corporate profits were running right around 6% of GDP. In the second quarter of 2026, they stood at about 13%, according to Commerce Department data. That's not just a more than doubling since 1999; it's also orporate profits are at their highest share of GDP on record, going back to 1947, topping the previous peak of 12.7% in 2021, and it's above every full year since the government's annual records begin in 1929.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

To be fair, investors who sold on Buffett's warning would have missed a lot. Profits have topped 6% of GDP in 95 of the 106 quarters since 2000, and stocks have soared.But his reasoning is worth a second look now. "If corporate investors, in aggregate, are going to eat an ever-growing portion of the American economic pie, some other group will have to settle for a smaller portion," he wrote. In other words, when profits take a record share of the economy, someone else, usually workers, is getting less. Some economists now think that is about to reverse.

Tech drove about two-thirds of this year's earnings growth, research firm TS Lombard estimated in a Nov. 5 report, with energy companies adding much of the rest.Much of that tech profit traces back to a handful of spenders. Here's what four of them paid for property and equipment, mostly data centers and the chips inside them, in the quarter that ended Sept. 30, according to their quarterly filings:

That's about $202 billion in one quarter, more than double the $97 billion a year earlier. Another important thing to note: One company's spending is often another's revenue. Data centers accounted for $89.0 billion of Nvidia's (NVDA +2.77%) $96.2 billion in sales in its quarter ended July 26, or about 92%. CoreWeave (CRWV +6.28%), which rents out AI computing power, had $103.7 billion in contracted future revenue as of June 30, but also $35.6 billion in debt and a $626 million quarterly loss.TS Lombard economist Dario Perkins estimates that more than 80% of AI-related revenue still comes from spending within the AI industry itself, rather than from outside customers paying for AI services. If that spending slows, he warned, those "paper earnings" will disappear.

Buffett's "smaller portion" argument is the part that could matter in 2027. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, the Labor Department reported Friday. TS Lombard expects that hiring to push wages up, raising companies' labor costs, while the firm's Freya Beamish expects the Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates.Investors got a preview of how fragile sentiment is. On Thursday, the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ +1.40%), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, fell 6.5%, its worst day since March 2020. It bounced 1.4% on Friday, and the U.S. stock market is still up about $5 trillion in value this year, according to Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok. But CoreWeave's bonds now yield more than 16%, CNBC reported, a sign lenders are nervous.

In the same 1999 article, Buffett pointed out that cars and airplanes changed the world, yet most of the companies that built them were terrible investments. His lesson: "The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry is going to affect society, or how much it will grow, but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage."For AI stocks, that means separating the companies that control their own fate from those that depend on someone else's budget. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta can choose to spend less, which would leave more cash for profits and buybacks. Nvidia has a powerful advantage, but much of its sales depend on those budgets. CoreWeave depends on them, as well as on borrowed money.

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB -0.25%), now run by CEO Greg Abel, gave its own answer on Saturday. In its third-quarter report, it said it bought back about $9.6 billion of its own stock during the quarter, the most in any quarter in its history based on its past filings, bringing the year's total to about $14.4 billion. A year earlier, it hadn't bought back any shares in the first nine months of 2025.Berkshire repurchases shares only when its CEO believes the price is below the company's intrinsic value, "conservatively determined," its filing says. In other words, while Wall Street argues about AI, Berkshire's best idea this quarter was a collection of railroads, utilities, insurers and manufacturers.This isn't a reason to dump tech stocks. But record profit margins rarely last forever. If you want to buy the dip, Buffett's advice would seem to favor durable businesses with cash to spare, and you should add gradually and watch Nvidia's next quarterly report, expected Nov. 17.

#3140. Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses

Vasanth Mudavatu, Senior Principal Software Engineer at a Fortune 50 company, dedicated to the security of generative AI and ML systems.

Enterprise AI security is no longer just about preventing inaccurate answers. It’s about preventing an automated system from using legitimate access to expose confidential information or execute unauthorized actions.

EchoLeak, which was disclosed in June 2025, was a Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that allowed a crafted email to trigger data exfiltration without requiring the victim to click a malicious link. Microsoft assigned it a CVSS severity score of 9.3, while NIST separately rated it 7.5.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability, and no evidence of exploitation in the wild was reported. This was a demonstrated vulnerability rather than a confirmed breach, but it exposed a consequential failure: External content could influence a system operating with access to internal information.

If an AI agent put customer data, revenue or reputation at risk today, could your organization explain what happened and stop it before the damage spread? The answer depends less on reassuring model behavior than on enforceable boundaries.

The framework below connects four activities: assessing six security blind spots, prioritizing findings, implementing controls in phases and verifying that those controls work.

Attackers can automate reconnaissance, credential harvesting and data extraction. Enterprises need to examine both how AI can be attacked and how it can accelerate attacks.

Being aware of the following six blind spots turn that concern into an actionable security assessment:

A downloaded model shouldn’t become a trusted production asset simply because it comes from a familiar repository. Modified weights, backdoor triggers and unsafe model-file deserialization are areas requiring scrutiny.

Recommended controls include verifying artifact signatures and hashes, documenting provenance, scanning inbound files and testing model behavior before deployment. Integrity verification establishes whether an artifact matches an approved baseline; behavioral testing examines whether it performs as expected. Neither replaces the other.

Disabling an agent isn’t necessarily the same as removing its access. Credentials, active tokens and downstream permissions may remain usable.

Agents need distinct identities, least-privilege access and short-lived credentials, and revocation workflows should be tested. Assessment should also consider combined permissions across tools, as individually acceptable capabilities may collectively create an unacceptable access path.

A useful operational test is straightforward: Disable an agent and verify that its downstream actions actually stop.

Inspecting the final response covers only one potential exit point. Sensitive information may also appear in tool-call arguments, logs, traces or data written to vector stores.

Monitor these boundaries, restrict outbound destinations and correlate activity across requests. That correlation matters because information can leave in small fragments rather than one easily detected transfer.

The assessment should follow the complete data journey, not just the conversation visible to the user.

The security boundary includes more than the model. Build workflows, libraries, containers and deployment dependencies also require review.

Scan inbound model artifacts, pin third-party GitHub Actions to specific commit hashes and maintain an AI-specific inventory of model and software dependencies. These measures help teams identify what they deployed and investigate compromised components.

The objective is traceability, knowing which artifacts and dependencies support each production capability.

A compromised agent may use legitimate tools and credentials to interact with connected systems. Shared memory and agent-to-agent communication introduce additional paths through which malicious instructions can propagate.

Organizations should authenticate communication, verify message integrity, inspect memory and implement per-agent quarantine. Additionally, review Model Context Protocol tool metadata for adversarial instructions or unapproved changes.

Trust should be established at each boundary rather than inherited automatically from another agent.

An agent inventory must capture more than a name. Security teams need ownership, approved capabilities, authorization context and a defined retirement process.

Automate discovery, log audits at the action level and decommission workflows that revoke credentials, address retained memory and preserve required audit records. These controls connect governance decisions to what agents do.

A gap analysis becomes useful when it drives priorities. Evaluate risks using likelihood, impact, difficulty of detection and an exposure multiplier for multi-agent environments.

Treat the resulting score as a prioritization aid, not an objective prediction. Organizations should document their assumptions and calibrate escalation thresholds to their own systems and business consequences.

• The missing control and supporting evidence.

• The test that will demonstrate closure.

Don’t consider a control complete merely because a policy or configuration exists. Closure should require evidence that it works.

The roadmap begins with agent discovery, model integrity checks, outbound monitoring, pipeline hardening and kill-switch implementation. Subsequent phases introduce managed identities, behavioral testing, inter-agent authentication, memory inspection and automated response workflows.

This sequencing provides a practical starting point—establish visibility and containment first and then deepen prevention and detection.

The strongest contribution of this framework is its operational focus. It asks teams to connect model provenance, agent permissions, runtime activity and incident response rather than assess each in isolation.

Leadership reporting should emphasize measurable coverage and tested effectiveness. Useful measures include the proportion of agents under governance, model integrity verification coverage, supply chain scanning coverage and decommissioning compliance.

These measures should be considered alongside the evidence used to close individual findings, connecting implementation progress to demonstrated control effectiveness.

For enterprise leaders, the goal isn’t to eliminate every uncertainty before deploying AI. It’s to make that uncertainty manageable with accountable ownership, observable actions and tested intervention paths. Governance sets expectations; operational evidence shows whether the organization can enforce them.​

#3139. Under Armour: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Monthly global product launches are replacing scattered regional marketing, a shift that tests whether full-price sell-through can rebuild while direct-to-consumer sales stay under pressure.

On its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, Under Armour (UAA -5.21%) announced that revenue declined 7% to $1.2 billion while reiterating its full-year operating outlook. Management is reducing operating complexity and cutting low-volume inventory to protect profitability. Three things management said stand out.

Management is trimming its product assortment to eliminate low-performing inventory. Reducing stock-keeping units (SKUs, or individual product codes) allows the business to lower costs and sell more goods without discounting.

Under Armour is moving its youth clothing line to a licensing partner, Centric Brands, to trim inventory exposure. This asset-light approach helps preserve cash while internal teams focus on core performance apparel.

Management is centralizing marketing under one global voice and launching one primary product story each month. Aligning regional teams behind unified releases aims to boost marketing efficiency and drive full-price sell-through.

Direct-to-consumer sales remain under pressure, but expense discipline is insulating operating margins. Under Armour relies on core strengths in football cleats and established apparel lines to support pricing discipline.

Long-term value depends on converting product innovation into full-price retail demand across global markets.

Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3136. Think It's Too Late to Buy Cloudflare Stock? Here's the 1 Reason Why There's Still Time

Cloudflare has nearly quadrupled in three years, but management says it has captured only about 1% of the market it's targeting.

Cloudflare (NET +9.91%) stock has gained roughly 280% over the past three years through Nov. 5, 2026. But it could still reward patient investors for one reason: The business remains small compared with the market management is targeting.

Cloudflare helps businesses keep their websites, applications, and networks fast and secure. At its June 9 investor day, management estimated a $238 billion addressable market for 2026, based on Gartner research. That's the potential annual spending in the markets its products serve, not a revenue forecast. Management projects that opportunity will reach $384 billion by 2029.

Against that backdrop, Cloudflare expects its full-year 2026 revenue to be nearly $3 billion -- representing only about 1% of the addressable market. It doesn't need to dominate every market it serves to become a much larger business. Winning even a modest share of that spending could support years of growth.

Cloudflare is growing rapidly. Third-quarter revenue grew 39% year over year to $783 million -- its fastest growth in nearly four years. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue to be up about 38% year over year, indicating strong momentum heading into 2027.

The stock is priced for growth, trading at 34 times trailing sales as of Nov. 5. Companies operating in an expanding market and growing revenue rapidly are usually worth holding at a premium. With just a tiny fraction of its opportunity captured, it's not too late to buy the stock. It looks more like a company in the early stages of growth than one nearing maturity.

#3135. 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow

Startups often move quickly because they have to, making the most of limited resources and adapting as circumstances change. As tech companies scale, added layers of process, approval and hierarchy can gradually slow decision making and erode the flexibility that helped them grow.

The good news is that companies don’t have to abandon the habits that fueled their early success as they expand. Here, Forbes Technology Council members share startup habits established tech companies should preserve—or relearn—to maintain their agility as they grow.

Established tech companies should preserve the startup habit of staying close to the raw customer experience. As organizations scale, dashboards and layers of interpretation can obscure what people actually struggle with. Leaders should keep speaking directly with customers and empower small teams to act quickly on what they learn. Scale should improve execution, not distance companies from users. - Leah Wang, Karpo

The tech market in the AI era is changing super fast—the cycles for product demands, work methods and tools, and customers’ needs and requirements have all become very short. The one thing companies must preserve is agility within the boundaries of their focus. It is easy to get lost and try to achieve everything, only to end up with nothing. Being able to stay agile while knowing the problem your company solves is critical. - Yoav Amitai, Elsight

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Startups are great at prototyping new products and services and moving on quickly from ideas during the research and development phase. As companies scale, this “create fast, test fast, decide fast” capacity is often diminished. One way to keep it alive is to engage early with a customer or partner to confirm requirements or do testing. It puts healthy pressure on the development process while gathering valuable external feedback on pricing, functionality and positioning. - Eva Rudin, Thales Cybersecurity

Preserve the willingness to challenge assumptions. Startups move quickly because they don’t treat “this is how it’s done” as an acceptable answer. As companies scale, process can quietly replace curiosity. The best teams keep questioning their own products, decisions and assumptions, especially when something appears to be working. Scale should give you more resources to challenge the status quo, not more reasons to protect it. - Alissa Knight, Assail, Inc.

Keep saying no to the wrong business. When you are small, you cannot serve everyone, so you get good at turning down the wrong customers and use cases, and that focus is half of why you survive. At scale, every deal looks worth taking, and the muscle for walking away weakens. You must protect it on purpose. The companies that keep rejecting what does not fit stay sharp long after they could afford to lose focus. - Vytautas Savickas, Oxylabs

Solve problems close to where they occur. As organizations scale, issues often get escalated to the most senior person rather than the person best connected to the customer or the detail of the issue. That introduces delays to fixes being made and promotes permission-seeking rather than judgment and accountability. Push authority down and let the people closest to the problem make the call. - Rob Sloan, Zscaler

Knowing when to stop is crucial. Startups have to focus because their resources are limited. The ability in a startup to know exactly what is going on means not only decisions to invest but also decisions to divest are made faster. - Véronique Özkaya, DATAmundi

AI-first thinking is the biggest thing established players need to adopt from the startup realm. New ventures have the luxury of AI being the starting point, not something they need to bolt onto old, outdated processes. That blank slate is a real edge—no legacy systems standing between them and AI-driven gains. So, I’d begin every problem by asking where AI can make the biggest impact and build from there. That mindset will define the future enterprise. - Tarek Nseir, Valliance

Preserve the habit of testing before debating. Startups rarely have enough data to eliminate uncertainty, so they build something small, put it in front of users, and learn. At scale, debate can become a substitute for discovery. Established companies should relearn how to turn unanswered questions into fast, low-risk experiments, using evidence from the market to resolve what meetings cannot. - Melissa King, Paylocity

Let the people closest to a problem try things without asking permission first. In many cases, our team members have made our most impactful suggestions. We discussed it, tried it out and looked at the results together. Nobody wrote a proposal. Give teams a sandbox, clear data and security rules, and a few weeks to test. You’ll learn more than you would from a six-month planning cycle. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society

Keep communication lines efficient. The best startups have an uncanny ability to throw unnecessary hierarchy to the wind and flatten communication lines. That’s how startups home in on solutions rather than simply admiring the problem. - James Stanger, CompTIA

Cross-department talk is essential. In a startup, everyone can talk to everyone without wondering about politics and the org chart. You never know where the next good idea will come from—it often comes from an “unexpected part” of the org chart. If Joe from team X is afraid of talking to Mary from team Y just because they don’t have the same boss, the company’s capacity to innovate is severely impacted. - Stephane Donze, AODocs

Startups move fast because they accept higher risk, while large organizations slow down to protect reputation, revenue and investors. As companies grow, they must consciously balance risk appetite to keep innovating. Teams should also keep the startup habit of “relentless iteration”—sharing early “sh***y first drafts,” as referenced by Brené Brown—for fast feedback instead of waiting for polish. - Mandy Andress, Elastic

Ship things that aren’t ready and learn from real users instead of extensive internal reviews. Process exists to prevent mistakes, but it also prevents speed and discovery. Talk directly to users without a layer of research, summaries or account managers in between. - Amy Gu, Dynamsoft

Create rituals early and maintain them throughout your growth. Startup life is hard. One of the things that inspires and preserves team alignment is the rituals created in early startup life that create an identity, a battle cry and a touchstone to the mission. As new employees join the company, these same rituals become part of their orientation, which helps encourage unity. - Amy Brown, Authenticx

Preserve fast, reversible decision making. Let teams run small, bounded tests without routing every choice through layers of approval, then use the results to adjust quickly. Reserve heavyweight reviews for decisions that are costly or difficult to undo—not every experiment. - Nagesh Nama, xLM Continuous Intelligence

Share the full picture with everyone. In a startup, the whole team knows the revenue, the biggest customer problem, and what worries the founders most. As companies grow, that context gets held back at the top, and teams start working on tasks without knowing why they matter. People make better decisions when they know what the company is facing. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

Preserve the startup habit of a hard work-in-progress limit. Early teams cannot pursue 20 “top priorities,” so starting one thing means stopping another. At scale, portfolios expand faster than capacity, and coordination becomes the bottleneck. Force every new priority to displace an old one. Speed comes as much from limiting concurrency as from moving faster. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Do it by hand before automating it. Startups run a new process manually for a few weeks and learn where it actually breaks. Larger companies jump straight to automation and lock in their guesses. In mature organizations we audit, roughly a third of flows either duplicate another or barely run. A month of manual work first is cheaper than a year of maintaining the wrong automation. - Sergii Grushai, Peeklogic

#3134. Why Sunrun Stock Surged 33.4% This Week

Investors warmed up to this solar stock after the company reported strong financial results.

A third-quarter earnings report featuring $1.1 billion in revenue sent Sunrun (RUN +1.11%) soaring 33.4% this week.

Sunrun stock changed hands at $9.98 as of the close on Friday, Nov. 6, up 33.4% from Friday, Oct. 30's close, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) fell 2.7%, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 4.9%.

On Wednesday, Sunrun reported third-quarter revenue of $1.1 billion, a 51.7% year-over-year jump that topped Wall Street estimates. Diluted earnings per share reached $0.56, beating the consensus expectation of $0.32 per share. That top-line surge came even as installed solar capacity dropped 15% year over year, because Sunrun completed a strategic shift toward direct-channel volume while scaling higher-margin battery storage attachments.

Management trimmed its full-year cash generation outlook to roughly $200 million, the bottom of its previous $200 million to $375 million target range. Even with that reduced guidance, direct sales volume grew 9% year over year as battery attachment rates hit a record 75%. This week's quarterly beat proves Sunrun can expand system margins through battery storage, but trimming guidance to the bottom of its range keeps cash generation on a tight leash.

Even after this week's rally, Sunrun remains down 55% from its 52-week high of $21.95, reflecting long-term investor anxiety over rising interest rates and complex project financing.

Sunrun trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 5, though that low multiple is heavily influenced by non-cash accounting adjustments and derivative gains. The company carried $15.3 billion in total debt, including lease obligations, as of Sept. 30, 2026, against $699.4 million in cash and short-term investments as of Sept. 30, 2026. Investors will watch the next quarterly earnings report scheduled for Feb. 25, 2027, to see if direct installation growth can offset higher funding costs.

Although Sunrun reported a strong quarter, investors must be cautious about warming up to Sunrun stock. While it shone brightly last quarter, reporting profits that exceeded analysts' expectations, the company is hardly in sound financial health.

Sunrun relies heavily on leverage to keep the lights on. As of the end of September 2026, for example, Sunrun had a net debt-to-earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) ratio of approximately 11.6. Taking this into account, along with the fact that the company has an interest coverage ratio of about 0.44, according to Morningstar, it's clear that Sunrun is best suited for those comfortable with a more speculative investment. For those who have lower risk tolerances, there are plenty of other solar energy stocks to consider.

#3131. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3130. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit by Age 62 to 80

Claiming at 62 versus 70 creates a gap that reshapes your entire retirement income picture.

Social Security provides a vital floor for your retirement, but it's meant to supplement your income rather than replace it entirely. The amount you receive depends heavily on when you choose to claim, making it one of the most consequential financial decisions you'll face.

The Social Security Administration (SSA) calculates your benefit based on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years, adjusted for inflation and run through a specific formula. Your final check size is then determined by your full retirement age (FRA) and the age you begin collecting.

Here is the average monthly retired-worker benefit by age, as of December 2025, the most recent data available.

The data reveals a clear increase between ages 62 and 70, with the average benefit growing by 59.7%. This represents a monthly gap of $850.28, or $10,203.36 per year.

Full retirement age (FRA) ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. If you claim at 62, you face a permanent reduction of up to 30%, while waiting until 70 earns you an 8% annual increase through delayed retirement credits.

A second pattern appears after age 70, as averages begin to decline slightly. This doesn't mean the SSA cuts benefits for individuals. Instead, older groups likely include more people who claimed early at permanent reductions.

Women also make up a larger share of the oldest groups because they tend to live longer. Because they often have lower lifetime earnings due to the gender pay gap and time spent caregiving, their presence in the data lowers the overall average among the oldest retirees.

Even at the age-70 peak of $2,274.68 per month, or $27,296.16 per year, benefits rarely cover every bill. That peak falls $34,135.84 short of the $61,432 average senior household spending reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027, adding about $82 a month on top of that age-70 benefit. While these adjustments are designed to keep pace with inflation, they often fall short.

The most useful number for your planning is the average that matches your own intended claiming age.

Even those who claim Social Security benefits at age 70, when they qualify for their maximum checks, rarely live comfortably on their benefits alone. You'll probably need other sources of retirement income to cover what Social Security doesn't.

Personal savings are your best bet if they're available to you. You're free to spend that money on anything you like, but remember it may have to last you 20 years or more, so choose a withdrawal strategy designed to make it last. If you don't have a lot of personal savings, you may need a job or other government benefits to supplement your Social Security checks.

Make sure you come up with a plan for how you'll cover your remaining living expenses before you apply for Social Security. If you're married, be sure to factor in your spouse's Social Security checks and personal savings as well, and make sure you're both on the same page about when each person plans to claim.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

#3122. Did Apple Just Get a Boost From Democrats? Data Center Moratoriums Could Benefit the iPhone Maker

Competition for this key component in Apple devices could come down.

Apple (AAPL -0.52%) issued a warning to investors when it shared its fourth-quarter earnings results at the start of November. Its huge profit margin on device sales could head in the wrong direction for the foreseeable future. The culprit: memory chips.

Memory chip pricing has soared over the past few quarters, driven by growth in AI data center spending. AI accelerator chips get packaged alongside high-bandwidth memory chips, which are effectively stacks of standard DRAM memory chips -- the same types of chips found in Apple's iPhone and MacBook, among other devices. Demand for those chips, while supply remains limited, has led to massive price increases, and Apple is finally starting to feel the pain.

The recent election, however, could provide some relief for Apple, given the growing potential for Democrats to impose AI data center moratoriums across the country.

Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate in this year's midterm election, paving the way for more federal regulation and policies that could curb the growth of AI. The more immediate impact, however, could come at the state level. Four of the biggest states for AI data center developments -- Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona -- will have Democratic governors once they're sworn in in January.

Many of those governors have announced plans to increase oversight and regulation of new data center construction (Texas did so even before Tuesday's election), aiming to mitigate any negative impacts on citizens. Venture Capitalist Brad Gerstner suggested that 25% to 35% of next year's data center build-out could be at risk of delays as a result of new governments across the country.

That could provide some relief for Apple. If data centers aren't going under construction, that means there's no place to put new server racks, and less demand for high-bandwidth memory chips. Reduced demand should put downward pressure on prices, limiting the impact of memory chip pricing on Apple's gross margin.

Apple management danced around whether it had already locked in pricing for some memory supply. All three major memory chipmakers, Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung, have shifted to signing long-term agreements to establish pricing ranges and provide more confidence in building new capacity. While that caps their near-term upside, it protects them from a major price collapse as they work to increase the total supply of memory chips.

Management did reveal that it increased purchase commitments by $33 billion last quarter, but not all of that is necessarily related to memory chips. Still, reports indicate that Apple did sign long-term agreements for at least some memory chip supply to ensure it would have enough chips to meet its expected device demand.

In the grand scheme of things, the memory crunch could play only a minor role in Apple's long-term earnings growth. Supply and demand will eventually reach equilibrium again, and Apple should see its component prices and gross margin return to normal levels.

Earlier this year, I wrote that Apple is best positioned among consumer electronics device makers in the face of rising memory prices. It had the option to hold prices steady to grab market share or raise prices to exercise its pricing power. It chose the latter, and amid a supply shortage for its components, that's a smart move. In the long run, the higher prices will stick, but the higher bill of materials won't.

That points to rising gross margin over the long run, even if the short term could see some pressure on its bottom line. The potential relief from a moratorium on data center building is just another bump in that upward trajectory. (In this case, to the positive side).

Investors should remain focused on Apple's fundamentals. Its ability to raise prices, introduce new products on both the high end (iPhone Duo) and low end (MacBook Neo), grow its services business, and effectively keep customers in its ecosystem are the factors driving earnings growth. That should result in sustained free cash flow, most of which it will return to shareholders through buybacks and dividends.

Recent developments sent shares to new all-time highs last week following their post-earnings pullback. There's a reason investors are paying a premium for the stock right now. The future remains bright for the iPhone maker.

Adam Levy has positions in Apple. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Apple and Micron Technology. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates dropped today, but inflation data could shake things up next week.

With the midterm elections behind us, mortgage rates are continuing their gradual slide this month. One factor is a sell-off in tech stocks, which can send investors toward the relative safety of bonds and help push mortgage rates lower.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Meanwhile, a stronger-than-expected jobs report could slow that slide by reinforcing expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

And a reminder: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.46% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3115. Here's What $10,000 Invested in Bloom Energy (BE) Stock Could Be Worth in 3 Years

This stock has soared in recent years -- but it's volatile.

If you'd invested in Bloom Energy (BE +3.42%), a company supplying fuel cells used in AI data centers, three years ago, you'd have done well. More than well, actually. A $10,000 investment would be worth more than $165,000! On an annual basis, that averages to a 155% gain.

The S&P 500 performed well above average over the past three years, but it only averaged annual gains of 21%, turning $10,000 into $17,857.

You might now wonder, what would $10,000 invested in Bloom Energy be worth three years from now? Well, with any stock, I would caution that no one can know exactly how it will perform over any particular period. That seems much more so for Bloom Energy, because its performance has been extremely volatile:

Data source: Morningstar.com, as of Nov. 6, 2026.

See? A bunch of down years and several years with whopping gains.

The stock's valuation can offer some insight. For example, the recent price-to-sales ratio of 17.2 is well above the five-year average of 3.35, suggesting that the shares are quite overvalued. The recent price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 130, meanwhile, is down from 1,086 in 2025, but is still quite high. This overvaluation would lead me to rein in my growth expectations.

Since no one can know how much Bloom Energy will grow, here are some scenarios:

#3106. Palantir Stock Just Fell 8 Days in a Row. History Says What Followed Its Only 2 Longer Losing Streaks.

Did the AI software company's two longer slides say anything about what happened next?

Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) stock closed lower for eight straight trading sessions through Thursday, Nov. 5. Over that span, shares dropped from $198.84 to $154.99, a fall of around 22%.

That put the AI software maker's stock about 26% under its record close on Oct. 9.

By my count of daily closes since Palantir started trading in September 2020, only two losing streaks have lasted longer. One was a 10-day slide ending May 10, 2021. The other was a nine-day slide ending March 1, 2023.

Each time, shares were up six months later. But a year out, the two cases ended up far apart. And two cases is a tiny sample, so I wouldn't rely on the streak to say much about what happens next.

Interestingly, both earlier slides were close in size to this one. The 2021 streak took the stock from $24.11 to $18.47, a fall of around 23%. The 2023 streak took shares from $10.11 to $7.69, a decline of around 24%.

(I measured what followed from each streak's final close, treating 21 trading days as a month.)

After the 2021 slide, Palantir stock gained around 31% in the next month and was up about 24% three months out. Six months later, it was about 41% above that final close. But a year after the slide ended, shares were down about 60% to $7.46.

The 2023 case went the other way over the full year. Shares were up only around 6% a month later. In the next three months, though, they rose by about 91%, and they were up 112% after six months.

Even more, one year out, the stock had more than tripled, gaining around 224% to $24.93.

The two seven-day streaks, which ended in September 2022 and June 2026, don't settle much either. After the 2022 slide, shares climbed about 16% in a month, dipped about 1% over three months, and were up about 12% after six months. A year out, the stock had more than doubled.

The June 2026 slide is too recent for a six-month read. But once it ended at $107.27, shares gained around 23% in the next month and about 80% in three.

So, after all four of Palantir's longest losing streaks before this one, the stock was up a month later. But with 12-month returns ranging from a 60% loss to a 224% gain, the streak arguably told investors little about the year ahead.

One difference between 2021 and 2023 sticks out to me, and it's the starting price. At $18.47, Palantir's stock traded at around 30 times its 2020 sales. At $7.69 in 2023, it cost under 9 times its 2022 sales. And Palantir lost money in both those years, though it had posted its first quarterly profit right before the 2023 slide started.

Today, Palantir's market value is more than 50 times its sales for the last four quarters, a higher sales multiple than in either case.

Sure, the business is very different now. Palantir's third-quarter revenue climbed 96% year over year to around $2.3 billion. This kept a streak of faster growth going, after rates of 70%, 85%, and 93% in the three quarters before that. And Palantir now turns a big part of its sales into profit, with a 47% operating margin last quarter.

Not every number is speeding up, though. The total contract value of the deals Palantir closed in the third quarter rose just 6% from a year before. The growth rate had already slowed sharply in the previous three quarters, dropping from 138% to 61% and then 49%. Deal timing can make the number lumpy. But if it keeps slowing, revenue growth might eventually follow.

Management's fourth-quarter revenue guidance of about $2.65 billion already implies growth of about 88%, down from the third quarter's 96%.

Palantir made $1.43 a share in its past four quarters. So at roughly $160 as I write, the stock trades at about 112 times earnings. Earlier this week, I put my buy price at 120 times those earnings, or about $172 a share.

In the end, the length of this streak doesn't tell me much about where Palantir stock heads next. What matters more to me is that shares now trade below my buy price.

Yes, a growth stock that just dropped 22% over eight sessions could easily keep swinging. But I think shares are worth a look at this level, and I'd build a position slowly instead of all at once.

#3102. Wall Street Is Ignoring Bristol Myers Squibb's Cash Machine -- and That's an Opportunity for Income Investors

Bristol Myers Squibb has a 4% yield and a 55% payout ratio, which should greatly interest dividend lovers.

Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY -1.57%) traces its history back to the mid-1800s. It is a proven survivor in the highly competitive and innovation-driven pharmaceutical sector. That can't save the company from the normal dynamics of the drug industry, as it works through a period of elevated patent expirations. Investor concerns about patent expirations, however, have turned the company into a dividend machine, yielding 4%. The average pharma stock yields just 1.4%.

Here's why Bristol Myers Squibb could be a buying opportunity for long-term income investors. And it all boils down to the success of the company's "growth portfolio," which is increasingly powering its cash flow.

The pharmaceutical sector follows a normal cycle that every company goes through. To simplify it, a company invests heavily in research and development to identify and secure approval for new drugs; the drugs have strong sales during a period of patent exclusivity; and then sales fall off when the patent expires and generic competition enters the market.

Investors inevitably get worried when patent expirations come up, because it means revenues are going to come under pressure. Right now, Bristol Myers Squibb has some big patent expirations on the horizon, and the stock's price has been relatively weak. However, dividend investors need to put this situation into perspective. The healthcare giant still has a well-covered dividend, highlighted by a 55% trailing 12-month payout ratio in the third quarter.

And revenues from what the company calls its "legacy portfolio" aren't exactly falling off a cliff just yet. In the third quarter, sales from this collection of drugs rose 1%. These drugs represent just over 40% of revenues. The other 60% is the cash flow machine you want to watch.

In the third quarter, the drugs Bristol Myers Squibb puts in its "growth portfolio" generated 12% revenue growth. The list of drugs here includes Opdivo Qvantig, Breyanzi, Reblozyl, Camzyos, and Opdualag. Don't worry too much about the names; just note that it is a fairly long list. This isn't a one-trick pony business. Bristol Myers Squibb is a respected, diversified industry giant with a long and successful history in drug development. And it is already seeing material success on that front.

To be fair, investors aren't exactly ignoring this fact. As the chart below highlights, the stock is up from its lows, and the dividend yield isn't as attractive as it was when it was roughly 6%. Still, the yield is well above the market average and that of the average pharma stock, so there's a very good reason for dividend investors to jump on this cash-flow machine.

The 40% of revenues that fall into the "legacy portfolio" is a problem. And investors need to monitor what's going on with that portfolio. However, it is entirely normal for drugs to become less profitable as generic competition enters the market. So Bristol Myers Squibb is just working through a transition period that it has worked through many times before. If history is any guide, it will survive this period in relative stride.

All of that said, the real issue for Bristol Myers Squibb is the drug Eliquis, which had sales of nearly $4.7 billion in the third quarter. It accounts for most of the company's $5.4 billion of "legacy portfolio" revenues. It will be a big hit when this drug loses patent protection, and there's a lot riding on finding a replacement.

But the "growth portfolio", which generates revenues of $7.6 billion, includes a dozen drugs, and revenue growth across the group has been strong. If you recognize the cash flow machine that's building in this portfolio, you might find Bristol Myers Squibb and its above-average yield an attractive addition to your passive income portfolio.

#3100. Higher Yield vs. Lower Cost: The Critical Differences Between HDV and VIG

VIG emphasizes dividend growers with lower costs, while HDV targets concentrated high-yielding stocks. One delivered 34.6% returns over the past year; the other offers greater stability.

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG -0.38%) focuses on companies with a history of increasing their payouts, while iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV -0.69%) targets a concentrated group of high-yielding domestic equities.

Dividend-focused investors often choose between maximizing current income or betting on long-term capital growth through dividend appreciation. VIG tracks companies that have consistently increased dividends, while HDV selects stocks offering notably high yields today. This comparison examines how their different strategies affect cost, risk, and portfolio composition.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The Vanguard fund is the more affordable choice, with a 0.04% expense ratio, which is exactly half the iShares fund's cost. However, investors seeking higher current income may find the iShares fund more appealing, as it offers a trailing yield that is double its peer's distribution.

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF holds 333 positions and emphasizes growth-oriented sectors. Its largest holdings include Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%) at 4.90%, Apple (AAPL -0.52%) at 4.89%, and Broadcom (AVGO +0.74%) at 4.30%. The portfolio leans heavily toward Technology at 27%, Financial Services at 21%, and Healthcare at 19%. The fund was launched in 2006. Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF has paid $3.65 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$248.24 share price, works out to a 1.5% yield.

iShares Core High Dividend ETF maintains a tighter portfolio of 74 holdings, focusing on stability and current income. Its largest positions include Exxonmobil (XOM +0.34%) at 9.61%, Chevron (CVX -0.15%) at 7.26%, and Abbvie (ABBV +1.06%) at 6.80%. This concentrated mix is heavy on Consumer Staples (27%) and Energy (25%), with Healthcare contributing 13%. The fund was launched in 2011. iShares Core High Dividend ETF has paid $0.96 per share over the trailing 12 months, which, on its recent ~$30.99 share price, works out to a 3.1% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

When comparing the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG) and the iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV), investors should consider several key factors. Let's see what they tell us about each fund.

First, we should examine each fund's strategy. VIG targets U.S. stocks with at least 10 years of growing annual dividend payments. HDV, on the other hand, targets top U.S. dividend-paying stocks based on yield. VIG also holds many more stocks, with around 330 names, while HDV holds about 75.

Two other important factors are historical performance and income potential. Since 2021, VIG has generated a total return of 60%, equating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.8%. HDV, meanwhile, has delivered an 83% total return, with a 12.9% CAGR. As for direct income potential, HDV delivers more. Its dividend yield of 3.1% is more than twice that of VIG's 1.5.%.

One final factor to weigh is cost. Here, both funds are quite affordable. VIG has the lower annual expense ratio, though, at 0.04%, while HDV's 0.08% is slightly higher.In summary, VIG and HDV both hold dividend stocks, yet they differ in many key respects. HDV delivers higher absolute income and has also generated superior total returns in recent years. As such, many income-oriented investors will favor HDV. That said, VIG could still appeal to extremely cost-conscious investors, given its lower expense ratio.

#3091. This Warren Buffett Dividend Stock Is the One I'd Buy With $1,000 in November

Warren Buffett's longtime investment offers a straightforward way to benefit from consumer spending.

A $1,000 investment doesn't need to prove its worth immediately. Indeed, the goal for investors should be to buy a piece of a business that can grow its earnings -- and distributions -- for years, and to hold onto that stake long term. American Express (AXP -1.23%) is one such company. Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA -0.01%) (BRKB -0.25%) longtime association with American Express might put it on some investors' watch lists, but its economics might be what earns it a place in your portfolio.

First, we need to understand American Express' business model. In a nutshell, the company provides a suite of payment-based services. It issues credit cards and charge cards (which are not the same thing), collects fees and interest from the consumers who use them, collects transaction fees from merchants that process payments on its cards, and offers lending services to borrowers. Overall, its business is solid. Revenue grew 9% year over year in its most recent quarter. Billed business increased by 8%.

American Express attracts an affluent customer base that is generally better able to weather economic downturns. Net card fees (the annual fees paid by cardholders regardless of spending volume) provide the company with a subscription-like recurring revenue stream that can help cushion the company from the impact of temporary consumer-spending slowdowns.

That said, like all lenders, its success depends in part on its ability to keep credit losses down. That means that the risk of a severe economic downturn that could lead to a spike in defaults is always one worth considering.

One reason that Berkshire Hathaway has kept American Express such a large part of its stock portfolio for so long is that the company continues to drive shareholder value. In part, it looks like this:

As you can see, its earnings per share have increased roughly threefold since 2016. Granted, there were a few dips along the way, but for the most part, earnings grew steadily. Similarly, the company's annual dividend payments have also nearly tripled.

However, even with its dividend growing nearly threefold in just 10 years, the dividend yield remains a modest 1.1% at the current share price. That means two things. First, management is prudent. They are ensuring that the company can withstand any credit losses that it may have to write off during an economic downturn. Second, by maintaining a moderate rate of dividend increases, management has left itself ample room to raise the dividend further and drive additional shareholder value if economic conditions improve.

The overall case for owning American Express stock is pretty straightforward: It's an iconic brand with a loyal, affluent customer base. Moreover, steady earnings and dividend growth make it a strong building block for a long-term portfolio. Finally, a $1,000 initial investment is a nice middle ground between making a stock a core investment and a symbolic one.

Now we must turn to valuation. Currently, American Express shares trade at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 18.4. That's just below its 10-year average P/E of 19.5. What's more, it's well below the S&P 500 average multiple of around 25.9. All in all, the stock is affordable, but it's not the cheapest equity you'll find on Wall Street.

As for risks, they are what you might expect for a financial stock. A recession is the main one. Economic downturns often result in slower consumer spending and a rise in unpaid bills -- both of which would dent American Express' bottom line.

In conclusion, American Express is my pick for a Buffett dividend stock to recommend investors buy this month. Its consistent revenue and earnings growth, coupled with rising dividend payments and an affordable valuation, mean it ticks all the core boxes for a Berkshire stock: It's an ideal investment to buy when you're ready to let compound growth and steady dividend reinvestment work over long-term horizons rather than chasing quick gains.

(NUTX -6.75%) reported a decline in total revenue for the first nine months of 2026 compared to the prior year, attributing the change to adjustments in historical collection data and revenue recognition patterns from 2025. Vivian Sanders: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Nutex Health, Inc.'s Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. My name is Vivian Sanders, and I'm happy to serve as your moderator today. We're truly grateful for your participation and your continued interest in our company as we share the highlights of another exceptional quarter.
